adventures-of-huckleberry-finn-chapters-: Huck's crisis of conscience — shall he free Jim or turn him in? — reaches its peak here, in the famous passage where he chooses to go to hell for his friend. Tom Sawyer's arrival then turns rescue into boyish farce. The moral heart of the novel.
arxiv-2512-00035:
Mislav Has, Tao Xiong, Fehmi Ben Abdesslem, and Mario Kušek test WebAssembly on resource-constrained Internet of Things devices. IoT hardware and software vary widely, which hurts portability and maintenance. WebAssembly, built for the web, is a portable, secure, and efficient runtime that could unify deployment.

Their study measures its performance, efficiency, and portability on limited devices. Evidence like this tells builders whether one binary can truly serve many tiny platforms. Portable runtimes would ease updates and security patching across device fleets. Portability across heterogeneous hardware is the problem statement, with WebAssembly tested as the unifying runtime answer.
arxiv-2512-00335:
Large language models consume enormous energy on graphics processors, which limits where they can run. Takuto Ando and Yu Eto study accelerating them on a coarse-grained reconfigurable array in 2025. Such arrays offer a trade-off between energy efficiency and programmability.

The authors work on efficient kernel mapping, placing the model's core computations onto the array's structure. They also carry out a comprehensive evaluation of the whole system, not just its peak speed. Hardware like this could bring capable language models to settings where power and cooling are tight. Coarse-grained arrays sit between fixed circuits and general processors in flexibility. Mapping is where such hardware usually succeeds or fails in practice.
arxiv-2512-00635:
Cryptographic chips can be mathematically secure and still leak secrets through power use and electromagnetic radiation. Archisman Ghosh surveys circuit-level countermeasures and proactive detection techniques for side-channel attacks in 2025, in an extended abstract. Internet-connected embedded devices make the exposure widespread.

Side-channel analysis exploits timing, cache behavior, photonic emission, and other physical traces. Buildable, low-overhead countermeasures can be added to designs without exotic fab steps. Proactive detection aims to catch leakage during design rather than after deployment, protecting devices from keys extracted by simply watching them work. Extended abstracts announce work in progress, inviting scrutiny before the full study lands. Low overhead matters because consumer devices cannot spare much power for defenses. For folks who ship small smart gear, the gain is a shield they can add at the fab stage. It is not a patch they must beg users to put on later.
arxiv-2512-00735:
A large team led by S Ivanov and A Kireev reports on light trapped by defects in a 2025 physics paper. They study topological dislocations, flaws that run through a material that is otherwise a neat periodic lattice. Far from the flaw, the lattice keeps its regular pattern.

Such dislocations show up in many systems, from crystals and sound-based lattices to light-based ones and matter waves. The team observes light trapping at these defects, in both the linear and nonlinear regimes. Trapped light stays near the defect instead of spreading away. Learning to control that effect could guide new designs for photonic devices.
arxiv-2512-00935:
Hunseok Kang, Doowon Koh, and Dung The Tran extend a classic partition theorem in a 2025 math paper. Raimi's theorem concerns splitting a space into parts with a surprising covering property. The authors move the result from its classical setting to the continuous world of the circle. Their new setting is the n-dimensional torus, a doughnut-like space in any dimension.

Building on recent work in finite groups, they prove that measurable partitions of the torus exist with a strong property. For any finite measurable cover, some shifted piece of the cover meets every part of the partition in positive measure. Such results link combinatorics, measure, and symmetry.
arxiv-2512-01735:
Marius Tacke and co-authors let language models design physics-constrained networks for mechanics. Agentic frames now spawn task-specific agents on demand. The team extends that idea to software modules. A module for a science task can be generated when needed, not hand-built.

Their case is constitutive modeling in solid mechanics. The generated networks must obey physics laws by construction. If the demo holds, labs could order bespoke solvers in plain words. Each solver would still respect the physics its task demands. Generated modules ship with their constraint code visible, so engineers can audit the physics before a design rests on its output.
arxiv-2512-01835:
Milo Bechtloff Weising studies a vast algebraic object: the infinite Hecke algebra of type A, built over a field where distance is measured in a non-archimedean way. His 2025 paper focuses on the case where the algebra's parameter is a pseudo-uniformizer, a special element of that field.

Weising looks at a family of representations called almost-symmetric, which must obey extra conditions from both topology and algebra. He then gives a complete classification of the irreducible ones, the basic building blocks that cannot be broken down further. For representation theorists, the work pins down exactly which building blocks this infinite algebra allows.
arxiv-2512-02135:
White dwarfs often show heavy elements in their atmospheres, pollution that should sink quickly, so something must keep delivering rocky debris. Isabella Trierweiler, Konstantin Gerbig, and Malena Rice test in 2025 whether slow orbital oscillations driven by a distant companion can do the delivering.

These von Zeipel-Lidov-Kozai oscillations need a three-body system tipped at a large mutual inclination to switch on. The authors add dissipative precession, a gradual swivel of the orbits, and check how often the mechanism triggers pollution. The result constrains a leading explanation for how dead stars come to eat their own planetary systems.
arxiv-2512-02435:
Zhongjian Qiao and seven co-authors work on teaching agents from logged data when the world changes. An agent trained for one setting may be deployed in another that moves in different ways. Logs from the new setting may be scarce, while logs from the old one are plentiful.

Mixing both datasets naively can hurt, since the old data follows different dynamics. The team's method filters the data, keeping samples that align in both dynamics and value. Cleaner training data should help agents adapt to a new setting without fresh trial and error in the real world. The filter keeps what helps and drops what would pull the agent off its course.
arxiv-2512-02735:
Anna Rodum Bjøru and four co-authors frame a causal way to explain black box AI models with concepts. Concept based explanations describe a model's choice in human ideas, like stripes or wings, rather than pixels. Good explanations must be understandable and faithful to what the model truly does.

Their framework intervenes on concepts and computes the probability that the concept suffices for the outcome. Both local explanations, for one case, and global ones, for the model overall, come from the same causal logic. Faithful concept explanations could build trust in AI used for lending, hiring, and care. A cause based score can be shown to a judge or a board in words they can grasp and probe.
arxiv-2512-02835:
Yifan Li and six co-authors make video segmentation explain its reasoning instead of hiding it. Referring video segmentation finds an object described in words, often involving motion, cause, or change over time. Past systems compress that reasoning into opaque embeddings, leaving the chain of thought untraceable.

ReVSeg uses reinforcement learning to reward a visible reasoning chain for each segmentation. Step by step reasoning can be checked, corrected, and trusted more easily. Transparent segmentation helps editors, annotators, and safety reviewers who must know why a system tracked one object and not another. Steps shown in the open can be taught, marked, and fixed, which is more than a lone black box score can give a class.
arxiv-2512-02935:
L. de Souza and four co-authors study clustering in active matter where particles slow down in crowds. Self propelled particles can pile up through simple excluded volume effects. Quorum sensing adds a second route: propulsion drops where local density runs high.

Using kinetic balance theory and simulations, the team finds the two routes interact in a reentrant way. Clustering dips through a clear minimum as sensing strength or persistence time varies. Non monotonic clustering warns designers of synthetic swarms that more sensing does not always mean more grouping. A dip, not a climb, is the shock here. More of a good thing can mean less of the clumps that labs have long taken as its mark.
arxiv-2512-03035:
Ibrahim Laiche and three co-authors learn control ready models of mechanical systems without ever measuring acceleration. Lagrangian systems describe machines from robots to vehicles through energy based equations. Non conservative forces, like friction, complicate both modeling and control design.

Their hybrid method derives and identifies physically consistent models, which model based control synthesis requires. Skipping acceleration measurements removes a noisy, costly sensing step. Consistent models learned from gentler data could widen model based control to machines where accelerometers are impractical or unreliable. Gentle data needs are a door for small labs. They lack the racks of big names but hold much of the skill that real world rigs need to work at all.
arxiv-2512-03135:
Bosons may host protected states at their edges, like fermions do. Alan Gardin, Emilio Cobanera, and Giuseppe Carlo Tettamanzi study that idea in this 2025 work. For fermions, a famous ten-fold scheme sorts insulators and superconductors by symmetry.

The authors seek a bosonic scheme as close as possible to the fermionic one. They focus on synthetic photo-magnonic crystals, systems that mix light and magnetic waves. They report symmetry-protected zero modes at the boundary that involve many bodies. Such modes could matter for future quantum devices. Bosonic edge modes could store quantum states in ways that resist local noise.
arxiv-2512-03335:
Designers build work step by step, refining as they go. Faizan Farooq Khan and co-authors model that process in this 2025 work. Most AI design tools treat synthesis as a single-step task, which understates how complex creative work is.

The authors present a layered design generation method that proceeds step by step. Each layer adds detail while keeping earlier choices in view. Stepwise tools fit how designers actually work. They could make AI help in layout, graphics, and product design feel more natural and controllable. Layered steps also let users intervene mid-design, not just judge the final output.
arxiv-2601-06635:
Juan Segura gives crushing and grinding a bold new frame in a 2026 paper. The old frame is a set of rate rules for how grain counts change. Those rules track the mean size of grains well through a grind.

But the old rules say nothing on how much counts swing round the mean. They say nothing on links between sizes, or on rules that hold at each scale. His new frame is built from the old rate rules' own inputs. Those inputs are the rate at which grains break and how the bits are shared out. The frame also fits a known chance-based way of writing such fields. The work gives mills and mines new tools for the spread of sizes. Swings in size can now be planned for, not just means.
arxiv-2601-07135: Xin-Rong Dai and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with decompositions for cyclic groups with 3 prime factors. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. We characterize the direct sum decompositions of the cyclic group ℤ ( p ​ q ​ r ) 2. Where p p , q q , and r r are distinct primes. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07235: Research by Agnivo Gosai and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with sentiment analysis on movie reviews. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. ZeinEldin, Ali Wagdy Mohamed, Seyed Jalaleddin Mousavirad, Independent Researcher, NY, USA; These authors contributed equally. The work presents a comprehensive survey of sentiment analysis methods for movie reviews. A benchmark task that has played a central role in advancing natural language processing. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07435:
A 2026 arXiv preprint was posted in 2026. It covers CP violating signal at DUNE in presence of nonstandard interactions and the role. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. Neutrino oscillation among the three active neutrino flavors is well established and supported by experiments at diverse length scales and energy scales.

It may be noted that five of the neutrino oscillation parameters in the three-flavor paradigm. Namely the three mixing angles and the two mass-squared differences are measured to a reasonable degree. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07935:
Yuxin Yang, Aoxiong Zeng, and Xiangquan Yang adapt large language models to specialist fields without erasing their general skill. Adapting to fields like medicine faces two challenges, they argue. The first is the stability-plasticity dilemma: learn clinical knowledge without catastrophic forgetting of general knowledge. The second is task interference, where sub-tasks compete for limited low-rank parameter space. Their 2026 preprint proposes a multi-task MoE-LoRA framework.

LoRA adapts models with small low-rank updates. A mixture-of-experts version routes different tasks to different updates, reducing interference. Sub-tasks like diagnosis, report summarization, and drug interaction prediction can then coexist. The goal is a specialized generalist, deep in one domain yet broadly capable. The paper serves teams adapting models for medicine and other professions. It names the failure modes before proposing its fix.
arxiv-2601-08035:
David Elsweiler argues that search systems should teach, not just retrieve. Information access systems like search engines and generative AI shape how people seek and judge information. Most are designed to optimize retrieval. They rarely help users develop better search strategies or critical awareness. His 2026 preprint rethinks search systems as instructive interfaces. It appears at a conference on human information interaction and retrieval.

A teaching search tool would leave users more skilled after each session. That goal changes interface design: hints, feedback, and reflection prompts become features. It also changes success metrics beyond speed and clicks. Elsweiler writes from information science, where user behavior is the core subject. The paper serves designers of search and AI assistants. It asks what users gain, not only what they find.
arxiv-2601-08535: Haricharan Balasundaram and Andrew Thangaraj wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how to gauge a spread from samples when extra facts are at hand. The base task is a classic one: learn a discrete distribution from samples drawn on their own. The new twist is side information on the spread. In large data sets, like text, such facts arise in a natural way. The sense and nearness of words can be read from how close their vector forms sit. That nearness gives the extra facts the method uses.
arxiv-2601-08635: R. Dengler wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on which stress tensor holds for light and fields inside a material. A dielectric is a material that does not conduct but can be polarized by a field. Dengler works out small-scale models in full detail. The results back one claim: a single, unique microscopic stress tensor exists in such a medium. The standard large-scale tensor of continuum electrodynamics holds a derivative of the dielectric coefficient. Dengler shows it is just the small-scale tensor, averaged over space.
arxiv-2601-08735: A. Deppman studies a key change in how quarks act when matter gets very hot and dense. In one old model, the shift from bound quarks to free quarks is sharp. In grid based work on real data, the shift looks smooth, not sharp. Deppman brings in a new lens called the thermofractal view to read this gap.
arxiv-2601-08835:
Vaarunay Kaushal and Taranveer Singh test if group talk helps chat models give a better joint answer. In group talk, more than one model shares views and they settle on one reply. Fans say the talk lifts quality. The pair ask if the same gain comes from a more plain trick: make many replies and just pick the best one.

Their test set is called DeliberationBench. It runs three forms of group talk next to that plain pick best base line. Each form is held to the same cost and pool size. A reader who builds model teams gets a fair check. It shows when group talk earns its cost, and when a plain pick does as well.
arxiv-2601-09035:
Aniesh Chawla and Udbhav Prasad test chat models on bad code by way of decompiled code. Decompiling turns a built program back into code a human can read. New chat models read code well. Bad code grows in craft each year. The pair ask if a model can sort a decompiled file as safe or bad with trust.

They run top models on such files and grade their calls. Good calls need more than key word spots. Bad code can hide its aim in plain code shapes. A reader in cyber work gets a first test of a new hunt path. It may let staff triage vast file sets fast, with care on edge calls.
arxiv-2601-09135:
Min Soe and five co-authors sim how light pulses bounce off a flat face that splits two stuffs. A pulse that hits at a slant makes short lived fields near the face. Those fields fade fast, but they shape what bounces back. The team uses a qubit grid method to run the sim. The method is near pure in its math, so wave power is kept well.

Good power care lets them trust the faint fade fields they see. Such fields test how a face acts in the first flash of a hit. A reader in light work gets a sim path that holds its sums true. It may aid work on fast light tools and thin films.
arxiv-2601-09735:
Gaetano Coccimiglio, Trevor Brown, and Srivatsan Ravi extend software transactional memory with dynamic multiversioning. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents Multiverse. Transactional memory lets programmers build concurrent data structures with atomic blocks, easing parallel coding.

Recent systems perform well on some workloads but share a limit. They struggle with long-running reads that touch many addresses which keep changing. Multiversioning keeps older versions alive so such reads can finish. The authors aim to bring that support without losing speed. Concurrent data structures underpin servers and databases alike, so the stakes here are broad.
arxiv-2601-10835:
Hieu Bui, Nathaniel E. Chodosh, and Arash Tavakoli ask whether vision-language models can read construction workers' behavior. Robots are joining construction workflows step by step. To work beside people safely, a robot must interpret what workers are doing. Vision-language models promise such reading without long domain-specific training.

The study is exploratory: it probes what these models get right and wrong on site imagery. Construction scenes are cluttered, dusty, and full of partial views. A model that shines on clean benchmarks may falter there. The results help robotics teams judge how far general models can be trusted around workers, and where custom training is still a must.
arxiv-2601-11035:
Long Ma and co-authors present a one-stop system for detecting AI-generated video. Generative models now make synthetic videos that look strikingly real. People struggle to tell them from genuine footage. Reliable detection is the counterweight. The authors say two key limitations have held the field back, and they set out to remove both in one system.

A single, complete detector could serve platforms that face many kinds of fakes. Fragmented detectors, each tuned to one generator, age fast as generators change. The paper frames detection as a product problem as much as a research one. Its audience is trust and safety teams who need one tool that keeps pace with synthetic media.
arxiv-2601-11135:
Van Thuy Hoang and O-Joun Lee predict molecular properties with context-aware graph causality in few-shot settings. Graph learning serves web-based drug discovery and protein tools. The hard case is few-shot: only a few labeled molecules exist for a new property. Standard models starve on so little data. The authors bring causal inference into the graph model.

Causal links, unlike raw correlations, may transfer to new properties with little data. Context awareness lets the model weigh which relations hold in which setting. The goal is predictions a chemist can trust from a handful of examples. The work serves drug hunters who often face exactly that scarcity for fresh targets.
arxiv-2601-11435:
Menglian Wang, Zhuanghua Liu, and Luo Luo speed learning across split machines. Their 2026 preprint tackles decentralized stochastic nonconvex optimization. The machines form a network with row-stochastic links. Each holds part of the data and part of the work.

Gradient noise in real tasks is often heavy-tailed. Wild outliers can wreck plain averaging across machines. The team gives a normalized stochastic gradient method for the case. It adds Pull-Diag gradient tracking to keep nodes in sync. The method reaches near-stationary points with optimal sample use. Communication cost stays near-optimal as well in their bounds. The work serves federated learning on messy real data.
arxiv-2601-11535:
Alexander Htet Kyaw, Haotian Ma, Sasa Zivkovic, and Jenny Sabin guide assembly with AR. Their 2026 preprint joins object recognition with hand tracking. Augmented reality can now overlay help on physical tasks. Assembly work is a natural fit for such guidance.

The team's workflow adapts instructions as the build goes on. It first identifies custom components in front of the user. Step-by-step instructions then appear in the headset view. The system detects deviations from the planned assembly. It updates the instructions based on the user's hands. Hands-on interaction thus drives the guidance in real time. Adaptive help could cut errors in complex custom builds.
arxiv-2601-11835:
Yufan Zhang, Jaromir Savelka, Seth Copen Goldstein, and Michael Conway track how student coding changed once large language models spread. These tools can boost output. They can also hide how much a student has truly learned.

Their study looks at both work habits and scores in that shift. Teachers face a new task: to grade skill when code may come from a tool. The team frame what to watch and how to test fairly. The work is set for the LAK 2026 meeting on learning analytics.  The study gives teachers a base for fair tests in a new era.
arxiv-2601-12035:
Qitong Liu, Hao Peng, Zuchen Li, and their co-authors spot social events and track how they change, with no labels. Social media volume makes hand work costly. Graph nets and pre-trained language models are the main tools, but training them eats resources.

Their method joins retrieval-augmented generation with structural entropy. Retrieval brings in past text to ground calls, while entropy guides how event groups form. A label-free tool could scale to new feeds fast. The work is set for the Web Conference 2026.  The tool is built for large, fast feeds of posts.
arxiv-2601-12135:
Fabricio Souza Luiz, José Carlos Bellizotti Souza, Luísa Toledo Tude, and Marcos César de Oliveira build stochastic dynamics from entropy in action space. In their form, the random term is the total action that links two points in spacetime. It is not the set of paths taken.

They make the Shannon entropy as large as can be, with a fixed mean action. That yields a Boltzmann-like spread over actions and end points. The route links dynamics to information in a new place. It may give fresh tools for noisy motion in physics.
arxiv-2601-12235: Koichi Inoue gives a new construction of a graph tied to the Chevalley group G2(2). He builds it from a U3(2) geometry, a unitary form. A past paper built the group with a 2-transitive action of degree 28 and gave a concrete tool to study it. A second build route can reveal new form in the same object. The graph is classed with generalized hexagons and unitary geometry. Such finite geometry objects link groups, graphs, and codes. Inoue's note adds a clean path to this one.
arxiv-2601-12535:
Ahmed Attia and Alham Fikri work on machine translation for low resource languages. These are languages with little paired text to train on. More paired data is now being gathered from such communities. Yet many ideas for better low resource translation remain untested, and the pair set out to try one.

Their method fine tunes a translation model with reinforcement learning, with no human labels. The trick is round trip bootstrapping: translate out and back, and learn from how well the trip preserves meaning. They build on the No Language Left Behind family of models. Those models already cover many low resource languages. A self supervised route like this could lift quality where paired data stays scarce.
arxiv-2601-12835:
Kui Wang Choi and Minming Li study fair division when goods arrive over time. Agents receive indivisible goods over multiple rounds, not all at once. Fairness must then hold in cumulative terms across the whole schedule. A split that looks fair in one round may drift unfair over many.

They investigate temporal envy freeness up to one good, and a stronger form up to any good. They also study an approximate version of the stronger notion. Temporal maximin share, a guarantee each agent can claim, gets treatment too. Scheduling adds a time axis that classic fair division lacks. Results here guide repeated allocations in workplaces, courses, and shared facilities.
arxiv-2601-12935:
O. D. Lunn and four co authors report a direct measurement of the orderphobic effect. Fluctuation induced forces drive organization and self assembly near second order phase transitions. The critical Casimir effect is the best known example of such a force. The orderphobic effect is a related phenomenon in this family.

Direct measurement is the contribution named in the title. Forces of this kind act at tiny scales and are hard to isolate in a lab. A clean measurement tests decades of theory about fluctuation forces. It also informs design of self assembling materials and colloids. The work sits in statistical physics and soft matter science.
arxiv-2601-13335:
Giana Deskevich and a large team hunted for shadow bands from a balloon in the path of the April 2024 total solar eclipse. Shadow bands are faint wavy lines that race on the ground just by totality. Their cause is still in doubt. One camp blames churn in the low air. A next camp blames a wave clash high past the air.

The team flew tools on a balloon to test where the bands are born. The eclipse fell on April 8, 2024. A balloon read can split low air from high air causes in a way ground tools cannot. For eclipse science, the hunt adds rare data to a long open ask.
arxiv-2601-13735:
Hojin Kim and Jaehyung Kim question a common way to pick the best AI answer in 2026. In Best-of-N selection, a model makes many answers and one is chosen. Probabilistic confidence scores often make that choice. High confidence is taken as a sign of sound reasoning.

The pair test if those scores truly track the steps of valid reasoning. They ask if scores reflect fluency, smooth text, more than logic. Valid reasoning needs each step to cause the next in a sound chain. If scores miss that, Best-of-N can pick slick but wrong answers.
arxiv-2601-13835:
Sam O'Connor Russell, Delphine Charuau, and Naomi Harte study how speech cues signal a turn to talk in 2026. Fluid turn-taking is a key challenge for human-robot interaction. A robot must know when a person has finished speaking. Self-supervised speech models now drive much progress in this task.

It is unclear if such models use prosodic cues, lexical cues, or both. Prosody is the rhythm and pitch of speech, while lexical cues are the words. Their vocoder-based approach controls each cue type in a clean way. Knowing which cue rules helps build robots that chat in a natural flow.
arxiv-2601-13935:
Anoushkrit Goel and co-authors segment white matter tracts in the brain with a GPT-style model in 2026. White matter tract segmentation maps the brain's wiring for study and surgery. The task is complex, as tracts differ among themselves and across subjects. Yet tracts keep a similar 3D structure across hemispheres and people.

Their framework, TrackletGPT, treats tract pieces as tokens in a sequence. Tracklets reintroduce sequential information that plain voxel methods lose. A language-like model can then learn tract patterns as a kind of grammar. Better maps aid the study of neurological disorders and neurosurgical planning.
arxiv-2601-14035:
A. Timsina and W. Korsch present a new way to measure how charged particles stick to surfaces in cold liquids in 2026. Ions and electrons can bind to dielectric surfaces inside cryogenic liquids. Liquid nitrogen is the test liquid in this work. Knowing binding energies matters for detectors that use such liquids.

The experimental technique watches charged particles build up on nonconductive surfaces. It uses the electro-optic Kerr effect, where an electric field changes how a material bends light. That optical signal reveals the surface charge as it grows. Rare-event detectors need this kind of surface knowledge.
arxiv-2601-14135:
Madhurendra Mishra, Zhen Qi, and Adarsh Ganesan find fractal patterns in a classic neuron model in 2026. The Hodgkin-Huxley model describes how neurons fire electrical spikes. The team applies temporal interference stimulation in a previously unexplored sub-Hz resonant regime. They uncover a nonlinear response they term multi-tongue frequency fractals.

Single-frequency driving yields a smooth resonant valley in the model. Dual-frequency excitation fragments that response into a hierarchy of tongues. The tongues are sharply modulated, and their number grows with observation time. The pattern reveals a clear self-similar architecture in neuron response. The tongues grow in a self-similar way as time goes on. Such rich response maps may help tune brain stimulation with more care.
arxiv-2601-14235:
Members of the LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration wrote this 2026 survey. The large team lists Eric Aubourg, Camille Avestruz, and many more. It covers where machine learning can help their work. The team studies dark energy and dark matter with data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. Its Legacy Survey of Space and Time will soon send back huge sets of images, catalogs, and alerts.

Old tools for sorting such data strain under that load. The authors argue that new methods must be strong on the facts, able to grow with the data, and safe to run day after day. Readers get a map of the tasks where AI and machine learning could help the survey reach its dark energy goals.
arxiv-2601-14335:
Seán Caulfield Curley, Karl Mason, and Patrick Mannion forecast local health in this 2026 paper. Their target is self-rated health, how people judge their own health, in small areas. They predict it for a future population, not just the present one. Each person's socio-economic traits feed the forecast.

The team uses an open-source microsimulation that projects Ireland's population into the future. In the simulation, each person carries demographic and socio-economic traits. Ordinal regression then maps those traits to health ratings, which come in ordered grades. The aim is long-term health estimates for small areas, the scale at which local services plan.
arxiv-2601-14435:
C. Estelle Smith, Alemitu Bezabih, Shadi Nourriz, and Jesan Ahammed Ovi present a design framework in this 2026 paper, set for the CHI conference. Their topic is spiritual care, support for a person's spiritual needs during illness and hardship. Such care matters for well-being, yet it stays under-explored in human-computer interaction research. Technology use in clinical spiritual care also lags behind other healthcare fields.

Past work by the group defined spiritual support through co-design workshops. Stakeholders from online health communities took part. The new framework, SPIRIT, builds on that base. It aims to support technology interventions for spiritual care, within the clinic and beyond it.
arxiv-2601-14935:
Lynn Heller, Sebastian Heller, and Martin Traizet study surfaces whose mean curvature stays the same at every point. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with such surfaces in flat three-dimensional space. The surfaces repeat by shifts that form a lattice pattern.

The team sets down a general formula for the volume these surfaces enclose. The formula links the volume to the surface area. It also adds a term of Wess-Zumino-Witten type and a new curvature term. The result extends the classic Minkowski formula, which covered only closed surfaces of this same kind.
arxiv-2601-15035:
Juan Marshall-Maldonado and Boris Solomyak measure how fast a class of flows forgets its past. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with suspension flows built over Salem substitutions. A substitution is a rule that grows strings of symbols step by step.

Weak mixing means the flow slowly loses all memory of where it began. The authors prove a rate for that loss. For almost every flow with a step-like roof function, the rate is just worse than a power of a double logarithm. The key condition is that the growth rate is a Salem number.
arxiv-2601-15435:
Megan K. Oxland, Matías Bravo, Laura C. Parker, and Claudia Del P. Lagos ask what shuts down star birth in satellite galaxies. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with quenching, the end of star formation. Observations chart quenching by mass and environment, but they pin down timescales poorly.

They also struggle to name the dominant process at work. The authors use the SHARK v2.0 simulation of galaxy formation. They study the role of gas stripping, where a satellite's gas is torn away. In the simulation they can watch that process and its effect on quenching directly.
arxiv-2601-15535:
Estefanía Duque Pérez, Lukas Jansen, and Benedikt Haeckener map Morocco's hydrogen prospects in a 2026 arXiv paper. Global demand for green hydrogen is growing fast. It is seen as a key tool for sectors that are hard to clean up. Morocco holds rich solar and wind resources. The country aims to capture up to 4 percent of the global PtX market by 2030. That would make it a strategic partner in Europe's energy transition.

The study tests how that path holds up under change. It varies demand scenarios and weather patterns. It also factors in efforts to cut emissions. Hydrogen output depends on sun and wind, so weather swings matter. For planners, the paper links ambition to conditions. It asks what Morocco's renewable build-out must survive to pay off.
arxiv-2601-15635:
Theodore Y. Faust, Arash A. Amini, and Mason A. Porter study communities in changing networks in a 2026 arXiv paper. A community is a set of nodes linked densely inside and sparsely outside. In temporal networks, these groups shift over time. Statistical inference is a growing way to track that structure. It fits a model and reads communities from the fit.

The authors focus on biases tied to community size. Inference may treat large and small groups unevenly. Such bias can distort maps of how networks evolve. Social, biological, and transport networks all change with time. Analysts who track their communities need to know where the method leans. The paper's warning is methodological: check the size effects before trusting the story a fit tells.
arxiv-2601-15735:
Takuya Nomoto and three co-authors set out a system for building magnetic structures in a 2026 arXiv paper. To predict how spins line up in a material is a basic step in magnetism. Their frame draws on oriented spin space groups, or SSGs. First, structures are built as fully symmetric forms of an SSG. Then they are rotated to fit the largest magnetic space group of that SSG.

The two levels get names: spin-symmetry-adapted structures, and oriented forms of them. The title adds high-throughput first-principles math as a use. Speed matters because candidate materials are many. A system that builds structures on its own can feed screening pipelines that hunt for new magnets. The frame turns symmetry from a check into a building tool.
arxiv-2601-15935:
Richard Stiskalek and Harry Desmond pair two cosmic probes in a 2026 arXiv paper. The thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect traces the pressure of ionized gas. It lights up galaxy clusters and the cosmic web. Constrained simulations rebuild the local universe's mass and velocity fields. They are digital twins, tuned to match the real nearby cosmos. The authors explore how the two tools inform each other.

The tSZ signal benchmarks how faithful the simulations are. In return, the simulations locate cosmic web structures. They supply positions, total masses, and density profiles for tSZ studies. Each tool thus covers the other's blind spot. Local-universe studies gain from that loop. It sharpens both the maps of nearby structure and the physics read from them.
arxiv-2601-16335:
Gustavo Gonçalves and coauthors test if bars in young star systems can be seen in fake views. Their 2026 preprint deals with barred star systems through time. Euclid views show bars fall from near space to a past shift of one. The TNG50 sim says bars should stay more oft than that. A clash of this kind may stem from view bias, not true counts.

The team makes fake Euclid like views of TNG50 systems. They then test how oft bars can be seen in those views. Miss rates at high shift would ease the clash much. The case study shows how to fair test sims next to views. It guards teams from false clash claims.
arxiv-2601-16535:
György Dósa, Zsolt Lángi and Zsolt Tuza ask how big a square can be clad by unit squares. Their 2026 preprint sets a clean maths task. Take a count n of unit squares, each of edge one. They must clad a big square with no gaps left. The aim is the most large edge the clad square can have.

That most edge is named S of n in the work. Small n can be solved by hand with care. Big n needs firm bounds and build tricks. Clean tasks of this kind test pack and clad maths. The team seeks sharp values and bounds for S of n.
arxiv-2601-16835:
Ke Ding, Bo Li, and Ankang Sun study fair pay when one boss hires many hands. A boss sets pay terms to spur work from each hand. Past work sought the boss's best gain from those terms. That aim can leave pay gaps that are vast and harsh. Their 2026 preprint adds a fairness curb to the task.

Their terms curb how far pay can spread among hands. The curb suits state work and worker co-ops. In such spots, fair pay is a core rule, not a wish. The team shows how to keep spur while pay stays even. This can guide real pact design in fair-first shops.
arxiv-2601-17035:
Christoph Bartneck, Richard Watt, Etienne Borde, and Pattara Klinpibul test a match rule to fix peer review. Peer review is key to science, but it crawls. Journals strain to find apt judges for each paper. Their 2026 preprint runs fake crowds to test a fix. The fix borrows the deferred acceptance rule from match work.

That rule pairs folks in a stable way from ranked picks. Here it pairs papers with apt judges. Fake runs set the rule next to the old way. Gains in speed or fit would help all fields. Match rules have fixed school and job queues before.
arxiv-2601-17335:
Angshul Majumdar asks if general AI can be defined in a strict way at all. Claims about AGI speak of existence, robustness, and self-checks as if they were fixed traits. Majumdar treats AGI as a distributional predicate. That means the claim rests on a task family, a task spread, a score rule, and set resource budgets. Change any one, and the claim can change.

In that frame, broad claims turn fragile. Some may even be undecidable, beyond proof or disproof. The work does not deny strong AI progress. It asks for claims that name their terms. Clear terms would make AGI debate more honest. Funders and labs could test what is said, not what is implied.
arxiv-2601-17435:
María Jesús Rodríguez-Sánchez and three co-authors propose a declarative layer for AI agents. Agents now plan, use tools, and split tasks. Many systems still fail in plain ways. They invent actions, make plans that cannot run, and coordinate poorly. The proposal sits in server ecosystems built on the Model Context Protocol.

A declarative layer lets builders state what agents may do in clear terms. Clear terms are easier to check than free text plans. That should cut brittle behavior across tools. The work speaks to teams that link many agents to live services. It offers a path to agents that stay within set bounds. Reliability, not flair, is the goal.
arxiv-2601-17635:
Gravity waves meet the stratocumulus-topped boundary layer in this simulation study. That layer is a sheet of low cloud over the ocean. Its breakup affects how much sunlight Earth reflects. The team uses large-eddy simulation to model the clash. The grid is five meters in the vertical and thirty meters across. A radiative-convective equilibrium state keeps the layer steady at start.

Gravity waves are then introduced through a set forcing. The study asks how prone the layer is to break up. Cloud sheets are a big unknown in climate models. Their breakup could shift warming forecasts. No author is named in the record. Fine grids give this test rare detail.
arxiv-2601-17735:
Kyungho Kim and five co-authors present ReFuGe for prediction on relational databases. Such databases store linked tables for web apps at scale. Prediction tasks on them have drawn fresh interest. Retrieval alone does not solve those tasks. ReFuGe uses LLM agents to generate informative relational features. Good features lift predictive performance in a direct way.

Feature craft is slow hand work in most data teams. Agents that mine linked tables could cut that time. They can join facts across tables humans might miss. The work targets web data as it lives, in tables. Better features mean better forecasts for churn, fraud, and demand. The agent design is the novel step.
arxiv-2601-17835:
Baowen Zhang, Chenxing Jiang, Heng Li, Shaojie Shen, and Ping Tan work on pulling true shapes out of a popular 3D method. Their 2026 preprint deals with Gaussian splatting. The method builds scenes from many soft blobs and renders new views fast and well. Getting a clean surface shape back out of those blobs is still an open problem.

Weak shape terms and loose fits leave methods with poor agreement between views. Stray blobs, called floaters, also throw off the result. The authors ground their method in geometry to fight both flaws. Clean shapes matter for robots, mapping, and any task that needs the world as a surface, not just a picture.
arxiv-2601-17935:
Daniel Commey, Matilda Nkoom, Yousef Alsenani, Sena G. Hounsinou, and Garth V. Crosby tackle money laundering that hops between firms. Their 2026 preprint presents FedGraph-VASP, a shared learning system for virtual asset service providers. These firms face a clash. Rules push them to catch laundering across firms. Privacy law pushes them not to share client data. Working alone, each firm misses patterns that cross chains and borders.

The team's design lets firms learn together without pooling raw data. Graph learning tracks how funds move between accounts. Federated training keeps the data at home, and post-quantum security guards the links. The aim is joint detection that respects privacy law.
arxiv-2601-18335:
Zexia Fan and co-authors teach sound localization systems to keep learning without forgetting. Their 2026 preprint deals with sound source localization, which finds where a sound came from. The method shines in controlled settings but struggles in the real world. Two imbalance problems bite. Within a task, some directions are far more common than others. Across tasks, new data skew and overlap with old. Both drive catastrophic forgetting as the system learns over time.

The authors propose analytic incremental learning with imbalance rectification. Analytic methods can update in closed form, which suits steady learning. Fixing the skew at both levels should keep old directions sharp. Hearing aids, robots, and smart rooms all need such ears.
arxiv-2601-18435:
Biraja Ghoshal and colleagues take on a hard task in eye care: to guess how bad a sight fault will be from a gene fault alone. The fault sits in a gene that helps the eye sense light. When it fails, sight fades over time. Two people with near twin faults can still end up with quite unlike sight loss.

The team looks for a sharp edge in how the gene's key part does its work at the scale of single atoms. Their claim is that a jump in how protons move through the part marks that edge. Past the edge, the fault turns harsh. If the claim holds, doctors could sort new cases by risk with more care. That would help them plan checks and care for each child in time.
arxiv-2601-18535:
Peter Balušík and Pavel Rajmic work on a fix for gaps in sound when the gaps are read as a map of tones over time. A tone map shows which tones sound at each beat. A flaw in the tape can knock out whole ticks of that map. The task is to fill the lost ticks in a way that sounds true. Time-based fills have a long past.

The tone-map form of the task is newer and less well served. Past fills can smear the tone or lose the phase, the part that sets how tones line up in time. The pair add phase care to the fill, so the built ticks keep the beat of the rest. A good fill could save tapes of talks and songs with short gaps. It could also help clean up calls and field tapes.
arxiv-2601-18735:
Jusheng Zhang and seven colleagues let a team of sight-and-text agents trade their doubts as if doubt were cash. Such teams can do more as one than each can solo. But to run many big agents at once costs a lot, and the cost grows fast as the team grows. Past team plans route tasks by gut rules that skip both cost and the shape of each agent's doubt.

A route that skips doubt can send a task to a sure but dear agent when a cheap, near-sure one would do. The team let agents state their doubt and trade tasks by worth and cost as one. That trade should cut waste while it holds the grade of the joint work. Sound trades could make big agent teams pay their way in real use.
arxiv-2601-18935:
B. Bercu and three co-authors prove a central limit theorem for a known random split model. The Ewens-Pitman model gives chances over ways to split a set of items into groups. It has two knobs that shape the splits, and one setting falls back to the classic Ewens model from population genetics.

A central limit theorem says how far the random counts stray from their mean, in a bell shaped way. The team works in the case where one knob grows large, using a martingale approach. Such results help geneticists judge whether a sample's family pattern is odd or just chance.
arxiv-2601-19435:
Shengwei Xu and four co-authors work out how ads could live inside chat model answers. Paying for large language models in a lasting way is an open problem. Search ads rested on static keywords, but chat users reveal their wants in passing, inside a flowing conversation, and those wants fade fast.

Ad insertion must catch that fleeting intent and place a fitting offer without wrecking the answer. The team studies the design of such a system. How this gets solved will shape whether chat tools stay free, and how much trust users keep in answers that also sell.
arxiv-2601-19535:
Manish Chandra, Debasis Ganguly, and Iadh Ounis work on retrieval-augmented generation, a method that lets language models look up text before answering. A retriever first finds passages that seem relevant to the question. The model then writes its answer using those passages. The catch is that a relevant passage may not actually help the answer get better.

Their system, LURE-RAG, re-ranks the found passages by utility instead. Utility means whether a passage truly improves the output for the task at hand, such as answering a question or summarizing for a query. The reranker is kept lightweight, so the extra step stays cheap. Putting helpful text first should raise answer quality without heavy cost. The work targets a quiet flaw in how most retrieval pipelines pick their evidence.
arxiv-2601-19635:
Shusen Liu, Pascal Jahan Elahi, and Ugo Varetto tackle a sharing problem in quantum computing. Quantum cloud services give each user's program an entire processor to itself. That monopoly blocks resource sharing and keeps costs high. It also prevents any quality-of-service tiers, where users could pay for better machines.

Existing quantum virtual machine designs try to split a processor among users. But they lean on the layout of one specific chip or on fixed templates. The authors propose DynQ, a dynamic virtual machine that ignores the chip's exact topology. It partitions the hardware using quality-weighted community detection, grouping good qubits together. Virtualisation transformed classical cloud computing. This work explores what it would take for quantum clouds to follow.
arxiv-2601-19735:
Francesco Sannino writes graduate-level lecture notes on one of particle physics' deepest puzzles. The strong CP problem asks why the strong force respects a symmetry it is allowed to break. The leading answer is the axion, a hypothetical particle that could also be dark matter. These notes introduce the problem and the axion from the viewpoint of effective field theory.

The notes are self-contained. They build the chiral effective theory of quantum chromodynamics and derive a potential that depends on the offending angle. Vacuum alignment, periodicity, and branch structure all follow from that potential. A clear path through this material helps new researchers enter axion physics. The notes serve courses and self-study alike.
arxiv-2601-19935:
Yiting Shen, Kun Li, Wei Zhou, and Songlin Hu build a benchmark for agents that must use long-term memory. Language model agents increasingly run complex, tool-based tasks over long periods. Memory should drive their actions, not just answer questions. Existing benchmarks mostly test passive recall of isolated facts in response to direct questions.

Their benchmark, Mem2ActBench, tests active memory use instead. The agent must apply what it remembers to execute tasks. That is the capability real deployments depend on. An agent can ace recall quizzes yet fail to act on what it knows. Measuring the gap guides memory design for autonomous systems. The work shifts evaluation from remembering to doing.
arxiv-2601-20135:
Domitilla Del Vecchio gives an overview of control systems engineering as used in synthetic biology. The field builds new functions into living cells, with uses such as cell therapy and guiding cells to change fate for regenerative medicine. A core problem runs through these uses: keeping the level of a key factor in the cell on target.

Cells face noise from their surroundings and from within, so open-loop designs often drift. Control methods add feedback that corrects the level as conditions change. Del Vecchio closes with a case study in cell fate reprogramming. The paper shows how tools from engineering can make living therapies safer and more predictable.
arxiv-2601-20435:
Aleix Roca and Vicenç Beltran rethink thread scheduling when a machine runs more threads than it can handle at once. High-performance computing and AI workloads now mix several parallel runtimes in one application, or share machines across jobs. Traditional operating system schedulers strain under these demands.

The authors present a user-space framework that coordinates multi-runtime and multi-process workloads. Coordinating above the operating system lets runtimes cooperate instead of fighting over cores. Better scheduling under oversubscription would raise the useful output of the clusters that train and serve large models. Less strife over cores means more work done per hour on the same chips.
arxiv-2601-21235:
Alok Abhishek, Tushar Bandopadhyay, and Lisa Erickson argue that current safety tests for large language models hide the harms that matter most. Models now work in high-stakes fields where a rare but severe failure can cause lasting damage. Most benchmarks still shrink social risk into one average score.

Their framework, called SHARP, builds risk profiles instead of single scores. It tracks how harm is spread out, how risk factors interact, and how bad the worst cases get. A single average can make an unfair model look safe. Profiles show which groups face the worst outcomes and where the danger concentrates.
arxiv-2601-21435:
Han-Chuan Kou, Zhi-Han Zhang, Xin-Hui Wu, Yan Zhou, Gang Chen, and Peng Li speed up a classic protocol for crossing a quantum phase change. Slow crossing follows a known scaling law for how many defects form. Rushing the crossing can backfire and create extra defects instead.

Their optimized protocol ramps the control field in a shaped way near the critical point. It keeps the classic scaling while taking much less total time. It also damps therise in defects that fast ramps often cause. Faster clean crossings help quantum devices and simulators that must change state without heating up.
arxiv-2601-21535:
Giacomo Greco and Domenico Marinucci study random fields spread over a sphere and how to make them sparse. Such fields model data on globes, from cosmic background radiation to climate maps. A simple new representation lets the authors compare several meanings of sparsity under rotational symmetry.

They also build sparse fields that mimic the spectra of popular non-Gaussian fields. The mimicry holds for both the basic power pattern and higher-order patterns. At the same time, the sparse form allows fast simulation. Fast, faithful simulation is gold for cosmology, where thousands of fake skies are needed to judge real ones.
arxiv-2601-21935:
Tom Yates and co-authors study belief propagation, a workhorse algorithm for drawing conclusions in probabilistic graphical models. The method passes messages between variables until they agree on a joint picture. Exact belief propagation quickly becomes infeasible as models grow, blowing past compute and memory budgets.

Cheaper variants exist, and the most popular one assumes every distribution is locally Gaussian, bell-shaped near each point. The team's 2026 preprint shows that belief propagation itself tends to converge toward Gaussian distributions in sparsely connected factor graphs. That result helps explain why the Gaussian shortcut works as well as it does. And it tells practitioners when the cheap version can stand in for the exact computation.
arxiv-2601-22035:
Longxuan Yu and co-authors study a freedom that diffusion language models have and ordinary ones lack. Autoregressive models must write left to right, in a fixed order. That hurts when the required output order clashes with natural reasoning, for instance when a format demands the answer before the explanation.

An autoregressive model must then commit to an answer before reasoning through it. Diffusion models generate in a different order, which could fit reasoning better. The team's 2026 preprint asks when output order stops reflecting reasoning order in these models. The answer shapes how structured outputs, from forms to code, should be generated when the reasoning must come first but the page layout says otherwise.
arxiv-2601-22135:
Zhexin Liang and co-authors relight whole photographs with a diffusion model guided by physics. Full-image relighting, changing a scene's light after the photo is taken, is hard for three reasons the authors name. Paired training data are scarce, physical plausibility is difficult to maintain, and data-driven priors generalize poorly.

Earlier attempts to bridge the gap between synthetic training scenes and real photos stayed suboptimal. The team's 2026 preprint, PI-Light, builds physics-inspired structure into the diffusion process for full-image relighting. Believable relighting serves film, e-commerce, and design, where reshooting under new light is costly. Physics guidance helps the model respect shadows and reflections instead of painting light on freely.
arxiv-2601-22535:
Yotam Dikstein, Max Hopkins, Russell Impagliazzo, and Toniann Pitassi build a new kind of error-correcting code. Their codes can be decoded locally, by reading only a small part of a message, and they list a few possible answers when noise is heavy. The codes reach rates and error tolerance close to the best theory allows.

The decoding runs very fast and with shallow circuits. Paired with older codes for low-noise cases, the work settles several long-open problems in coding and complexity theory. Such codes help protect data and also power proofs about hard problems.
arxiv-2601-22635:
Claudio Guarcello, Alexander Dubkov, and Davide Valenti survey how noise can help systems escape stuck states. Many systems, classical and quantum, relax slowly through metastable states — traps that look stable but are not the true rest state. Their 2026 preprint spans systems from memristors to Josephson devices.

Noise, long seen as a foe, can give the kick that frees a stuck system. The survey links Lévy flights, quantum escape, and axion hunts with Josephson gear. One frame for many fields can spark cross-field tricks. The work is a map of noise as a tool.
arxiv-2601-22735:
Zhidian Huang and a large team ask whether reasoning multimodal models actually think in a sound way. New models reason step by step about images and text. Their 2026 preprint, MM-THEBench, probes whether that thinking cuts hallucination, or adds new kinds of it.

Self-checking thought can steady a model, yet each extra step can also drift. The bench sorts those gains and harms across tasks. Honest grades for reasoning are now a core need. The work gives the field a shared test. It asks a sharp question in its title, and answers with data.
arxiv-2601-22935:
Evgeny Grigorenko and four co-authors protect private code used by AI autocomplete tools. Modern coding editors use language models to suggest code as you type. Training those models on user code risks leaking that code through the model itself, a new kind of data exposure.

Their approach applies differential privacy, a method that adds measured noise so single examples cannot be traced. The trade-off is between suggestion quality and privacy strength. Safer training would let firms use smart coding help without risking their source code. Privacy protection at training time is the focus, since a released autocomplete model cannot be un-trained once it leaks code.
arxiv-2601-23035:
Samir Adly, Vinh Thanh Ho, and Huu Nhan Nguyen study a fast gradient method with a fading regularizer. Their algorithm targets smooth convex minimization, where the objective's gradient changes at a controlled rate. It comes from discretizing a damped inertial system, a model of motion with friction.

A Tikhonov regularizer that vanishes over time steadies the path without biasing the end point. Explicit, step-by-step versions suit real computation better than continuous models. Faster convex solvers sit under logistics, imaging, and machine learning pipelines. Vanishing regularization is the balancing act: strong enough early to guide the iterates, gone at the end so the true solution remains.
arxiv-2601-23135:
Cheng Ge, Caitlyn Heqi Yin, Hao Liang, and Jiawei Zhang explain why a popular training method needs its normalization step. Group Relative Policy Optimization, or GRPO, trains language models without a separate critic network. It compares answers within a group per prompt and normalizes by variance.

Why that normalization helps, and when, was unclear. The authors give a local-curvature view of the adaptive gradients involved. A clear reason for a standard trick helps practitioners tune it instead of trusting habit. Per-prompt baselines replace the critic, so understanding the normalization explains the method's core stability trick.
arxiv-2601-23235:
Barron K. Nguyen, Laura K. Schaefer, Fei Dai, and Héctor E. Delgado-Díaz model the air of the rocky planet 55 Cancri e. The planet is an old, dense world orbiting a K-type star, larger and heavier than Earth. Webb observations suggest a carbon-rich atmosphere over a global magma ocean hotter than any on Earth.

The authors test how tidal heating and the planet's volatile budget shape the outgassed atmosphere. Matching the observed carbon gases constrains what the interior holds. Lava worlds like this are natural labs for planetary origins.

Audubon issued volume three of his Ornithological Biography in 1835. The work stands as the prose companion to The Birds of America. Species accounts march on through the birds of the young republic. Audubon's years in forests, swamps, and coasts stand behind every page.

He records how each bird feeds, nests, migrates, and sings. Encounters with hunters, settlers, and wild weather enliven the science. The accounts mix exact detail with a storyteller's pace. Volume three holds the middle of the five volume set. Its pages widen the record his pictures made famous. Naturalists quote these observations to this day. berzelius-theorie-proportions-1835:
Berzelius states his full atomic-weight system in his Theory of Chemical Proportions, in French from 1835. Decades of exact trials stand behind the tables in this capstone work. The great Swedish chemist sums up a life spent weighing the elements with unmatched care and patience.

His system gave later chemists the firm numbers they needed. On such weights the periodic table would one day be built with confidence. He also defends his views against rivals in clear, firm prose. The book closes an era in which one man's laboratory set the measures for a whole science coming of age.
boerhaave-elements-chemistry-1735:
Herman Boerhaave's Elements of Chemistry, in Peter Shaw's 1735 English version, was the eighteenth century's leading textbook of the science. Boerhaave taught at Leiden, and students crossed Europe to hear him lecture. He made chemistry a fit and honored study for a university, not a mere trade secret.

Order, clarity, and trial mark every part of his vast course. Furnaces, salts, metals, and medicines fall into one clear system here. Shaw's version carried the master's voice to the English-reading world in full. The book laid a foundation stone of Enlightenment chemistry, and its influence ran through lecture halls for decades after.
buchner-dantons-death-1835:
Georg Büchner wrote Danton's Death in 1835, at the age of twenty-one, while hiding from police pursuit. The text here is the German original, since no English translation is in the public domain. Danton, hero of the French Revolution, has tired of blood and wants the Terror stopped.

Robespierre and Saint-Just, cold and certain, move to destroy him for that mercy. Danton drifts, jokes, and despairs, yet will not flee or fight in time. Büchner built the play from historical sources, letting real speeches carry the scenes. Its weary, brilliant talk sounds startlingly modern. Critics now rank the play as the birth of modern political drama.
calderon-life-is-a-dream-1635:
Pedro Calderon de la Barca wrote Life Is a Dream in 1635, a Spanish verse drama of the Baroque age. Prince Segismundo has been locked in a tower since birth. A prophecy said he would become a cruel king. His father the king tests him by giving him one day of freedom.

Segismundo acts with rage, is returned to the tower, and is told it was all a dream. Later a revolt frees him for real, and he must choose how to rule. The play asks whether life itself is a dream. It is the most famous drama of Spain's Golden Age.

The talk lays bare how the doomed operation was run, and judged, from the top.
