cia-03153735: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1957/12/07, a CIA publication. The December briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
cia-03155135: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1957/07/12, a CIA publication. The July briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
cia-06828435: OHB MAIN CAFE 11/6/17, a CIA document. The dated cafe file. This file preserves that declassified paper. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
coriolanus-pg1535: Pride destroys Rome's greatest general in this edition of Shakespeare's austere tragedy: Coriolanus, hero of the wars, cannot stomach the people's voice and turns his sword on Rome itself. Only his mother Volumnia, kneeling before him, can turn him back. Politics, honor, and maternal power in magnificent, uncompromising verse.
croll-basilica-chymica-1635:
Oswald Croll, a German physician in the circle of Paracelsus, wrote Basilica Chymica, shown here in its 1635 form. Croll taught that chemical medicines, made by art, could heal better than the old herbal mixtures alone. His book became a leading guide to Paracelsian pharmacy.

Recipes give salts, oils, and spirits drawn from metals, plants, and minerals, with the steps for making each one. Croll also set out the doctrine of signatures, which held that a plant's shape hints at its use. Doctors and apothecaries used the book across Europe. It shows chemical medicine taking shape inside an older world of signs and likenesses.
doe-osti-2998720-measured-reaction-rate-: Uranium and plutonium samples got their reaction ratios, and this DOE report measures U-235, U-238, Np-237, Pu-239. The pages detail the foil results. The nuclear data folks get their numbers. The samples were actinide. The ratios were reaction rate. The folks were nuclear data.
elliotson-human-physiology-vol1-1835:
John Elliotson sets out the human body in the first volume of his Human Physiology, from 1835. Elliotson was London's most fashionable physician and a star lecturer. His textbook bridged orthodox medicine and the mesmerism that would soon define, and then destroy, his public standing in the medical world.

Organs, tissues, and functions are laid out in systematic order here. The writing aims at students yet carries a controversialist's spark beneath. Within a few years, mesmeric trials would cost him his hospital post. The volume shows establishment medicine at its most ambitious, by a man standing, unknowing, on the edge of a spectacular fall from grace.
elliotson-human-physiology-vol2-1835:
Elliotson continues his systematic textbook in the second volume of Human Physiology, from 1835. The body's functions unfold in ordered detail for the medical student. Its author writes on the very eve of the scandal that would exile him from respectable medicine into the mesmeric camp for good.

Senses, nerves, and the machinery of life fill these careful pages. Elliotson's fame as a lecturer rests on clarity like this throughout. Orthodox in form, the book hides no hint of coming disgrace. Readers meet the establishment's physiology at full stretch, from a physician whose later fall makes the calm competence of these volumes read almost sadly.
elliotson-human-physiology-vol3-1835:
Elliotson completes his Human Physiology with this third volume, from 1835. The system of the body stands whole at last for his students. Within a few years, his public mesmeric demonstrations would cost him his hospital post and his good name among the faculty of London medicine.

Generation, growth, and the mind's link to the body close the course. The physiology itself remained a landmark text despite its author's disgrace. Elliotson later founded the Zoist to plead the mesmeric cause in print. The three volumes together capture a moment when one textbook could carry a man from fame to exile, while the work outlived the scandal.
europmc-pmc10353935:
Patel and colleagues built a better gene-based risk score for heart artery disease in 2023. The Genes & Health Research Team and the Million Veteran Program shared data for the work. A polygenic score adds up many small gene effects into one risk number. The new score, GPSMult, drew on gene data from five ancestry groups.

The data held over 269,000 cases and over 1,178,000 controls. Patel also folded in gene data for ten risk traits, such as blood fats. In UK tests, the top fifth of scorers had three times the risk of the middle group. The score beat all past scores in African, European, Hispanic, and South Asian groups. It also flagged 3% of healthy people whose risk matched that of patients.
europmc-pmc1044835:
Iacoboni and colleagues used brain scans in 2005 to test how people read the aims of others. Mirror neurons are brain cells that fire both when a person acts and when they watch the same act. Past work tied them to naming an act. The team asked if they also grasp why the act is done.

Twenty-three people watched hand grasps in the scanner. Some clips showed a grasp with no setting, some a setting alone, and some a grasp in a setting that hinted at drinking or cleaning. Iacoboni found a clear rise in signal for grasps in a setting. The hot spot sat in the lower front of the brain, in mirror areas. The result says the motor system infers aims on its own.
europmc-pmc10558035:
Huang and Li built compleasm in 2023, a faster tool to grade how complete a genome build is. A genome build may miss genes, which then warps all later work. The standard grader, BUSCO, checks for a set of genes kept near unchanged across species. It runs slowly, most of all on huge genomes.

Their tool pairs a fast protein aligner with the same gene sets. Huang reports a 14-fold speed gain on human builds. It also scored the full human build at 99.6% complete, close to the 99.5% from gene labels. BUSCO had scored the same build at just 95.7%. The code is free on GitHub for any lab to use.
europmc-pmc1084335:
Bolzer and colleagues mapped every chromosome inside human cell nuclei in 3D in this 2005 paper. Chromosomes are the bundled strands of DNA that carry genes. How they sit inside the nucleus, the cell's control centre, may affect how genes are used. Past studies clashed on whether their layout follows a fixed order.

The team built tools to chart all chromosomes at once in skin cells. Small chromosomes sat nearer the centre, they found, while large ones sat nearer the edge. This held in resting and growing cells and in a second cell type from birth fluid. The pattern followed size, not gene richness, in these flat nuclei. The authors note that round nuclei in other cells follow a distinct rule, so layout rules vary by cell type.
europmc-pmc11223835:
Galaxy Community reports the 2024 state of a global platform for data analysis in biology in this paper. Galaxy lets researchers run complex analyses through a web interface without local computing power. Most services are free to use, and the user base broadens each year. Stability, tool variety, training, and support draw users in.

Recent work applies user experience design to improve accessibility and tool discovery. A redesigned ToolShed, the platform's app store, is part of that push. Two technical directions stand out: access to graphics processors for cutting-edge methods, and support for licensed tools. The Galaxy Training Network has grown its course portfolio and linked lessons directly to tools. Job scheduling and the interface were improved. The authors also describe resourcing public services to run more shared workflows.
europmc-pmc1523235:
Cells that build tissue, fibroblasts, behave unlike twins in each body site. Rinn and co-authors mapped their gene programs in 2006, sampling 43 sites across the human body. The question was whether each site is specified on its own, or reads its place on a body map.

A set of 337 genes sorted all samples by their site of origin. The genes varied along three axes: head to tail, limb base to tip, and skin versus deep tissue. Many were pattern genes, including HOX genes whose embryo layout persists in adult cells. Rinn argues fibroblasts keep a lasting memory of position.
europmc-pmc1635535:
A jumping gene from fish can haul cargo too big for virus tools. Balciunas and co-authors harnessed the Tol2 transposon in 2006. Viruses and transposons insert DNA into genomes, but falter beyond about 8,000 letters.

Tol2 efficiently integrated pieces larger than 10,000 letters into human cells. The team trimmed it to a minimal form, miniTol2 at 5,800 letters, that still works in zebrafish and human cells. Both forms fixed a missing enzyme in an animal model of hereditary tyrosinemia, a liver disease. Balciunas offers Tol2 as a nonviral truck for large therapeutic genes.
europmc-pmc1762435:
Oxygen-starved cells tune their blood vessel signals with tiny RNAs. Hua and co-authors mapped that tuning in 2006 for VEGF, a key vessel growth factor, in a human tumor cell line. Computer analysis predicted 96 microRNAs could regulate VEGF.

Expression profiles across five cell lines showed only some candidates were actually present to act. Different cells used different subsets of the 96. Some microRNAs co-regulated several vessel factors at once. Multiple microRNAs could cooperate at separate binding sites or compete for one. Hua lays out coordinate and competitive principles for how microRNAs jointly govern a gene.
europmc-pmc2125335: A medical paper on the action of optochin on type strains of pneumococci. The drug's effect. This article preserves that pharmacology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2126335: A medical paper on effect of bile on the clotting time of blood. The bile-thinned blood. This article preserves that hematology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2130935: A medical paper contributing to the pathology of experimental virus encephalitis, herpetic. The brain virus. This article preserves that neurology. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2140435: A biology paper on the reciprocal relation between the osmotic pressure and the viscosity of gelatin. The gel's physics. This article preserves that biophysics. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2140535: A biology paper on the phagocytosis of solid particles, carbon and quartz in various solutions. The eaten soot again. This article preserves that cell biology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
europmc-pmc2141035: A biology paper with a study of the bactericidal action of ultra violet light, the effect of varying factors. The killing rays. This article preserves that bacteriology. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2225435:
García-Lerma and a large team tested HIV prevention drugs in macaques in 2008. With no effective vaccine, pre-exposure prophylaxis, taking antiretroviral drugs before exposure, is a leading prevention idea. The team used a repeat-exposure model with fourteen weekly rectal virus challenges. Six monkeys per group received daily emtricitabine alone, an oral two-drug combination, or a stronger injected combination. A fourth group got the strong regimen only around each challenge.

Risk of infection fell 3.8-fold with the single drug and 7.8-fold with the oral combination, compared with eighteen untreated controls. Both reductions were statistically significant. The work used a macaque model of rectal transmission of the virus. All six monkeys on the strong daily regimen were protected. All six on the intermittent regimen were also protected. Breakthrough infections showed blunted virus levels, and drug resistance appeared in two of six cases.
europmc-pmc2491635:
Strobl and colleagues fixed a bias in how random forests rank the importance of input factors in 2008. Random forests are models built from many decision trees, prized when inputs are many and tangled together. Their importance scores guide screening in fields like gene studies, but the scores favour inputs that move together with others.

The authors traced the bias to two causes. First, tree building itself prefers such linked inputs when choosing splits. Second, the standard score shuffles one input on its own, handing its linked partners an extra edge. Their fix shuffles each input only within groups matched on its partners, so each factor is judged on its own effect alone. In tests, this conditional score tracked each factor's true impact far better. They urged its use when tangled inputs make the standard ranking hard to trust.
europmc-pmc2527135:
Jones and colleagues studied in 2008 what a gene-tagging enzyme called Dot1L does in developing mammals. Dot1L adds a chemical mark, methylation, to one spot on histone H3, a protein that packages DNA. In yeast the mark helps silence genes near chromosome ends, but its role in mammals was unclear, so the team bred mice lacking the enzyme.

Embryos without Dot1L grew poorly, showed blood vessel defects in the yolk sac and swollen hearts, and died around day 10 of development. Stem cells taken from them had lost the H3 mark entirely. They also carried weaker silencing marks at chromosome centres and ends, wrong chromosome counts, overlong chromosome ends, and slow growth. The work ties Dot1L to keeping silent DNA regions intact during development.
europmc-pmc2581435:
Towner and a large team of collaborators reported in 2008 the discovery of a new Ebola virus species behind a haemorrhagic fever outbreak in western Uganda. In November 2007, cases appeared in Bundibugyo District. The known Ebola species, Zaire and Sudan, kill 53 to 90 percent of patients, so identifying the culprit fast mattered. The team tested blood from the first 29 suspected cases.

Standard antibody and antigen tests plus a new random-primed sequencing method identified an Ebola outbreak caused by a previously unknown species, named Bundibugyo ebolavirus. Its genome is only distantly related to Côte d'Ivoire ebolavirus from western Africa. It diverges enough from all known ebolaviruses to matter practically. The authors warn that diagnostic tests, antivirals, and vaccines designed against the known species may miss or fail against this one.
europmc-pmc2628535:
Brenk and colleagues described in 2008 how they assembled screening libraries for drug discovery against neglected diseases, working from 2.3 million commercially available compounds. A new discovery operation for diseases of the poor needed libraries chosen with limited money and staff. The team defined rules to drop unwanted chemical groups and criteria to enrich for lead-like compounds, molecules simple enough to optimise later.

They selected 222,552 compounds for a computer-screening library. A diverse general screening library took 57,438 more. A focused set aimed at kinase enzymes took 1,697, built from key fragments mined from the literature and patents. Testing showed the general library spanned broad lead-like chemical space with high purity and suitable solubility for biochemical screening. The authors draw lessons for compound selection in resource-limited academic settings.
europmc-pmc2631735:
Hooper reviewed in 2001 the emerging mechanisms by which bacteria resist fluoroquinolone antibiotics, a widely used drug class. These drugs kill by jamming two bacterial enzymes, DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, that manage DNA tangles. Resistance had followed broad use, and Hooper catalogues the routes bacteria take.

Most resistance comes from mutations in the target enzyme genes that blunt drug binding. Bacteria also mutate genes controlling the pores that let drugs in and the efflux pumps that throw drugs out. Species needing only one mutation, like Staphylococcus aureus, turned resistant first. Species needing several mutations followed later. These include Campylobacter and the gonorrhoea bacterium. Animal drug use and person-to-person spread helped them along. Hooper warns pneumococcus resistance, then low, needs close watching.
europmc-pmc2674935:
Hessell and co-authors tested in 2009 whether a famous HIV-blocking antibody could protect monkeys at strikingly low blood levels. The antibody, 2G12, locks onto sugars on the virus surface and neutralizes many strains. Most such antibodies need high levels to protect, which had dimmed hopes for an antibody-based vaccine. Earlier hints suggested 2G12 might be an exception.

The team dosed five monkeys and exposed them to a monkey-human hybrid virus through the vagina, mimicking sexual transmission. At blood levels so low they barely registered, three monkeys were fully protected, with no sign of infection at all. One showed a delayed, smaller infection, and one was not protected. Comparisons with a rival antibody found no edge for 2G12 in reaching the vaginal surface or in calling in killer cells, leaving its unusual strength unexplained.
europmc-pmc2677735:
Xilouri and colleagues showed in 2009 that faulty alpha-synuclein harms brain cells in part by jamming one of the cell's recycling routes. This protein clumps in Parkinson disease. Cells clear proteins two ways through their acid sacs: a bulk route, and a targeted route called chaperone-mediated autophagy, which walks single proteins to their doom.

In rat and human cell lines switched to make the faulty protein, the targeted route faltered and overall protein clearing fell. In mature nerve-like cells, both normal and faulty protein slowly killed, and the harm partly depended on the jammed route. The bulk route ramped up to compensate. In real neurons grown from rat brain, only the faulty form caused both the jam and the extra death. Easing the jam lessened the killing, pointing to a drug target.
europmc-pmc2685735:
Terwilliger and colleagues improved in 2009 the way crystallography software judges its own work while solving protein structures. To read a protein's shape from X-ray data, scientists build an electron-density map, a cloud picture of the molecule. Automated solving makes choice after choice, and each choice needs a reliable score for how good the current map is.

The team tested ten candidate scores against known answers. The winner was skewness, a measure of how lopsided the density values are; good maps skew in a characteristic way. They wrapped that score in a Bayesian method, which weighs new evidence against prior expectation, inside the PHENIX AutoSol wizard. The wizard now picks paths and stops bad branches with better judgment. Sharper self-scoring matters because structure solving is increasingly done by software alone, overnight, on hundreds of targets.
europmc-pmc2721635:
Melman and co-authors tested in 2009 whether parasitic worms from Kenya had grown less sensitive to praziquantel, nearly the only drug used against schistosomiasis, a widespread worm disease. Heavy reliance on one drug raises fears of resistance. They took Schistosoma mansoni isolates from workers in Kisumu who face constant exposure through their jobs.

Larvae from patients treated before were less sensitive in lab tests than larvae from untreated patients. One isolate from a man never cured despite many treatments was clearly less sensitive in mouse and adult-worm assays too. A sub-line kept apart for three years regained sensitivity, which suggests the trait fades without drug pressure but could spread as treatment expands.
europmc-pmc2740835:
Lemey, Rambaut, Drummond, and Suchard introduced in 2009 a Bayesian framework for phylogeography, the study of how viruses spread across places over time using their genetic family trees. Past work mostly used model-free shortcuts that gave little sense of timing. Probabilistic evolution models, by contrast, can date dispersal events while allowing for uncertainty in the tree itself.

Their method maps locations onto sampled, time-scaled trees and uses a variable search to pick the simplest set of dispersal routes that fits the data. Priors can encode sampling patterns or rival hypotheses about spread. Tests on bird flu H5N1 origins and on rabies in West African dogs showed timed routes and epidemic cycles that sustain the virus locally.
europmc-pmc2777335:
Sprong, Cacciò, and van der Giessen, with the ZOOPNET network and partners, genotyped in 2009 Giardia duodenalis isolates from people and animals to judge how often animal strains infect humans. This gut parasite causes giardiasis worldwide and spreads through stool, water, and food. Its seven genetic groups differ in host range, and two of them occur in humans and many mammals.

They characterized nearly one thousand human and over fourteen hundred animal isolates, building almost four thousand sequences from four gene loci into a shared European database. At coarse resolution, both human-infecting groups looked zoonotic, able to pass from animals. Under strict multi-locus definitions, though, only two genotypes of one group clearly qualified, and none of the other. Mixed genotypes within single isolates appeared repeatedly. Real zoonotic potential is evident, they conclude, but its size is still unmeasured.
europmc-pmc2810335:
Khallou-Laschet and colleagues tracked how macrophages, the eater cells inside artery plaques, change character as fatty deposits grow in mice prone to clogged arteries. Macrophages come in an attacking type, M1, and a repair type, M2. The 2010 team told them apart by which version of an enzyme called arginase each type makes.

Young plaques held almost only repair-type cells, which helped vessel wall cells multiply in lab tests. Older plaques flipped to mostly attack-type cells, and worse disease tracked with that flip. Lab experiments showed fully set cells could still swap types, so the change likely happens inside the plaque rather than by new arrivals. Reversing it might slow disease.
europmc-pmc2845135:
Seyfried and Shelton argued in 2010 that cancer is, at root, a metabolic disease of broken cell energy systems. Normal cells draw most usable energy from oxygen-based burning in mitochondria, the cell's power units. Most cancer cells instead lean on a cruder sugar-fermentation route, even when oxygen is plentiful, a pattern noticed by Warburg generations ago.

The authors review evidence tying that energy failure to nearly every cancer hallmark, from runaway growth to spread. Gene instability itself, they contend, may flow from faulty energy metabolism rather than sitting at the top of the chain. If the view holds, prevention and treatment would shift toward guarding mitochondrial function and starving the backup energy route tumors depend on.
europmc-pmc2877735:
Van Vliet, Harmsen, de Bont, and Tissing argued in 2010 that gut microbes help drive mucositis, the painful gut injury that often forces cancer treatment to pause. The classic model of mucositis runs through five phases of damage and healing and gives microbes no role. Yet gut bacteria clearly shape several bowel diseases, and chemotherapy itself slashes the gut's anaerobic bacteria just as mucositis peaks.

The authors set out five candidate pathways linking the microbial community to each stage of injury, from the first tissue damage to bacterial escape through the broken lining. Microbe shifts could amplify inflammation, weaken the mucus shield, and slow repair. Testing those routes could open probiotic or antibiotic strategies to protect patients and keep chemotherapy on schedule.
europmc-pmc2936535:
Hershberg and Petrov asked whether mutation itself leans in one direction across bacteria, in a 2010 evolution study. Mutation supplies the raw variation for selection, yet its habits were thought to differ widely between species.

They used clonal disease bacteria that evolve under unusually weak selection, letting mutation patterns show with little filtering. Across five pathogens from four broad groups, mutation consistently favoured the bases A and T, even in genomes rich in G and C. Changes from C or G toward T or A drove the trend. Base makeup, they argue, must also reflect selection.
europmc-pmc2948035:
Guerrero-Bosagna and colleagues examined sperm DNA in rats three generations after a pregnancy exposure to vinclozolin, a hormone-disrupting farm chemical, in a 2010 study. Earlier work showed such exposure produced disease in later generations without direct contact.

Scanning promoter regions genome-wide, they found dozens of stretches with altered chemical marking in the third-generation sperm, and confirmed a set of them with a second method. Most confirmed regions shared a common short DNA motif, rare among random promoters. One case turned out to be a copy number change rather than a marking shift, hinting early marks may seed later genetic faults.
europmc-pmc2987835:
Bos and colleagues hunted effector proteins from the green peach aphid, a sap-sucking pest, in a 2010 functional genomics study. Aphids inject saliva that calms plant defences such as sap tube clogging, and the responsible molecules were unknown.

Starting from salivary gland gene tags in public data, they picked forty-eight candidates sharing features with known pathogen effectors and tested each in a model plant leaf. One, named Mp10, triggered leaf yellowing and local cell death and made a virus carrying it recognisable to tobacco defences. A plant helper protein long tied to disease resistance proved necessary for that response.
europmc-pmc2993935:
Martínez and co-authors fed volunteers two kinds of resistant starch and tracked changes in gut microbes in a 2010 trial. Resistant starch escapes digestion and feeds bowel bacteria, but its forms differ chemically and may act differently.

Ten people ate crackers carrying one starch type, a modified type, or plain starch for three weeks each in a blinded rotation. Gene tag sequencing showed both resistant types shifted the faecal community in distinct ways. The modified type lifted whole bacterial groups and multiplied certain bifidobacteria up to tenfold in some people, while the natural type favoured other named species.
europmc-pmc3020935:
Rossin and co-authors tested whether genes in genome regions tied to immune diseases physically interact as proteins, in a 2011 study of rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn's disease. Scans had flagged over a hundred and fifty regions, but the disturbed biology behind them stayed murky.

Building protein interaction networks from genes inside the flagged regions, they found far more links than chance allows, confirmed by several shuffling tests. Network members clustered in tissues relevant to each disease. Proteins in the networks but outside the flagged regions also proved enriched for new associations, giving the networks power to nominate fresh disease genes.
europmc-pmc3031535:
Harvey and coauthors showed in 2011 that plants keep a backup weapon against viruses when their first defense is knocked out. Plants fight viruses by chopping viral RNA, using proteins called Argonautes. The main fighter, AGO1, is itself targeted by proteins that many viruses carry. The team tested plants missing each of ten Argonaute proteins against two real viruses.

Plants missing AGO2 became far sicker than normal plants and let both viruses build up faster early on. Healthy plants raised their AGO2 levels after infection. The authors propose a layered defense: when viral blockers disable the first layer, that loss frees the second layer to switch on. The backup does not cover every virus, since a third virus was unaffected. The model helps explain how plant and virus counter moves evolve together.
europmc-pmc3072935:
Gagliardi, Brouwers, Palda, Lemieux-Charles, and Grimshaw asked in 2011 why clinical guidelines are so often ignored. These documents are the evidence summaries meant to guide care. The team also asked whether guidelines could be built for easier use. They coined a framework of implementability: features of a guideline that help or hinder its uptake. The team built the framework from the implementation literature, then checked twenty high quality guidelines against it.

The framework holds twenty two elements grouped under headings such as usability, adaptability, and how use is evaluated. Most guidelines were long walls of graded evidence and tables. Few offered versions for different readers, plain summaries, patient discussion aids, cost notes, or tips for local promotion and monitoring. No topic area did consistently better. The authors say closing those gaps may require new setups for who writes guidelines and how. Testing the framework comes next.
europmc-pmc3118335:
Sascha Keller and colleagues tested tiny cell-made sacs from body fluids as a diagnostic tool in a 2011 paper in the Journal of Translational Medicine. Cells shed these sacs into blood, urine, saliva, and other fluids, and each sac carries proteins and RNA from its parent cell. The team asked whether that cargo survives well enough to read.

Sacs purified from pregnancy fluid, saliva, and urine carried the expected marker proteins, and their RNA stayed intact, shielded by the sac wall from enzymes that would destroy it. RNA from pregnancy fluid even revealed a gene variant and the sex of the unborn child. Since collecting fluids is gentle, the authors present sacs as a promising window into the body's gene activity.
europmc-pmc3186735:
Mark Tremblay and colleagues reviewed sitting behaviour and health in school-age children in a 2011 paper. Evidence was growing that sitting harms health independently of exercise, but youth data had never been gathered fully. More than two hundred studies covering nearly a million participants met their criteria.

Across study types, more sedentary time tracked with worse health in a dose-wise fashion. Television dominated the measures, and more than two hours daily was tied to poorer body composition and fitness, lower self-esteem, weaker social behaviour, and lower school achievement. Trials that cut sitting time lowered body mass index modestly but significantly. The authors conclude any reduction in sitting helps, with television time the clearest target.
europmc-pmc3263635:
Marianne Baird and colleagues examined creatine kinase as a marker of exercise-induced muscle damage in this 2012 paper in the Journal of Nutrition and Metabolism. The enzyme leaks into the blood when muscle is injured, and its blood level is widely used to diagnose heart attacks, muscular dystrophy, and brain disease. Its use after exercise is more controversial.

The authors review the evidence and opinion on whether raised levels after physical activity genuinely reflect muscle damage and whether they should worry anyone. They stress that unchangeable traits such as ethnicity, age, and sex shift the enzyme's baseline, so the upper limit of normal may need resetting for different groups. They also call for standardized testing protocols and stronger guidelines, arguing the field's scientific integrity depends on treating this everyday measurement more carefully.
europmc-pmc3265535:
Kathrin Ziegelbauer and colleagues pooled the evidence on sanitation and intestinal worm infections in this 2012 systematic review and meta-analysis in PLoS Medicine. More than a billion people carry soil-transmitted helminths, the roundworms, whipworms, and hookworms that spread where human waste contaminates soil and water. The infections cling to poverty, poor hygiene, and missing or inadequate toilets.

By combining the available studies, the authors find that access to sanitation is associated with a clearly reduced risk of catching these worms. The result strengthens the case for building and using proper sanitation. It is not only a matter of dignity and general hygiene. It is also a measurable defense against a vast, neglected burden of disease. It also gives control programs a firmer evidence base for investing in sanitation alongside deworming medicine.
europmc-pmc3289635:
Poland and his co-authors introduced a cheaper way to map genes in barley and wheat in 2012. Both crops have huge genomes, which makes full sequencing slow and costly for breeding work. Their method uses two cutting enzymes to sample only part of the genome, then reads those pieces for many plants at once.

Applied to breeding populations, the approach placed tens of thousands of single letter variants onto existing reference maps for both crops. The authors also built a fresh wheat map using only markers from the new method. Because each sample costs little, they argue the technique can support association studies and breeding programs that select plants using DNA markers.
europmc-pmc3325235:
Kohane and colleagues used electronic health records to count the other illnesses that travel with autism, in a 2012 study. Earlier estimates came from studies of fewer than two hundred patients, too small to measure rare conditions well. Querying records across four Boston hospitals, the team profiled more than fourteen thousand people under thirty five with autism spectrum disorders.

Epilepsy stood out, affecting roughly one in five patients, many times the hospital wide rate. Schizophrenia, bowel disorders, brain structure differences, sleep problems, and a muscle disease all appeared far more often than in other patients. Some conditions, including schizophrenia and inflammatory bowel disease, grew more common as patients moved from childhood into young adulthood. The authors say care for autistic patients must plan for this broad medical burden, not just developmental support.
europmc-pmc3329435:
Bloemberg and Quadrilatero presented a faster way to type muscle fibers in rats, mice, and people, in a 2012 methods paper. Muscle is a patchwork of fiber types that differ in speed and fuel use, and the proportions vary from muscle to muscle. Older staining methods are slow and can blur types together, while antibody based fluorescence can reveal several fiber proteins at once on a single slice.

Using multicolored glowing antibodies, the team sorted pure and mixed fibers across ten muscles each from rats and mice, plus a human thigh muscle. Mixed fibers, carrying two fiber proteins at once, turned up in every species and formed a sizable share in some muscles. The paper also reports fiber sizes and fuel burning enzyme activity by type, offering a reference dataset alongside the protocol.
europmc-pmc3369835:
Zug and Hammerstein re-ran a contested estimate in 2012: how many insect and other arthropod species carry Wolbachia bacteria. These microbes live inside host cells and twist how their hosts reproduce. An earlier study had put the share of infected species at about two thirds.

Using a newer survey that tested more animals per species and picked species more randomly, the pair arrived near forty percent. That is lower than before, yet still a striking share of land arthropods. Within a species, they found, usually nearly all or very few animals are infected. Wolbachia also stayed the most common reproductive parasite in the survey.
europmc-pmc3414035:
Li and colleagues reported new variants of a pig coronavirus in 2012 after outbreaks swept vaccinated Chinese herds the year before. The virus causes porcine epidemic diarrhea: severe gut illness, vomiting, and watery diarrhea that kill suckling piglets in droves. Infection rates had jumped despite wide vaccine use, suggesting the field virus had changed.

The team sequenced the full spike gene, the virus's key weapon, from samples collected at nine hard-hit farms with heavy deaths. Three new variants emerged from the sequences. finney-lectures-revivals-1835:
Charles Grandison Finney was the lawyer turned evangelist who led the Second Great Awakening across upstate New York. His Lectures on Revivals of Religion, published in 1835, turn his practice into a teachable method. Finney insists that a revival is not a miracle dropped from heaven.

A revival, he argues, is the right use of means: preaching that presses for decision, prayer meetings, and the anxious bench for seekers. Critics called his methods machinery, but his converts filled churches and fueled reforms from temperance to abolition. The lectures remain the manual of American revivalism as science and method.
frus-1861-d135:
On 6 July 1861, William H. Seward sent William Dayton a letter full of hopes for a quick win. The letter is document 135 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

July orders from Washington carried hopes of a quick win in Virginia. Seward's tone to Paris was bold in those weeks. The letter belongs to the last confident days before Bull Run taught both capitals that the war would be long. Bold words abroad rested on the loans and levies Congress voted that July. Loans and levies at home were the hard facts beneath his boldest phrases. Hard facts at home underwrote every bold phrase.
frus-1861-d235:
From his post abroad, Mr. Murphy wrote to William H. Seward on 27 May 1861. It stands as Document 235 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. The date falls in the opening months of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d35:
On 21 August 1861, William H. Seward wrote once more to Henry Sanford in Belgium. The letter is document 35 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

By late August the Union cause abroad rested on habit as much as hope. Seward's task was to keep neutral courts neutral, month after month. A routine letter to Brussels may look slight, but a hundred such letters were the wall the Confederacy could not climb. Routine, in this record, was not the foe of policy but its chief tool. The wall held because a hundred hands kept laying its plain, dated bricks.
frus-1862-d135:
On 29 August 1862, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 135 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d235:
William Stuart wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 6 September 1862, the same day Seward wrote twice to him. The Stuart letter is Document 235 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Same-day traffic in both directions marks a live matter moving between the legation and the Department. September 1862 gave both offices urgent business, with Lee in Maryland and Europe debating whether to step in. A letter in this exchange belongs to the small group of papers that show Anglo-American dealings at their most active that summer. Each note was numbered and docketed by clerks, which is why the file reads so evenly.
frus-1862-d335:
Document 335 is the second Dayton report dated 14 October 1862, printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, sent both reports to Secretary of State William H. Seward the same day.

An envoy's second letter of the day often carried the softer material: impressions, private remarks, the tone of a room. In Napoleon III's Paris, such things were policy, since one man's leanings drove the state. This report's value lies in that register, complementing the formal account in its mate. A steamer's sailing day set the legation's week, and Dayton wrote against that clock.
frus-1862-d35:
Circular No. 9 went out from the State Department on 17 March 1862. It stands as Document 35 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It belongs to the winter of the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers see how Washington kept many far-flung posts working from a single set of orders. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d435:
On 9 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Gabriel García Tassara, Spain's minister in Washington. The note is Document 435 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress with the annual message.

Seward wrote a week before Antietam, while Lee's army stood on Union soil and every foreign legation in Washington waited on the result. His notes to ministers like Tassara in those days carried a steady message: the government was unshaken and expected its rights respected. Spain, with Cuba in play, heard that message directly. The letter is part of the September file in which Seward held the diplomatic line until the army could help him.
frus-1862-d535:
Answering the Dutch minister's same-day notes, Secretary of State William H. Seward replied to Roest van Limburg on 9 June 1862. The letter is Document 535 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

Seward's answering note closed the first round of the June exchange, though the Dutch file ran on through the autumn. His method with resident ministers was to meet formal notes with formal notes, each complete in itself, so that the record could speak later. That is exactly what the printed volume does with this run of letters. A reader who follows the sequence from Document 527 gets a short, complete course. It teaches how the Union handled a friendly power's complaints during the blockade.
frus-1862-d635:
Townsend Harris, the first American minister to Japan, wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State Lewis Cass on 1 August 1860. It is Document 635 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the oldest paper in this run of the Japanese file.

Harris wrote before the Civil War, under President Buchanan. He wrote from the post he had won by the treaty of 1858. That treaty opened Japan to American trade. His letters from Edo reported the hard birth of that new relationship. Ports were opening and officials were learning new forms. A lone minister was insisting on the treaty. The State Department printed such back papers with the 1862 volume because the Japanese correspondence ran as one story across the change of administrations.
frus-1863p1-d135:
March closed as it had run, with a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams dated 28 March 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. This letter is document 135 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Seward closed the month as he had run it: by feeding the London brief in short, clear sheets. His pair of 28 March answered the flood of Adams mail that month. This letter opens the pair. It shows Washington's hand on the brief at the end of a hard month, when the ship fight and the claims all pressed at once.
frus-1863p1-d235:
Washington's orders to London on 13 July 1863 came in this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 235 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Seward's orders set the line Adams had to press on the British government. They told him what to demand, what to soften, and when to wait. It was written in the month of Gettysburg and Vicksburg, twin Union wins that changed how Europe judged the war. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d335:
In Washington on 10 December 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 335 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

The two men met and wrote constantly, and both knew a quarrel between their countries could hand the South its independence. That shared fear kept the tone correct even when the words were sharp. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d35:
Judah P. Benjamin, the Confederate secretary of state, wrote this letter to John Slidell on 26 September 1862. Slidell was the South's envoy in Paris, charged with winning French backing. The letter is document 35 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

These papers are the other side's mail: letters from Richmond's state office to its men in Europe, printed in the Union's own record. Benjamin's letters armed his envoys with the South's claims and hopes. This one shows the Confederacy's foreign push at its height. It was run from Richmond by a man who wrote with great skill for a cause that needed friends abroad.
frus-1863p1-d435:
The date 31 March 1863 heads a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the spring of 1863. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d535:
A dispatch dated 26 May 1863 went from Assistant Secretary of State F. W. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d635:
A 8 October 1863 dispatch from the American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams reached William H. Seward, Secretary of State. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the autumn of 1863.

That autumn the sharpest issue was the pair of ironclad rams built for the Confederacy at Birkenhead. Britain held them back, and this mail ran while that fight played out. Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d135: Charles Bohlen wrote a second memorandum on November 16, 1943, a week after his first in this series. It is Document 135 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Bohlen was traveling with the president's party as its Russian hand, and his papers helped shape the American approach to Stalin. The record gives the author and the date only. The memorandum is preserved in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d235:
Joint Staff Planners drafted a proposed agenda, marked Enclosure A, for President Roosevelt's first meeting with Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek at Cairo. Prepared aboard the Iowa between 15 and 19 November 1943, the paper went straight to the President and was never approved by the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

Seven items are listed for the Americans to raise. They are Chiang's account of the situation in China, China's view of Soviet help in the war, and the state of operations against Japan. The rest are Chinese aid for the north Burma campaign, air bases, supplies, and the equipping and training of Chinese forces. A second list prepares Roosevelt for Chinese questions, most of them postwar, about bases, mutual security, and continued American aid after Japan's defeat.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d335:
Assistant Secretary of War John McCloy sent Secretary of War Henry Stimson a secret priority telegram from Cairo on 27 November 1943, numbered 10064. It reports his talk of the day before with Foreign Secretary Eden about the European Advisory Commission in London.

Eden, McCloy says, plainly prizes the commission and will not see its authority cut down, and he wants a small, good American staff sent to London at once to help Ambassador Winant. In exchange, Eden agrees that the commission's draft recommendations go to the Combined Chiefs of Staff for comment before reaching governments. He also drops the push to move the Combined Civil Affairs Committee to London. McCloy calls the deal entirely satisfactory and the best arrangement possible, and asks for Stimson's views.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d35: On October 4, 1943, Roosevelt wrote to Stalin, in a letter kept as Document 35 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. October was the month the three foreign ministers were to meet in Moscow, and the leaders' letters that fall ran alongside the planning for it. The record names the date and the two men only. Printed in the Foreign Relations series, the letter forms part of the final approach to Tehran.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d435: Document 435 in the Cairo-Tehran volume is an editorial note, not a wartime paper. State Department historians wrote such notes to guide readers through the file. A note can supply background, name the people involved, or point to related papers nearby. The volume covers the Cairo and Tehran conferences of late 1943. There Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin planned the war's next phase. Readers meet this note as a signpost placed by the editors.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d535:
Ambassador Averell Harriman closed the year with another report to President Roosevelt from Moscow on December 30, 1943. It was his fourth direct cable in ten days. The State Department printed it in its Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

A year-end report from Moscow let Roosevelt take stock of the alliance as 1944, the year of the great invasion, was about to open. Harriman's stream of cables had made him the President's chief interpreter of Soviet behavior. For readers, this message ends the volume's December run with the Soviet question still at the center of Allied fortunes, exactly where Tehran had left it.
frus-1944-quebec-d135:
General William O'Dwyer, chief of the Economic Section of the Allied Control Commission for Italy, reported to Roosevelt on September 8, 1944. Years of Fascist and Nazi rule and battle destruction had left the Italian people in serious plight. His report moves through health, jobs, and transport before turning to Italy's political status.

O'Dwyer warned that malnutrition would bring serious illness between January and July 1945 unless food and shipping increased. Demolished power plants meant mass unemployment, and without food and power he foresaw rioting and anarchy. He urged ending the confusion between defeated enemy and co-belligerent, abolishing the Control Commission in liberated Italy, and handing government to the Italians and civilian experts.
frus-1944-quebec-d235:
Deane wrote to General Spaatz on September 15, 1944, urging that no date be set for reducing the American shuttle-bombing bases in Russia. The Soviets had told London they would cooperate in Warsaw aid under a prearranged plan, and Deane and Burrows had asked the Red Army staff for an immediate meeting. No Soviet reply had yet come, while the Red Army stood in Praga, across the river from Warsaw.

American participation would probably be limited to the single Frantic 7 mission, Deane judged. Even so, closing the bases now would make further missions impossible before the battle was decided. Politically, he and Harriman agreed, that would put America in a most disadvantageous position, and might suggest the insurgents had been abandoned.
frus-1944-quebec-d35:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on August 29, 1944, as the Quebec Conference came within a fortnight. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Churchill's late-August letters rehearsed the arguments he would carry to Canada: the endgame in Europe, the treatment of Germany, and Britain's place in the Pacific war. He liked to arrive at a conference with his case already stated in writing. For readers, this message shows the Prime Minister loading his brief for Quebec, in a correspondence that had become the alliance's chief instrument of decision.
frus-1945-50-intel-d135:
The National Intelligence Authority wrote to Representative Clare Hoffman on 26 June 1947. A letter from the secret board to a member of Congress is a rare outward paper in the volume. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Congress held the money and was then writing the law that would replace the authority with a statutory agency. Answering a representative's inquiry put the board's case on a new kind of record: one the public's branch could read. Readers can mark the widening circle here. A system born in secret directives now had to explain itself to legislators. It was the open season of the National Security Act, weeks before that act remade it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d235:
A memorandum from the General Counsel of the Central Intelligence Agency (Houston) reached Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter on 2 September 1948. The State Department prints it as document 235 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. It was a season of stock-taking: the CIA was a year old, and its friends and critics were both writing things down.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d335:
Formal minutes cover the 3d Meeting of the National Security Council, held on 12 December 1947. It survives in print as document 335 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. By law the CIA now stood where the Central Intelligence Group had stood, and the National Security Council sat above it.

A set of minutes does one job well. It fixes what a body took up and what it settled, in the order the items came up. Such pages are often the only proof of when a choice was made, and by whom. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d35:
Stone of the Budget Bureau wrote to Appleby, the bureau's assistant director, on 26 October 1945. The Budget Bureau's papers run through the volume like a spine. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

By late October the bureau was deep in the arithmetic of the postwar intelligence house: which units survived, at what strength, on whose budget. Stone's inside memorandum shows the bureau talking to itself as it formed the advice the president would hear. Readers should not mistake these dry papers for minor ones. In Washington, the bureau that prices a plan often decides whether the plan exists at all, and this volume proves the point repeatedly.
frus-1945-50-intel-d435:
National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 9, issued on 10 March 1950, is document 435 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The out of order date is itself a clue to how the series grew. Older numbers were revised or filled in long after higher ones appeared. Placed at the end of the volume's run of directives, No. 9 shows the Council still working through its first set of rules on the eve of the Korean War. The volume's editors placed the directives together, so readers can trace the rule book as one growth.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d135:
Ends and means for Germany's economy are set out in a briefing book paper of 11 January 1945. “Economic Policies Toward Germany” was prepared for the President's trip and is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It looks past the first occupation months to the lasting aims.

In the end, the paper says, the goals are to end German self-sufficiency and strip away the tools of economic aggression. For a long control period, policy must first cut Germany's war potential and help the victorious countries rebuild. Economic disarmament would bar the making of arms and all aircraft, wreck the special plants for them, and watch for secret war work. Limits on key goods and on metal and chemical exports are also weighed.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d235:
Wait, Stettinius advised on Iran on 18 December 1944, gently setting the President's plan aside. His memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, answers Roosevelt's direction that Harriman raise the Soviet quarrel with Stalin. News from Tehran had changed the picture.

Ambassador Morris reported on 8 December some hopeful news. Since the Iranian government resigned last month, no Russian act can clearly be read as fresh meddling. The trouble touches Iran's home affairs, where an approach now might stir the Russians to a harder policy than ever. As long as the tension may be easing, sending Harriman to Stalin would be a mistake. The Department watches events closely and keeps Harriman posted, ready when the right moment comes.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d335:
No record of what was said at this meeting has ever been found, and this note says so at the start. Times and names come only from the official trip log, which shows the talks ran until 4 p.m. Years later, in 1954, H. Freeman Matthews added a written memory of the session.

Matthews could not recall the subject. But he noted that most such meetings briefed the President on the morning's foreign ministers' session. They also readied him for the afternoon agenda. The note is honest about the hole in the record. It fills it with nothing stronger than a careful guess.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d35: New Year's Eve brought a Churchill message to Roosevelt on 31 December 1944, filed as document 35. It appears in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences, published by the Department of State. A prime minister writing on the last night of the year underlines how continuous this diplomacy was, with the winter conferences now only weeks away.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d435:
Late on February 9, 1945, after the plenary, Britain tabled its revised formula on the Polish government. A new situation, it begins, has been created by the complete liberation of Poland by the Red Army. That calls for a fully representative provisional Polish government, more broadly based than was possible before western Poland was freed.

The government should rest on the provisional government then functioning in Poland, plus other democratic Polish leaders from inside Poland and abroad. It should be called the Polish Provisional Government of National Unity. Molotov, Harriman, and Clark Kerr would consult in Moscow, first with the present government's members. This text became the spine of the final Yalta formula.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d135:
Robert Murphy reported on the delegation's housing from Hoechst on July 10, 1945. His telegram is document 135 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference, answering Washington's invitation and its request that he arrange quarters for the State Department party.

The arrangements look reasonably satisfactory, Murphy says. The Secretary will likely live in the President's villa and use a second villa as his office, with rooms for Dunn, Clayton, and Matthews. Three more villas will billet the rest of the party, each person with an individual room, and small bungalows are set aside for Harriman, Pauley, and Murphy. A small apartment house gives some twenty rooms of office space. Officers who knew Yalta and Tehran judge the setup far more convenient than those conferences.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d235:
A briefing paper urged bringing Italy back into world bodies quickly, in a paper dated July 6, 1945. The paper is document 235 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It seeks British agreement that the United States and Britain should lead in restoring Italy to international life without waiting for a final settlement of her status.

Italy should join the United Maritime Authority now, the paper argues, rather than after signing a peace treaty, as the British prefer. She should also return to the International Labor Organization. On the world security organization, it recommends asking British support for a public American pledge: if Italy declares war on Japan, Washington will back her admission at the earliest date. Such steps, it says, would raise Italian morale and strengthen moderate elements, without weakening Allied claims in the final settlement.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d335:
Agreed allied propaganda in Germany is urged in a memorandum by the Joint Staff Planners. Reports from supreme headquarters, it says, showed that clashing official announcements from the several zones had already affected German minds. In the American zone, Germans heard one version of policy; elsewhere, they heard others.

If the lack of coordination went on, the planners warned, harmful reactions could spread through every zone. The memo sets out the American policy for control of public information in Germany, agreed by the Joint Chiefs, the State Department, and the Office of War Information. Its plea is simple: the four occupiers should tell Germans one story, not four.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d35:
Molotov wrote to correct the record in this letter to Harriman of May 26, 1945, given here in translation. During that day's conversation between Stalin and Hopkins, the place for the pending heads-of-government meeting had been mentioned. It had been said that Stalin's message to Truman spoke of the region of Berlin.

For accuracy, Molotov writes, the Berlin area was named not in that message. It appeared in his own answering telegram to Joseph Davies. Davies, citing a conversation with the President, had recently raised both the meeting and its place. The letter is a footnote in ink — and a sign Moscow was already steering the summit toward Berlin.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d435:
Suggested American policy toward Poland is summarized in a briefing book extract dated June 29, 1945. On population transfers, the summary draws a firm line. The United States should help, where its aid is requested, with the transfer of minority groups. Managed movement is one thing; forced movement is another.

Washington should not permit, the paper says, the forced repatriation of Poles now in the West. Nor should it allow the uncontrolled deportation, by Poland's unilateral action, of the eight to ten million Germans formerly living in the areas claimed by the Soviet-sponsored Polish government. The extract is one section of a longer Poland paper printed in several parts.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d535: Mail weights between two embassies are reported in Ambassador Murray's airgram from Tehran of July 11, 1945. It answers a Department request of the previous December. The table gives mail sent from the American embassy at Tehran to the American embassy at Moscow in June 1945. Figures are in pounds, for June 9, June 25, and June 30. Courier mail totaled 1,011 pounds. Navy courier mail made up 648 of that. Non-courier mail totaled 3,199 pounds, with 251 pounds of Navy mail inside it.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d635:
James Dunn, an Assistant Secretary of State, sent Secretary Byrnes a memo from Potsdam on July 14, 1945. Extracts form document 635 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers. Dunn reports a two-hour talk that day with Sir Alexander Cadogan, the top career man in Britain's Foreign Office.

The extract kept here covers Iran. Cadogan set out Britain's wish to get out of Persia, as the text also calls Iran. London proposed a concerted withdrawal of British and Soviet forces by stages, starting with Tehran. British officers wanted a small force left to guard the oil fields. Foreign Secretary Eden, Cadogan said, would insist all troops go, leaving a trained police force, if that would coax the Russians to withdraw in full. Cadogan warmly backed a gradual exit by all three forces.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1035: Ambassador John Winant sent this telegram from London to Philip Mosely at Potsdam on July 18, 1945. It is the full text of the message printed in extract just earlier in the volume. Winant reports that no word has reached the Soviet embassy in London from Moscow. Without that word, the Soviet side cannot clear or sign two pending papers. One is the agreement on additional requirements to be imposed on Germany. The other amends the agreement on zones of occupation in Germany.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1135:
From London, Ambassador Winant cabled the Acting Secretary of State on 23 July 1945. A week into the Potsdam talks, his embassy kept up its reports on British politics and press response to the summit. The election that would change Britain's government hung over every report.

Winant's dispatches gave Washington a read on its closest ally that no other post could give. He knew the British leaders, their parties, and their press at first hand. This cable is one part of that running London account. It helped the home office judge how much weight British words at the table would carry at home.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1235:
A second Sato cable to Togo bears the date 25 July 1945. The pair of reports shows the Moscow embassy working to the last hour before the Allied terms appeared. Sato summed up his channel's state: open in form, empty in fact.

The exchange between these two men is the volume's secret spine. Allied leaders read it through codebreaking while they weighed how to end the Pacific war. Each Sato report told them Japan's bid for Soviet help was failing. This one, from the eve of the declaration, confirmed it. Tokyo would face the Allied terms with its Moscow hope already spent.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1335:
From Tehran, Ambassador Wallace Murray sent a second cable in two days to the acting secretary of state, dated 28 July 1945. His post in Iran put him close to Soviet and British moves in the region. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Back-to-back cables from one embassy show a post working a fast-moving story, not a single event. Readers can watch how an ambassador framed facts for Washington readers who were busy with the Potsdam talks. The pair of Murray cables, read together, gives a ground-level view of diplomacy in Iran at the end of the Second World War.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-135:
Emile Despres, adviser on German economic affairs, wrote this memorandum on July 29, 1945. Germany's economy lay at the center of the Potsdam bargaining. What the beaten country could produce, pay, and export shaped every other question. Despres gave the delegation expert counsel on that ground. His memo was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

An adviser's memo states a problem and weighs the choices. Despres wrote as a specialist for men who had to decide quickly. Readers see the economic thread of the talks in expert hands. The paper shows how deeply the settlement rested on questions of coal, food, factories, and cash.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-35:
Department of State minutes record the foreign ministers' meeting of July 20, 1945, at 11:30 a.m. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Molotov sat in the chair, and the morning's story was mostly one of papers not ready.

The German economic paper came first on the agenda, but it was not yet finished. The question had to go over until tomorrow. The Polish paper was no further along, Vyshinsky reported. His committee had met the day before and that morning without producing a report, though he hoped for results by night. The third item, the Council of Foreign Ministers, bred a procedural tangle instead. Byrnes thought a subcommittee had the draft in hand. Molotov answered that no subcommittee had been appointed, and asked whether a general drafting committee covered all questions.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d735:
Byrnes wrote to Grew, his acting deputy in Washington, on July 21, 1945, in document 735. The Secretary reported from the conference's first week. Grew needed the feel of the talks, not just their texts. This letter kept the home office aligned. It was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Letters from the Secretary to his deputy show trust in action. Byrnes could not run Washington from Potsdam, so he armed the man who did. Readers learn what the travelers thought worth cabling home. The document also reveals workload: a summit abroad and a department at home, bound by a daily flow of paper.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d835:
Kennan answered the Acting Secretary from Moscow on July 17, 1945, in document 835. The chargé replied as the Potsdam Conference opened in Germany. Kennan's letters from this period are prized for their clarity. This one joined the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

A Kennan reply joined reporting to judgment. He did not merely list events; he read them. Readers get the Soviet capital interpreted by its sharpest American observer. The document shows the embassy's value while its chief bargained abroad. Moscow still had a voice in Washington that week, and it spoke in Kennan's prose.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d935:
William Clayton's statistical paper of July 26, 1945, works through the math of one-time reparations removals. It finds 40 percent of German factory and mining output in the Russian zone. Most of that industry, though, uses small units of light trades like textiles and printing, which peacetime Germany should keep.

The zone's true removal potential is therefore put at 30 percent. The Ruhr holds 42 percent of the German total. If Russia is owed half of all removals, 20 percent must come from elsewhere. The paper proposes assigning half the Ruhr removals, with only half of that counted as reparations. The rest would be traded for goods from the Russian zone.
frus-1969-76v17-d135: A 1969-1976 FRUS editorial note on the final arrangements for the China opening. The trip. This note provides that context. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.

gao-gaoreports-gao-06-535: America's message to Muslim audiences needed work in 2006, and GAO's report says State Department efforts lacked key communication elements. The findings target the gaps. The report warns that the diplomacy of persuasion needed sharper tools. The efforts had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-635: Medicare's cancer-seed payments needed a new formula in 2006, and GAO's report says rates for the radioactive sources could be set prospectively. The findings do the math. gao-gaoreports-gao-06-735: Visa bids tied to sex crimes got a GAO review in 2006, and the report weighs when the crimes may be told to the hopeful migrant. The findings parse the policy. The report warns that the newcomers deserved to know the truth. The rules had to be clear.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1035: No Child Left Behind left schools guessing in 2007 — GAO's report says the Education Department owed clearer rules and a harder look at compliance traps. The findings walk the line between high standards and fair play for the schools graded under the landmark law.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-335: The Capitol's preservation purse got audited in 2007, and GAO's report grades the fund's financial statements for 2005 and 2004. The findings deliver the formal opinion for the record. The report shows the marble halls get the same ledger check as the war rooms.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-35: Farm conservation for endangered species needed coordination in 2007, and GAO's report shares stakeholder views on participation. The findings gather the voices. The report warns that the plow and the prairie chicken needed a truce. The programs had to work together.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-535: College sports were booming in 2007 — GAO's report tracks the trends in NCAA teams and players. The findings lay out who played what, where the growth ran, and what the money looked like. The report brings data to the eternal campus debate: big-time sports, big-time questions.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-735: Customs needed better data to catch fakes in 2007 — GAO's report says sharper analysis would help the border agency fight counterfeits. The findings press for smarter targeting of shipments. The report's logic: the knockoff trade leaves tracks, if anyone bothers to look.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-35: This 2007 Government Accountability Office report looks at state and local fusion centers — the offices where police, federal agents, and analysts share intelligence about terrorism and crime. GAO found federal help was easing some of the centers' growing pains, from funding to data access. The report takes stock of an intelligence-sharing experiment that grew rapidly after 9/11 and asks whether Washington's support was keeping up.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-535: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at VA Health Care: Facilities Have Taken Action to Provide Language Access Services and Culturally Appropriate Care to a Diverse Veteran Population.
