gautier-mademoiselle-maupin-1835:
Theophile Gautier published Mademoiselle de Maupin in 1835, a French novel famous for its preface as well as its story. The preface argues that art need not serve morals or use. In the tale, a young woman travels disguised as a man named Theodore. Two lovers are drawn to Theodore without knowing the truth.

Letters and confessions slowly reveal desires that cross the lines of the age. Gautier writes lush, jeweled prose about beauty in all its forms. The novel shocked many readers of its time. Its defense of art for art's sake shaped later writers, including Oscar Wilde. It remains a landmark of French Romantic fiction.
gogol-taras-bulba-1835:
Nikolai Gogol published Taras Bulba in 1835, a historical novel about Cossacks in Ukraine. Old Taras is a fierce Cossack leader with two sons, Ostap and Andriy. He takes them to the Cossack camp and then to war against Poland. Battles, raids, and sieges fill the story.

Andriy falls in love with a Polish noblewoman and betrays his own side. Taras must answer that betrayal in the harshest way. Ostap shows steady courage to the end. Gogol writes with energy and pride in Cossack freedom. The book is a rousing, violent tale of loyalty, family, and war on the steppe.
hor-phrenologic-being-three-phrenologica: Horae phrenologicae, three phrenological essays, 1835. The phrenological hours. This book preserves that work. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
hutcheson-considerations-on-patronages-1:
Francis Hutcheson published his Considerations on Patronages in 1735, entering a live fight in the Church of Scotland. Lay patrons claimed the right to appoint parish ministers, while many churchmen held that congregations should choose their own pastors. Hutcheson, a Glasgow professor and Presbyterian minister's son, defended the church's side.

The pamphlet argues from both Scripture and the nature of religious office that forced appointments corrupt the ministry. It joins deep thought about conscience and authority to the hard politics of Scottish church life. Hutcheson is better known as the philosopher of the moral sense, and that wider thought shows here in his care for free consent. The piece shows the Scottish Enlightenment at work in the pulpit's defense, where philosophy met parish quarrels.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-metals-10735:
Metals known to the ancient Hebrews — gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, and lead — are surveyed in a Jewish Encyclopedia article by Joseph Jacobs and Samuel Krauss, published in 1906. It opens with a puzzle: Deuteronomy calls the Promised Land rich in ore, yet Palestine itself had almost no metals and imported nearly all of them.

Section by section, the article traces where each metal came from, from gold of Ophir to iron from the north, and unpacks the Hebrew names and Talmudic lore for each. Gold gets seven Talmudic varieties, silver doubles as the word for money, and tin likely arrived through Phoenician trade. Later parts list metal terms in the Talmud, from unstamped silver coins to Corinthian brass.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-milk-hebrew-hal:
Milk in the Bible and Talmud is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia article by Isidore Singer, Julius H. Greenstone, and Cyrus Adler, published in 1906. A land flowing with milk and honey is its most famous phrase: milk stands for life's necessities, honey for its luxuries. The article gathers every kind of evidence, from poetry to dairy practice.

Goats and sheep supplied most of Israel's milk, the writers note, because the hill country suited cows poorly, so cows' milk stays rare in the text. Milk was kept in buckets and skins and served as a refreshing drink at meals, as Abraham served his guests in Genesis. Ben Sira ranked it among the principal things needed for human life, and Deborah called it a cup fit for nobles.
mellon-ms-6-alchemical-miscellany-1435: Mellon MS 6, Alchemical miscellany, 1435. The medieval miscellany. This book preserves that manuscript. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
nasa-tm-19680016260-lunar-explorer-35: In July 1967, NASA parked a satellite in orbit around the Moon — Explorer 35. This 1968 report covers Lunar Explorer 35 and its mission to measure the Moon's magnetic fields, particles, and plasma. The orbiter mapped the lunar environment for Apollo's planners.
on-the-functions-of-the-brain-and-of-eac: On the Functions of the Brain, 1835. The brain's functions. This book preserves that work. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Later readers can locate it. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
openalex-w1999469035: Pressed plants are treasure chests of DNA — if you can unlock them. A 2012 study compared DNA extraction protocols to boost yield from herbarium specimens. The head-to-head test found the best way to open the chest.
openalex-w2027420135: Ecologists compare species counts — but the stats are tricky. A 2013 study tackled the problem with calls based on overlapping confidence bands. The paper gave ecologists a sound way to judge real differences in richness.
openalex-w2076380535: Soybeans fight drought with chemistry. A 2012 study compared chemical shifts in tough and tender soybean types under water stress. The work mapped the shifts behind the tough plants' edge in the field and greenhouse.
openalex-w2098635935: Ecology needs indigenous partners — not just subjects. A 2014 paper calls for deeper ties between university and indigenous community partners in fieldwork. The work laid out principles for genuine teamwork in the field — respect first, data second.
openalex-w2136004435: ICU delirium is common — data was local. A 2010 study studied delirium in critical care worldwide. The one-day survey mapped a frequent source of ICU harm — confusion, counted at last now — the ICU's hidden plague.
openalex-w2144820135: Primates got a DNA family tree. A 2011 paper built a molecular phylogeny of living primates. The genomic work tackled a complex, messy taxonomy with little consensus — our family, sorted at last for all — primates' true tree.
openalex-w2224020635: Counting the particles born in lead-lead collisions tells physicists about the hot matter they create. This 2013 Physical Review C paper measures how many pions, kaons, and protons emerge at mid-rapidity in 2.76 TeV collisions, tracking how the yields change from peripheral to central hits. The species-by-species breakdown probes how the quark-gluon plasma cools into ordinary matter.
openalex-w2253902135: Soil microbes run the planet's life-support systems — but does having more kinds of microbes mean ecosystems do more jobs at once? openalex-w2308570835: In the debris of LHC collisions, protons and neutrons sometimes stick together into light nuclei — even antimatter ones. This 2016 Physical Review C paper studies production of (anti-)deuterons and (anti-)helium-3 in lead-lead collisions with the ALICE detector. The spectra harden with collision centrality, and combined fits probe how these fragile clusters assemble in the fireball's aftermath.
openalex-w2606932135: The heartbeat's strength is tuned by cAMP signals confined to nanoscale neighborhoods inside heart cells. openalex-w2800397035: Cognitive load theory was built for solo learners — but much learning happens in groups. The collaborative cognitive load theory explains when working together helps thinking — and when it just adds overhead.
openalex-w2962705835: Severe RSV infection kills infants — but a high-fiber diet protected mice, via gut microbes. openalex-w2974427135: Electrons and photons trigger the recording of everything from Higgs decays to exotic searches. This 2020 European Physical Journal C paper evaluates ATLAS electron and photon trigger performance during Run 2, spanning 5 GeV to several TeV. openalex-w4391112535: Secondary prevention after heart disease prevents recurrences — yet practice lags guidelines. openalex-w7172453835: Strong legs keep the elderly independent. This study followed 93 adults, median age 85, for a year to link function-focused training with leg strength. The authors measured the payoff of targeted exercise. A geriatrics study of training that keeps people on their feet.
openalex-w7206152235: Paperwork runs a police force, and in Alagoas the military police handle theirs through Brazil's electronic information system, the SEI. This paper studies how administrative processes are managed there and proposes a complementary management system to fix gaps the author found. It is a practical piece of public-administration engineering: part diagnosis of how the current digital workflow falls short, part blueprint for improving it.
openalex-w7214901235: Hard ceramics shatter, yet at tiny scales they can bend. This review sums up new work on bendability at room heat in oxide ceramics: nano poke tests and atom models. The authors tied inner structure to flex. A materials review of brittle stuff learning to give.
philip-dru-administrator-a-story-of-tomo: Written anonymously by Colonel Edward House — President Wilson's closest adviser — this political novel imagines a benevolent strongman remaking America. Philip Dru seizes power to enact sweeping reforms, from banking to labor laws. Part utopia, part warning, it is a fascinating glimpse into progressive-era dreams of government.
plos-pbio-0020235:
Jess H. Leber, Sebastián Bernales, and Peter Walter studied a cell stress response in yeast for PLOS Biology in 2004. When misfolded proteins pile up in a cell compartment called the endoplasmic reticulum, the cell mounts the unfolded protein response. A sensor named IRE1 is its best-known trigger.

The team found a way the response can be tuned even without IRE1. That backup gain control shocked a field that saw IRE1 as the sole master switch. Extra control layers make the response more flexible, able to match its strength to the load. The finding is basic cell biology with wide reach, since this stress response is tied to diabetes, cancer, and brain disease.
plos-pone-0000035:
Cristina Aguayo-Mazzucato, Carmen Sanchez-Soto, Victoria Godinez-Puig, and co-authors studied the insulin system in the first days of life for a 2006 paper. Pancreatic islets are the small clusters of cells that make insulin. After birth they are rebuilt as the body shifts from life in the womb to feeding on its own.

The team tracked that restructuring inside a postnatal critical window, a short period when the islets change shape and reset how they release insulin. Windows like this matter for diabetes research: faults laid down in the first days can echo for a lifetime. The study maps what normal development looks like so that abnormal development can be recognized.
plos-pone-0000135:
Priya Chikhlikar, Luciana Barros de Arruda, Milton Maciel, and colleagues published this vaccine study in PLOS ONE in 2006. They built a DNA vaccine that joins an HIV-1 protein, Gag, to a human protein called LAMP-1. The team tested this chimera in rhesus macaques, monkeys used as a stand-in for human immune responses.

As the title reports, the vaccine drew out a broad immune response, both cellular and antibody-based. Blending a viral protein with a routing protein is a trick meant to show the virus to more parts of the immune system. The results informed later work on DNA vaccine design against HIV.
plos-pone-0000235:
Javier Pérez-Tris, Olof Hellgren, Asta Križanauskienė, and colleagues published this parasitology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It studies within-host speciation of malaria parasites, the splitting of one parasite lineage into distinct species inside a single host animal. That idea challenges the usual picture of species splitting across separated places.

If new malaria species can arise side by side in one bird or mammal, parasite diversity may grow faster than expected. The authors present evidence bearing on that process. The work matters for tracking the many malaria relatives in wild animals, some of which can cross into new hosts.
plos-pone-0000335:
Stefan Wuchty published this network biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. The interactome is the web of interactions between a cell's proteins. Studying the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum, the author examines its rich-club phenomenon. This is a core of highly connected proteins that also connect to each other. He asks whether it is an artifact of the data or a signature of the parasite's lifestyle.

Malaria parasites live inside host cells and rewire them, which could shape their protein web. Distinguishing a real signature from a data artifact is the paper's task. The answer bears on using network maps to find drug targets in the parasite.
plos-pone-0000435:
Bjoern Seidel and colleagues tested whether a prion disease can wait in soil and still infect, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Scrapie is a fatal brain disease of sheep caused by prions, misfolded proteins that resist breakdown. The team used strain 263K and asked whether it can transmit disease by the oral route after persisting in soil over years.

Their title states the answer: yes, it can. Soil-bound prions would explain how pastures stay infectious long after sick animals are gone, a serious problem for farmers and wildlife managers. The work adds hard evidence to fears that prion contamination of land is durable and hard to clean.
plos-pone-0000535:
Toomas Timpka and colleagues wrote a protocol for spotting toddlers headed for lasting obesity, published in PLOS ONE in 2007. Their high-precision protocol identifies preschool children at risk for persisting obesity, the kind that does not resolve as the child grows. The aim is to target help where it will matter most.

Most heavy toddlers slim down; a minority carry obesity into adult life with its disease risks. A precise protocol avoids both missing that minority and labeling the majority wrongly. Prevention programs are expensive to run for everyone, so risk identification decides whether early intervention is practical at all.
plos-pone-0000635:
Keizo Sugaya, Shiro Matsubara, Yasuhiro Kagamihara and colleagues studied a mutation tied to Huntington's disease onset, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The mutation stretches a polyglutamine tract, a run of one amino acid repeated too many times. Stretched proteins can change shape, misfold, and gather into aggregates such as amyloid fibrils, which are toxic to cells.

The team reports that the expansion creates a pathological epitope, a distinctive patch the immune system can recognize. That patch is linked to nucleation, the first seed from which aggregates grow. Pinpointing the seed step matters, because blocking nucleation could, in principle, delay the disease whose onset this patch helps set.
plos-pone-0000735:
Mathias Streitz, Lydia Tesfa, Vedat Yildirim and colleagues looked for a blood-cell sign of active tuberculosis, in PLOS ONE in 2007. T-cell responses to tuberculin have low diagnostic specificity in populations vaccinated with BCG. Tests using subunit antigens such as ESAT-6 and CFP-10 can diagnose latent infection. No reliable immunological test, though, could confirm active pulmonary tuberculosis.

The title reports their marker: tuberculin-reactive T cells lose a certain surface receptor in active disease. A test separating active from latent infection changes treatment decisions and contact tracing. Patients with active disease need urgent therapy and isolation; latent carriers need a different path entirely.
plos-pone-0000835:
Tomohisa Horibe and Nicholas J. Hoogenraad found a control switch for the cell's response to stress inside its mitochondria. Mitochondria are the cell's power plants. When bad, unfolded proteins pile up inside them, the cell nucleus turns on genes for helper proteins that clean up the mess. The team had helped find this response, called the mitochondrial unfolded protein response, in mammal cells.

Their title reports that the Chop gene holds an element that boosts this response. One stretch in one gene's control zone thus helps run a whole stress program. That is a firm handle on a pathway that counts in aging and in diseases where nerve cells die. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2007.
plos-pone-0000935:
Miriam Podtschaske, Uwe Benary, Sandra Zwinger and colleagues showed how T cells turn a graded signal into an all or none reply, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Making interleukin-2 is a key step when helper T cells switch on. It drives their growth and shapes both attack cells and the regulatory cells that calm them.

The team found that inside each cell, activation of the factor NFATc2 is digital: fully on or fully off. Stronger stimulation recruits more cells rather than pushing each cell harder. That design keeps responses decisive instead of half hearted. It also changes how immune drugs and vaccines should be judged, cell by cell.
plos-pone-0001035:
Matthew Loza, Charles McCall, Liwu Li and colleagues assembled a gene set for studying inflammation genetics, in PLOS ONE in 2007. New links keep appearing between inflammation gene variants and common diseases. Testing those genes fairly requires a systematic list, not a grab bag of favorites.

The team gathered inflammation related genes into a pathway focused panel for genetic analysis. A defined panel lets studies compare results on the same ground. It also keeps attention on genes with a plausible shared role, rather than scattered single hits. Their assembly work is infrastructure: unglamorous, and exactly what later association studies stand on.
plos-pone-0001135:
Cutting out a tumor is not always possible, so doctors look for ways to kill one in place. Bassim Al-Sakere and co-authors report an early test of such a method in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The method is irreversible electroporation, which uses short, strong electric pulses to destroy tissue without heat.

The team reports the first successful use of the technique against aggressive skin tumors implanted in mice, with minimal invasion. Because the pulses do not cook tissue, nearby structures may be spared in ways heat-based methods cannot manage. The paper is a proof of concept in animals, not yet a human treatment.
plos-pone-0001235:
Rice feeds half the world and serves as the model plant for cereal genomics. Kouji Satoh and colleagues mapped the full-length copies of its genes and measured their activity, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Rice has a considerably smaller genome than other monocots, which made it the first cereal sequenced.

Accurate genome sequences of the indica and japonica varieties existed, but knowing where genes start and end, and when they switch on, needed more work. The authors combine full-length cDNA mapping with microarray expression analysis to describe gene organization in rice. Such maps underpin breeding and functional studies.
plos-pone-0001335:
Some tuberculosis is smear-negative: the standard microscope test cannot see it, and diagnosis is hard. Blood-based immune assays had shown promise for such cases. Ronan Breen and colleagues combined immune tests and sputum checks in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Lung fluid sampling lets both kinds of test run at once. Until now, that had only been possible with invasive procedures.

The authors report rapid diagnosis of smear-negative tuberculosis using this combined approach, in people with and without HIV. With HIV, such disease is more common and more deadly. A fast route to diagnosis that avoids invasive sampling fills a real gap.
plos-pone-0001435:
Jeffrey Bhasin and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on sex based gene control in mouse immune cells. Many trait gene sites act in one sex but not the other. Why that is so was not well known. The team read gene use in immune cells from a cross of mouse strains, split by sex.

They mapped sites where gene variants steer gene use in a sex linked way. The maps show that males and females run some of the same genes on unlike settings. That helps explain why some ills and drug effects split by sex. It also urges care in pooling male and female data in gene studies.
plos-pone-0001535:
Say Viengchareun and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on milk hormones and brown fat in newborns. The hormone prolactin and kin drive breeding and milk making. Their receptor is rich in brown fat, the tissue that burns fuel for heat. Yet its job in fat was not known. The team tested mice that lack the receptor.

They show the signal is vital for brown fat work around birth. A growth factor acts as a key go between in that path. Newborns rely on brown fat to hold body heat. The work thus ties a breeding hormone to a core survival task in the young.
plos-pone-0001635:
Jacob N. Barney, Thomas H. Whitlow, and Arthur J. Lembo rebuilt the invasion history of two non-native plant species for a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Records of where invading plants spread, and when, are rarely kept well, which makes invasion patterns hard to study at the scale of whole regions. The team turned to herbarium records, the pressed plant specimens stored by botanical collections.

By mapping dated specimens and studying the spatial trend, they traced how each species moved across the landscape over time. The full text gives the maps, the likely entry points, and the places the authors flag as at risk of future invasion. Land managers can use such reconstructions to spot where a plant will spread next and where control work is best spent first.
plos-pone-0001735:
Simone Kurt, Anke Deutscher, John M. Crook, and their co-authors modeled how the hearing brain separates sounds in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The brain breaks the world into discrete objects of perception. When similar objects appear at once, it must segregate and selectively address them. Models aim to solve this with winner-take-all circuits, where the strongest signal suppresses the rest.

The team studied global winner-take-all inhibitory interactions in auditory cortex and how they enhance contrast between sounds. The full text gives the model and the neural data it explains. Sharper contrast in hearing helps listeners follow one voice in a crowd, and the same principle guides design of hearing devices and speech software.
plos-pone-0001835:
Dick S. J. Groenenberg, Albert J. Beintema, René W. R. J. Dekker, and their co-authors used ancient DNA to settle a bird dispute in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. A persistent controversy surrounds the flightless island hen of Tristan da Cunha, Gallinula nesiotis. Some believe it went extinct by the end of the nineteenth century; others suppose it still inhabits Tristan. The status of the related name Gallinula comeri was also disputed.

DNA from museum specimens let the team test the hens' identity and relationships. The full text gives the sequences and the family tree. Ancient DNA turns museum skins into evidence, resolving extinction questions that field surveys alone cannot answer.
plos-pone-0001935:
Yoni Haitin and co-authors probed how a heart and nerve channel senses voltage, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The channel, Kv7.1, opens and shuts in response to electric charge, and faults in it cause disease. Its voltage sensor is a helix called S4 that moves when the charge shifts, which in turn works the channel gate.

How S4 moves was unclear. The team swapped single building blocks of S4 for a tagged form and tracked the effects. They report that a second helix, S1, constrains S4 in the sensor. A clearer picture of the sensor helps explain channel faults and may guide drugs that tune them.
plos-pone-0002035:
Jing-xin Zhang, Gretchen Diehl, and Dan Littman worked on making mouse T cells host HIV, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. A small animal model of HIV would speed drug and vaccine work, but the virus fails to copy itself in non-primate cells. Most past work used fibroblast cell lines, not the T cells the virus attacks in people.

The team relieved a block that stops HIV before it joins the host genome, and charted further blocks in primary mouse T cells. Each block named is a step a model must clear. The study shows how many locks keep HIV a primate virus.
plos-pone-0002135:
Yuyan Zhu, Huayan Hou, William Nikolic, and co-authors studied brain immune cells in Alzheimer's disease, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Microglia are the brain's own defense cells, and in this disease they switch on in ways that may harm nerve cells. Signals through pathways called MAPK drive much of that response when the cells meet amyloid-beta, the protein that builds up in patients' brains.

Earlier work by the group showed that a surface protein called CD45 calms this response. Here they point to a related form, CD45RB, as a drug target. Adjusting it might lower the harmful side of microglial activity while leaving the brain's defenses in place.
plos-pone-0002235:
Petra van der Stoop and co-authors asked what a chromatin protein does for mouse embryonic stem cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Ring1b, also called Rnf2, is a core part of Polycomb repressive complex 1, a system that switches genes off by marking histone H2A. Embryos cannot develop properly without it.

To learn its role in early development, the team studied Ring1b in mouse embryonic stem cells, the cells that can form any tissue. They report that it helps keep those cells stable in their undifferentiated state. The finding ties a gene-silencing machine to the balance stem cells strike between staying young and growing up.
plos-pone-0002335:
Jacques Prudhomme, Eric McDaniel, Nadia Ponts, and co-authors mined sea bacteria for new malaria drugs, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Malaria kills about 2 million people a year. Rising drug resistance and the lack of an efficient vaccine make fast, broad antimalarial drug discovery urgent.

The team turned to marine actinomycetes, bacteria famed for producing antibiotics, as a new source of compounds against the human malaria parasite. Ocean microbes make chemical defenses unlike those of land species, so their extracts may hold scaffolds the parasite has never met. Screening programs like this widen the pipeline for a disease that keeps outrunning its medicines.
plos-pone-0002435:
Huurman and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Volkert A. L. Huurman, Robert Hilbrands, Gabriëlle G. M. Pinkse, among others. Its subject is cellular Islet Autoimmunity Associates with Clinical Outcome of Islet Cell Transplantation. Islet cell transplantation can cure type 1 diabetes (T1D), but only a minority of recipients remains insulin–independent in the following years.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002535:
Siawaya joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Joel Fleury Djoba Siawaya, Teri Roberts, Chantal Babb, among others. Its subject is an Evaluation of Commercial Fluorescent Bead-Based Luminex Cytokine Assays.

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002635:
Jason Ivanoff and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was fMRI evidence for a dual process account of the Speed-Accuracy tradeoff in Decision-Making. The catalog record names Jason Ivanoff first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. The speed and accuracy of decision-making have a well-known trading relationship: hasty decisions are more prone to errors while careful. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002735:
A 2008 study by Patricia Chastagner and colleagues in PLOS ONE takes up AIP4/Itch regulates notch receptor degradation in the absence of ligand. Authorship is credited in the record to Patricia Chastagner and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. The regulation of Notch signaling heavily relies on ubiquitination events. It goes on to note a further point. Drosophila Su(dx), a member of the HECT family of ubiquitin-ligases, has been described as a negative regulator of Notch signaling. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002835:
K. Mathias Wegner and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on clustering of drosophila melanogaster immune genes in interplay with recombination rate. The full author list in the catalog record begins with K. Mathias Wegner, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Gene order in eukaryotic chromosomes is not random and has been linked to coordination of gene expression, chromatin structure and also recombination rate. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002935:
José Rodríguez, Victoria Jones, Masashi Tabuchi and co-authors studied new neuron growth in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease in 2008. In adult mammals, new neurons are added mainly in two brain areas. One is the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus, a region central to learning and memory.

In a triple transgenic mouse carrying Alzheimer's-linked changes, growth of new neurons in that region was impaired. The title states that result plainly. Published in PLOS ONE, the finding links the disease model to a loss in the brain's own renewal, which may worsen memory failure.
plos-pone-0003035:
Tarja Sironen, Jonas Klingström, Antti Vaheri and co-authors described Puumala hantavirus pathology in macaques in 2008. Hantaviruses cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and a lung syndrome in people worldwide. Leaking capillaries sit at the center of these diseases, but how the leak develops had remained unknown.

Macaques offer a close model of human infection. The PLOS ONE study sets out the pathology of Puumala infection in them, testing ideas about how the disease unfolds. A faithful animal picture is a step toward treatments for a virus group with few options. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003135: Igor F. Tsigelny and colleagues published a PLOS ONE study in 2008 on how hybrid oligomers, mixed clusters of proteins, form. The title links that process to the joint development of Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease in the brain. No abstract text beyond the title was supplied, so this record states no methods or findings.
plos-pone-0003235:
Yuji Yoshiike, Ryoichi Minai, Yo Matsuo and colleagues study amyloid oligomer shape in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Recent in vitro and in vivo studies suggest that destabilized proteins with defective folding induce aggregation and toxicity in protein-misfolding diseases. One such unstable protein state is called amyloid oligomer, a precursor of fully aggregated forms of amyloid. Detection of these oligomers was the challenge addressed.

The authors examine amyloid oligomer conformation in a group of natively folded proteins. Readers learn how a toxic intermediate can arise even from proteins that normally fold well. That idea widens the search for what makes proteins dangerous in diseases like Alzheimer's.
plos-pone-0003335:
Ismael Galván and Carlos Alonso-Alvarez link an antioxidant to a bird signal in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. To understand how traits used in animal communication evolved and are maintained as honest signals, researchers need to understand mechanisms that prevent cheating. It has been proposed that honest signaling is guaranteed by costs associated with signal expression. The team test a cellular cost mechanism.

The title reports that an intracellular antioxidant determines expression of a melanin-based signal in a bird. Readers learn how a bird's internal chemistry could keep its colour badge honest. Costly signals are a central idea in how animal displays can be trusted.
plos-pone-0003435:
Kuo-Liong Chien and co-authors followed heart risk in Chinese adults for this 2008 study. They measured the wall thickness of the carotid artery in the neck. They also noted plaque, fatty buildup inside that artery. Data on these measures were still limited for Chinese groups.

The team ran a community cohort and tracked new disease over time. Thicker walls and plaque each pointed to more heart disease and stroke ahead. Both signs came before illness, not after it. Simple neck scans may flag at-risk adults early in this population. Both measures can be taken with a painless neck scan rather than any surgery.
plos-pone-0003535:
Tamara E. King and co-authors built a model of prostate cancer in bone for this 2008 paper. Cancers of prostate, breast, and lung often spread to bone. Tumor cells grip bone using adhesion receptors called integrins. That spread also causes severe, hard-to-treat bone pain.

Their new xenograft model placed human cancer in mice for study. A receptor, alpha 6 integrin, played roles in migration and bone pain. The model lets drug hunters test pain relief in a living system. It ties tumor movement and suffering to one molecule. Bone pain is often the worst part of late prostate cancer for patients.
plos-pone-0003635:
Akira Katoh, Peter J. Chapman, and Jennifer L. Raymond published this neuroscience study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Good movement needs control of both force and timing, and timing can improve with practice. The team asked which molecules let animals learn that timing. They worked with mutant mice.

Mice with faulty P/Q-type calcium channels could not adjust the timing of their movements through learning. Normal signaling through these channels was needed for that change. The result ties a basic skill, learning when to move, to one type of channel in the brain's motor circuits.
plos-pone-0003735:
Benjamin J. Dubin-Thaler, Jake M. Hofman, Yunfei Cai, and colleagues published this cell mechanics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Actin-based movement and force drive immune response, tissue building, and cancer spread. Cell spreading is a favorite model for studying that machinery. The team measured it with care.

They quantified how fast cell edges move and how hard cells pull on their substrate. The numbers revealed distinct motility modules, separate units of the spreading process. Breaking crawling into parts gives researchers targets for work on immunity, development, and metastasis. Each module can now be studied, and perhaps tuned, on its own.
plos-pone-0003835:
So-ichi Tamai, Kamon Sanada, and Yoshitaka Fukada published this neuroscience study in PLOS ONE in 2008. New neurons are born throughout adult life in a few brain regions, including the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus. There, progenitor cells keep dividing and giving rise to fresh neurons. Brain clocks shape much of this tissue's activity.

The team found that adult neurogenesis in the hippocampus depends on the time of day. The birth of new neurons rose at certain hours and fell at others. The rhythm suggests the brain schedules its own renewal by the daily clock.
plos-pone-0003935:
Stefan Kempa, Julia Krasensky, Silvia Dal Santo, and co-authors studied a plant stress hormone in 2008. Dryness, salt, and cold all harm plant growth and yield. The hormone abscisic acid, or ABA, guides how plants respond to such stress. Its role in switching genes on was already well established.

Their PLOS ONE article gives ABA a central role in sugar handling under stress. Plants shift how they store and use carbohydrates when conditions worsen. Linking that shift to ABA helps explain how plants budget energy in drought. Crop scientists can use the insight in breeding tougher plants.
plos-pone-0004035:
Daniel Rubinoff and Johannes J. Le Roux examined sudden leaps in moth evolution in 2008. Saltational evolution means a lineage changes fast and far beyond its relatives. Gradual change is the dominant model in evolutionary biology. Sudden leaps are rarely invoked as an alternative.

Their PLOS ONE article reports evidence in the sphinx moth genus Proserpinus. Repeated and independent leaps appear in that peculiar group. Documenting such events tests the limits of gradual models. The moths offer a rare case where rapid change left clear traces. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004135:
Wai Fook Leong and colleagues published this bone study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Osteoporosis, a disease of weak bones, is among the most common of all diseases. Drugs can slow bone loss or build new bone, and finding targets for bone-building drugs requires knowing how bone-forming cells, called osteoblasts, mature.

The study looks at palmitoylation, the attaching of a fatty molecule to proteins, and its effect on osteoblast growth. The authors report that this process controls how a signal protein called BMP switches on Osterix, a factor osteoblasts need to mature. The result names a possible new target for drugs that build bone.
plos-pone-0004235:
Yonatan Mahller and colleagues published this childhood cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Neuroblastoma, a tumour of young children, often goes into remission but commonly relapses. The cancer stem cell theory blames rare tumour-initiating cells that resist conventional therapy and regrow the tumour.

The team report that neuroblastoma cell lines contain pluripotent tumour-initiating cells, cells able to make many cell types and seed new tumours. They also show these cells are susceptible to a targeted oncolytic virus, a virus engineered to attack cancer. A therapy that reaches the relapse-causing cells could change this disease.
plos-pone-0004335:
Elsa Youngsteadt and colleagues published this Amazon ecology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Across lowland Amazonia, arboreal ants collect the seeds of specific plants and cultivate them in nutrient-rich nests. These ant-gardens are diverse yet obligate and species-specific symbioses: the ants depend on their plants for nest stability, and the plants depend on the ants.

The team studied species-specific seed dispersal in this mutualism, asking how ants choose the right seeds. A gardener that plants only its own crop keeps the partnership pure. The study shows the precision inside one of the tropics' neatest arrangements.
plos-pone-0004435:
Routine liver blood tests are among the most common checks in medicine. Nilufer Rahmioglu, Toby Andrew, Lynn Cherkas, and co-authors asked how much of their variation is inherited, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Doctors use these tests to judge liver health, track disease, judge treatments, and spot liver harm from drugs. Levels differ from person to person for many reasons.

The study splits those reasons into genes and life experience, a field called genetic epidemiology. Knowing how strongly genes set each test protein helps doctors read odd results. A level that looks abnormal may be normal for someone's family line. The work also points to gene hunts that could reveal new facts about how the liver works and fails.
plos-pone-0004535:
The worm C. elegans can show gene interactions more clearly when its diet is tuned just right, show William Mair, Siler Panowski, Reuben Shaw, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dietary restriction, eating less without malnutrition, lengthens life in many species and lowers the risk of age-related disease. Its lifespan effect is conserved from worms to mammals, which makes the small worm a useful test bed.

To find genes behind the effect, researchers combine dietary restriction with gene changes, a method called genetic epistasis analysis. The trick is choosing a restriction level strong enough to reveal interactions but not so harsh it swamps them. The authors optimize that level for C. elegans. A well-set dial makes gene discovery faster and cleaner for the whole aging field.
plos-pone-0004635:
Premature babies breathe in measurably different patterns from full-term babies, show Philipp Latzin, Stefan Roth, Cindy Thamrin, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Preterm infants with bronchopulmonary dysplasia, a chronic lung disease of prematurity, have structural changes in their lungs. Those changes have functional consequences for lung volume, ventilation inhomogeneity, and respiratory mechanics.

Some studies had shown lower lung volumes and increased ventilation inhomogeneity in these infants. The team measured lung volume, breathing pattern, and ventilation inhomogeneity in preterm and term infants for direct comparison. Precise measurements matter in neonatal care: they show which babies' lungs are coping and which need more support, and they give trials of new therapies an objective yardstick.
plos-pone-0004735:
Megan Sellick and colleagues tested how isotope levels vary in bird tissue by place, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Isotopes in tissue can reveal where a bird has been, since food and water differ by site. In theory, a single capture could show past moves and spread of that bird.

In practice, the basic maps of how isotopes vary were still thin. The team measured strontium and hydrogen isotopes across places. Better base maps make bird tracking from feathers more trusty. That helps guard migrants whose routes cross many lands. Future studies can use these results to refine both methods and theory.
plos-pone-0004835:
Maj-Britt Pontoppidan and colleagues studied spatio temporal spread of dead Ophiocordyceps infected ants, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Parasites likely play key roles in structuring host groups. Many adaptively manipulate host behavior, so extended phenotypes of parasites and their distributions in space, and Time are potentially key ecological variables for knowledge transmission dynamics in tropical forest ecosystems.

Infected ants die in clustered graveyards above ground. Fungal positioning maximizes spore spread to new hosts. Graveyard patterns reveal manipulation precision. Rainforest ecology includes such hidden control. Such evidence helps the field move from broad claims toward tested detail. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is. Such work helps guide care, field work, and lab work in the years ahead.
plos-pone-0004935:
Some chemicals can mimic hormones and disturb development. They can come from industry or from plants themselves. Genistein is one such plant-made compound, found in soy. Sana Sassi-Messai and colleagues studied it in PLOS ONE in 2009. They asked how genistein affects zebrafish development. Zebrafish are a standard model for early growth.

The team found the compound acts through two different pathways. A single natural chemical can scramble development by two routes at once. The work adds zebrafish evidence to wider concerns. Hormone-like substances are reaching water and wildlife. Studies like this show why their effects deserve close tracking.
plos-pone-0005035:
Membrane proteins run the cell's exchanges with the outside world. They are hard to study because they shun water. Myriam Reffay and colleagues tracked them in model membranes. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They followed how membrane proteins associate with each other. The setting was artificial membranes that mimic real ones.

The tracking reveals rules of protein matchmaking in the membrane. Association depends on the membrane setting as much as the proteins. The work offers a window into stubborn machinery. Membrane proteins include many drug targets. Understanding their partnerships helps design better medicines. It also helps explain how receptors and channels organize themselves.
plos-pone-0005135:
Prochlorococcus is a tiny ocean microbe. It has the smallest genome of any photosynthetic organism. Erik Zinser and colleagues tracked its daily routine in PLOS ONE in 2009. They followed its transcriptome across the day. They also measured its photophysiology and cell cycle. At temperate latitudes, sunlight varies predictably each day.

The microbe choreographs everything to that light cycle. Genes, light use and division march in step. A minimal cell times its life to the sun with precision. The work is a masterclass in doing more with less. Prochlorococcus fixes vast amounts of carbon in the oceans. Its daily rhythm shapes ocean productivity. Understanding it matters for the planet's carbon budget.
plos-pone-0005235:
Daily body clocks run on gene feedback loops, but nerve activity may tune them too. Kilman and colleagues tested that tuning in fruit flies in PLOS ONE in 2009. They disturbed dynamin, a protein that handles membrane traffic inside cells.

The team used a temperature-sensitive, faulty form of dynamin to perturb the system on demand. The title states the result: perturbing dynamin has potent effects on the fly's circadian clock. That finding ties everyday cell traffic to the timing system, a link that clock research had left unclear. The fruit fly is cheap and fast to breed, so a clear result there can guide work on clocks in larger animals and in people.
plos-pone-0005335:
Polycomb proteins keep gene patterns locked in as an embryo develops. In plants and animals, a complex called PRC2 marks genes with a chemical tag, H3K27me3. Exner and colleagues studied the plant protein LHP1, which reads that tag, in PLOS ONE in 2009.

LHP1 resembles the animal reader of the same mark. Its chromodomain proved essential for binding H3K27me3 and for normal Arabidopsis development. A single reading domain thus carries much of the plant Polycomb system's memory, showing how deeply this gene-silencing machinery is conserved. Corn, wheat, and rice all use this same lock-and-key gene system, so a plant model result here can guide work on the crops that feed most of the world each year.
plos-pone-0005435:
Michael Long and Fabio Rossi reported a warning for mouse genetics in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. A widely used system lets scientists switch genes on or off in chosen tissues of mice. Reporter strains show where the switch has worked by turning on a visible marker.

The authors found that gene silencing can block the switch in adult cells for two common reporter strains. When that happens, the marker stays dark even though the system should have worked. Workers who use these mice need to know that a dark result may mean silencing, not a failed gene change.
plos-pone-0005535:
Salomon Israel and co-authors studied giving behaviour in lab games for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. In the Dictator Game, one person decides how to split money with a stranger, keeping the rest. People often give more than pure self-interest would predict.

Earlier work had tied giving to a variant near a gene for the oxytocin receptor. The team tested that link in the game and in a survey of social values. Their results support a role for the receptor gene in how generous people are, adding gene evidence to the study of kindness.
plos-pone-0005635:
Michael Walsh and co-authors studied a new adenovirus that causes eye infections in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. In 2005, an outbreak of a severe eye disease was traced to a virus strain not previously known to cause it. The disease, epidemic keratoconjunctivitis, usually comes from a few set strains.

Gene study showed that swapping of parts between strains had reshaped this virus's targeting. The swap changed which tissues it infects. Tracking such swaps helps health officials spot new outbreak strains early. Eye outbreaks spread fast in clinics and schools, so spotting a new strain early can limit their reach.
plos-pone-0005735:
Martin Lubin and Adam Lubin proposed in 2009 a way to kill only those tumor cells that lack a certain enzyme. The enzyme, MTAP, sits near a famous tumor guard gene on chromosome 9. Both genes are often deleted together in lung and pancreas cancers, brain tumors, and bone cancers.

Cells without MTAP depend on backup routes that normal cells can do without. The authors lay out a strategy that exploits that dependence to strike the tumor and spare healthy tissue. Such selective killing is the goal of modern cancer drug design. The paper maps the logic and the cancers where it could apply.
plos-pone-0005835:
Pedro Vera and co-authors blocked two cell-surface proteins inside the rat bladder in 2009 and prevented inflammation triggered by substance P. An immune factor called MIF is released by bladder lining cells during irritation. It rides in complexes that latch onto surface receptors CD74 and CD78-family proteins.

Blocking those receptors from inside the bladder lumen stopped the inflammatory changes. Local blockade is attractive because it avoids whole-body immune suppression. Painful bladder conditions lack good treatments, so a defined target pair is welcome news. The work also clarifies how MIF signals in the bladder wall.
plos-pone-0005935:
Inside each cell, small sacs called endosomes ferry cargo from place to place. Sigrid Skånland, Sébastien Wälchli, Andreas Brech and colleagues studied how one ferry protein, SNX4, does its job in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. SNX4 belongs to the sorting nexin family, proteins that guide traffic inside the cell.

The team found SNX4 working in a complex with clathrin and with dynein, a motor protein that hauls cargo along cell tracks. That team-up helps explain how endosomes move toward the Golgi, the cell's shipping hub. The work fills in one route on the cell's inner map, basic knowledge for anyone studying how cells sort their goods.
plos-pone-0006035:
A mother's surroundings can shape her young, even in plants. Nianjun Teng, Biao Jin, Qinli Wang and colleagues tested that idea across an unusually long run in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper grows Arabidopsis under raised carbon dioxide for fifteen generations and checks each new generation for lasting maternal effects on growth and development.

None were detectable, the title states plainly. A null result over fifteen generations carries weight, since shorter tests can miss slow effects or invent them from noise. The finding tempers claims that high carbon dioxide will echo through plant families, and it sets a careful bar for studies of how the changing air shapes crops.
plos-pone-0006135:
A sperm channel thought to work alone turns out to take partners. Cheng-Tao Yang, Xu-Hui Zeng, Xiao-Ming Xia and colleagues paired Slo3 with its regulator family in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies Slo3, a potassium channel tuned by pH and voltage and found mainly in sperm. It also studies how Slo3 interacts with the beta subunits of the KCNMB family.

One partner stands out: beta4 selectively modulates Slo3's expression and function, the title reports. Channel properties in lab systems had differed from those in real sperm, and a partner subunit can explain the gap. Sorting the channel's true team matters for fertility science, where this current helps set sperm behavior.
plos-pone-0006235:
Fear learning and place learning rely on different brain circuits, and a single gene can split them apart. Duong Huynh and colleagues studied mice lacking ataxin-2 in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The team had earlier built these knockout mice and found no obvious faults in brain structure.

Behaviour tests showed dissociated changes: fear and spatial learning did not move together. Networks in the amygdala and hippocampus differ in how much they depend on the gene. Models where the two memory systems separate are rare and valuable. They let researchers study one system without disturbing the other.
plos-pone-0006335:
Women burn more fat than men during endurance exercise, and their muscles may be primed for it. Amy Maher and colleagues measured global mRNA content in human skeletal muscle from both sexes in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Several fat-oxidation genes were already known to show higher message levels in women.

The study extends that pattern across the muscle's full message set. Higher fat-burning messages offer a molecular basis for the exercise difference. Sex differences at this scale affect training and metabolism research design. Studies pooling men and women may blur real effects.
plos-pone-0006435:
Evan Kingsley, Marie Manceau, Christopher Wiley, and co-authors studied dark fur in deer mice for PLOS ONE in 2009. Dark, or melanic, forms of mammals offer a clean system for a big question. When the same trait evolves more than once on its own, what genes change each time? The answer shows how genes and development limit or channel evolution.

The title states their result: melanism in Peromyscus mice comes from separate mutations in the same gene, Agouti. Evolution reused one gene through different changes. That pattern tells scientists how much freedom evolution has when it solves the same problem twice. The mice make the lesson concrete.
plos-pone-0006535:
Umesh Yadav, Kota Ramana, Leopoldo Aguilera-Aguirre, and colleagues tested an enzyme blocker against allergic airway inflammation in PLOS ONE in 2009. Bronchial asthma involves persistent inflammation of the airway and subsequent airway hyper-responsiveness. It is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality. The team studied aldose reductase, an enzyme in sugar metabolism.

Their title reports that inhibiting aldose reductase prevents experimental allergic airway inflammation in mice. A metabolic enzyme thus joins the list of asthma targets. Blocking it may calm several inflammatory steps at once. The mouse results justify further study toward human asthma treatments.
plos-pone-0006635:
Joost Smolders and co-authors linked vitamin D status with regulatory T cell function in multiple sclerosis in PLOS ONE in 2009. In several autoimmune diseases, including MS, compromised regulatory T cell function is believed to be critically involved in disease. Vitamin D has repeatedly been tied to MS risk. The team correlated vitamin D status with regulatory T cell function in patients.

Their title reports a positive correlation: better vitamin D status, better regulatory function. Correlation is not causation, but it motivates intervention trials. If raising vitamin D restores regulation, a cheap supplement could help. The study connects two active MS research threads.
plos-pone-0006735:
Hortensia de la Fuente and co-authors measured gene changes in immune cells exposed to ultraviolet light in PLOS ONE in 2009. UV radiation affects the skin deeply. It also influences the wider immune system. Dendritic cells, which start immune responses, change behavior after UV exposure. Which genes drive those changes had not been mapped before.

The team used human dendritic cells grown from monocytes. They exposed the cells to solar-simulated UV radiation. Then they identified genes that responded to the exposure. The gene list explains how sunlight can dampen immune activity. It may also point to how UV contributes to skin disease and cancer risk.
plos-pone-0006835:
Konstantin A. Tsetsarkin and colleagues studied mutations helping chikungunya virus use a new mosquito in PLOS ONE in 2009. Between 2005 and 2007 the virus caused its largest recorded epidemic. Unusually, the mosquito Aedes albopictus was a principal vector. A single earlier mutation had boosted spread in that species. The authors examined mutations in the E2 glycoprotein.

E2 sits on the virus surface and contacts host cells. Some E2 mutations worked only together with others, an effect called epistasis. Their roles differed between albopictus and the classic vector, Aedes aegypti. Mapping these interactions explains how the virus adapted. It may also help predict future vector shifts.
plos-pone-0006935:
Claudia Baltzer, Stefanie Tiefenböck, Mark Marti, and colleagues studied fat tissue in fruit flies in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mitochondria make energy from nutrients inside cells. They also supply building blocks for fatty acids and amino acids. Their mass and activity must match the nutrients available.

Working in the adipose tissue of Drosophila, the team asked how nutrition controls mitochondrial production. They traced the control to two factors, Delg and Cyclin D with its partner Cdk4. The pathway links food signals to the cell's energy machinery. It offers a model for how animals adjust metabolism when diet changes.
plos-pone-0007035:
Emmanuelle Deniaud, Joël Baguet, Roxane Chalard, and colleagues raised levels of a common transcription factor in PLOS ONE in 2009. Sp1 switches on a vast number of genes. Those genes cover tasks from cell growth to cell death. Sp1 levels climb sharply when cells turn cancerous.

The team asked what that extra Sp1 does on its own. Overexpression disturbed gene programs across the cell. It also held back the cell cycle. The result shows a single overactive factor can scramble a cell's whole schedule. That scrambling may be part of how transformation begins.
plos-pone-0007135:
Nicholas Graves, Adrian Barnett, Kate Halton, and colleagues priced a health coaching program in PLOS ONE in 2009. Chronic disease rates keep climbing. Broad, cheap programs that raise activity and improve diet are in demand. The intervention they studied delivered coaching by telephone to adults with poor activity and diet habits.

The team calculated the program's cost-effectiveness. Phone delivery reaches people far from clinics at modest cost. If the benefits per dollar stack up well, health systems can justify wide rollouts. Their analysis gives decision makers the numbers behind a simple, scalable idea.
plos-pone-0007235:
Walter S. Leal, Yuko Ishida, Julien Pelletier, and colleagues studied smell proteins in a serious crop pest in 2009. The navel orangeworm moth damages almonds and pistachios in California. It is the most serious insect pest of those crops, and growers want greener control methods such as pheromones.

Pheromone control depends on understanding chemical communication in the moth. The authors identify olfactory proteins that mediate that communication. Their findings could guide traps or mating disruption tools. Such tools would reduce insecticide use while protecting valuable nut harvests from this persistent pest.
plos-pone-0007335:
Edwin Nuijten, Robbert van Treuren, Paul C. Struik, and colleagues found new rice types arising in West African fields in 2009. Two rice species coexist in West Africa, African rice and Asian rice. Experts once thought the two could not hybridize without biotechnology, because their crossing barriers seemed too strong to overcome naturally.

Farmers' fields told a different story. Hybrid progenies appeared to occur without lab help. The authors use AFLP genetic analysis on field plants. They present evidence for new rice types of interspecific hybrid origin. Their finding matters for breeding, since natural hybrids may carry useful trait combinations.
plos-pone-0007435:
Srinivas Garlapati and Ching Wang published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their subject was a virus that infects Giardia, the gut parasite behind a common diarrheal illness. Most viruses start making proteins at a special entry site for ribosomes. That site usually sits near the start of the genetic message. The giardiavirus entry site breaks that pattern.

In this virus, key parts of the entry site sit in places not seen in better-known viruses. That odd placement still manages to recruit the parasite's protein-making machinery. Giardia is an early-branching form of life, and its virus shows a distinct solution to a universal problem. The study widens what biologists know about the ways protein production can begin.
plos-pone-0007535:
Shireen Kahai and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the small RNAs that steer bone formation. MicroRNAs silence genes after their messages are made. One of them, miR-378, drew the team's attention in bone-building cells called osteoblasts. They traced how it controls a protein named nephronectin, which helps those cells mature. The chain ran through another target, an enzyme called GalNT-7.

By targeting GalNT-7, miR-378 regulates how much nephronectin the cells produce. That regulation in turn modulates osteoblast differentiation, the maturing of bone builders. Small RNAs thus sit inside the control circuit for bone growth. Understanding such circuits matters for diseases of weak or excess bone. The study maps one complete chain from tiny RNA to cell fate. Each link is a place where the process could be tuned.
plos-pone-0007635:
Kelly Gorres, Khian Hong Pua, and Ronald Raines published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the metal-binding clasp shared by a family of enzymes. These iron-using enzymes hold their iron with a motif of two histidines and one carboxylate. The family performs many oxidative reactions, including modifying the amino acid proline. The team focused on prolyl 4-hydroxylase, an enzyme needed to build collagen. They tested how strict the motif's requirements are.

Changing parts of the clasp showed how much variation the enzyme tolerates. Stringency data tell chemists which features are non-negotiable for activity. That knowledge guides enzyme engineering and drug design alike. An enzyme that builds collagen is also a target in fibrotic disease. The study is basic enzymology with practical edges. It measures how tightly nature's design is locked.
plos-pone-0007735:
Ida Chiara Guerrera and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It searches blood plasma for fat patterns tied to cystic fibrosis. Cystic fibrosis is an inherited disease that damages the lungs over time. Doctors need better markers of how severe the lung disease is.

The team adapted tools built for proteins to read lipids, the fats in blood. They compared samples from thirty-three patients. Certain phospholipid signatures tracked the severity of respiratory disease. If confirmed, a blood fat test could help doctors follow lung decline. It might also flag patients who need closer care.
plos-pone-0007835:
Isao Oze and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It reviews twenty-seven years of phase III trials in advanced small-cell lung cancer. This cancer spreads fast, and the extensive form is hard to treat. Whether outcomes had truly improved over decades was unclear.

The authors formally assessed results across trials for patients with extensive disease. Their verdict, stated in the title, is disappointing. Survival gains over the period were slight at best. The review makes the case plainly. It shows why fresh ideas, not small tweaks, are needed for this disease.
plos-pone-0007935:
Yassine Sakar and colleagues traced a gut hormone circuit in rodents for PLOS ONE in 2009. The hormone is leptin, made in the gut wall, and the circuit runs through GLUT2 and GLUT5, proteins that move sugars across the gut lining. Sugar handling in turn shapes liver work.

The team found a loop that feeds back on itself: gut leptin adjusts the sugar movers, and that change links onward to liver function. The loop helps keep blood sugar steady after meals. It also gives a fuller picture of how the gut and liver talk to each other through the day.
plos-pone-0008035:
Benjamin Tiede and colleagues built a mouse that lets them trail breast stem cells without harming the animal, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mammary stem cells rebuild the gland in each pregnancy, but their hiding places and habits were largely guesswork. A single marker that lights these cells was the key.

With the marker in place, the team followed the cells through pregnancy in living mice. They could see where the cells sit and how their numbers swell and shrink. That living record should help both nursing science and the study of breast cancers that may start in such cells.
plos-pone-0008135:
Jennifer Prescott and colleagues mined a long study of teachers for links between childbearing history and lymphoma in PLOS ONE in 2009. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is a blood cancer tied to immune quirks. Female hormones tune the immune system, so pregnancies, hormone use, and like factors might shift risk.

The California Teachers Study gave a large group with detailed histories to test many such factors at once. Some factors tracked with risk and others plainly did not. Sorting the two helps aim future work at the hormone paths most worth a closer look.
plos-pone-0008235:
Edward O. Ronan and colleagues tested a tuberculosis vaccine in mice in a PLOS ONE study from 2009. In lung infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis, immune responses arrive late. Specific immune cells may not appear in the lungs before two weeks. Even the standard BCG vaccine leaves this early gap. A faster response could limit the infection sooner.

The team immunized mice with a recombinant adenovirus vaccine. Vaccinated mice resisted the early growth of the bacteria after infection. Beating the usual delay is a promising sign for vaccine design. The study supports adenovirus platforms as candidates for better tuberculosis protection.
plos-pone-0008335:
Shengjun Wang and colleagues studied an enzyme that trims sugar chains in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Peptide: N-glycanase detaches sugar chains from proteins by cutting a specific bond. In yeast, the enzyme binds a partner protein called Rad23p through its front end. That front section is called the N-terminus. The team tested what happens when it is deleted.

Removing the N-terminal part enhanced the enzyme's deglycosylation activity. A section that mediates binding apparently also restrains cutting. The result clarifies how this enzyme is regulated. Such enzymes help cells dispose of faulty proteins.
plos-pone-0008435:
Edith Tong and co-authors study salt stress in cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. When salt around a cell is too high, a protein called OREBP turns on genes that help the cell cope. OREBP is also called TonEBP or NFAT5. It is the only known factor of its kind for this task in mammals. The authors look at the DNA it binds.

They find that high salt can clear nucleosomes from those binding sites. Nucleosomes are spools that DNA wraps around. Clearing them may open the sites so OREBP can act fast. The work shows a step in how cells meet salt stress.
plos-pone-0008535:
Cheryl Tan and co-authors find a gene controlled by gene-switch groups in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Two groups, Polycomb and trithorax, set which genes are on in each cell type. They do this by adding marks to chromatin, the packed form of DNA. Those marks can silence a gene or switch it on. The team had earlier found a link to complexes called MLL and SET1.

They show the gene Fgfr3 is a target of these complexes. Control involves two proteins, Ap2delta and Ash2l. Fgfr3 sends growth signals in bone and other tissues. The work ties the marks on DNA packing to control of a key growth gene.
plos-pone-0008635:
Hunter Fraser and co-authors study how stable traits are across yeast in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Some strains keep a trait steady despite noise or gene changes. That steadiness is called robustness. It was not known how much robustness varies between individuals. It was also not known if buffers against noise also buffer gene changes. The team measure robustness across many yeast strains.

They find robustness differs by strain and can be passed on. In short, steadiness itself is a heritable trait. Buffers against noise and against gene changes partly overlap. The work turns a classic idea into a trait that can be measured and mapped.
plos-pone-0008735:
Geetha Govind, Omprakash Mittapalli, Thasso Griebel, and colleagues compared two kinds of caterpillars on tobacco plants. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Wild tobacco defends itself with poisons switched on by jasmonate signals. Specialist caterpillars handle those defenses well. Generalist caterpillars eat many plants and struggle more. The team removed plant defenses step by step for a fair test.

Newborn larvae fed on plants with graded defense levels. Gene activity in the larvae showed how each kind coped. Specialists adjusted smoothly while generalists showed stress. The contrast reveals why some pests shrug off plant poisons.
plos-pone-0008835:
André Schütte, Jana Hedrich, Walter Stöcker, and colleagues silenced a cutting enzyme in zebrafish embryos and watched vessels grow. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Meprins are metalloproteases, enzymes that snip other proteins. Their exact jobs in the body stayed vague despite many known targets. Growth factors and structural proteins are among those targets. Morpholino tools can block one gene at a time in fish embryos.

Blocking meprin alpha 2 changed blood vessel growth in the embryos. The change revealed a pro-growth role for the enzyme. Vessel biology gains a new named player. Such enzymes may become targets for controlling vessel growth.
plos-pone-0008935:
Elsa Jourdain and colleagues infected mallard ducks with flu virus under controlled conditions for PLOS ONE in 2010. Mallards are dabbling ducks that carry bird flu in the wild without getting very sick. Wild waterfowl are the main natural home of mild avian influenza viruses. Those viruses can sometimes change into forms that threaten poultry or people.

The team recorded how the infection ran its course in these natural hosts. They tracked how much virus the ducks shed and for how long. Data from real infections help scientists judge how flu spreads through wild flocks. That knowledge feeds models of when and where outbreaks in farm birds might start.
plos-pone-0009035:
Ben Lehner asked whether the genes that cushion yeast against one kind of trouble cushion all kinds, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Switching a gene off often changes a yeast cell surprisingly little. That toughness is called robustness, and it matters for disease and evolution. Trouble can come from the environment, from chance, or from mutations.

Lehner compared gene lists for each kind of buffering. Largely the same genes softened all three sorts of knocks. Robustness looks like one general system, not separate fixes per problem. That unity shapes how organisms can evolve and how gene faults cause disease.
plos-pone-0009135:
Jesse Wiley and co-authors rescued a stressed brain protein pathway with a simple chemical, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Alzheimer's disease, inherited or not, leaves the same pattern of brain damage. That match hints that cell stress can copy the effect of inherited mutations. Stress in the endoplasmic reticulum can shut down the cutting of APP.

APP is the parent protein of the amyloid that clumps in Alzheimer's brains. Phenylbutyric acid relieved the stress effect in cultured neuronal cells. APP cutting resumed and the stressed cells escaped death as a result. A stress-relieving chemical may be worth testing against this disease.
plos-pone-0009235:
Karina Stucken and co-authors published this genome study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cyanobacteria come in many forms, from single round cells to long filaments. Some kinds build colonies and filaments with specialized cells for different jobs. Others make toxins that can poison water supplies.

The team compared the smallest known genomes among multicellular and toxic cyanobacteria. They worked out the minimal gene sets tied to traits like filament building and toxin making. A stripped-down genome shows which genes a trait truly needs. The comparison also hints at how these bacteria evolved their complex forms from simpler ancestors.
plos-pone-0009335:
Genevieve Phillips and co-authors published this hair analysis study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Scientists read trace metals in hair to learn about the dead and the living. Hair samples serve archaeology, forensics, and toxicology as records of the body. The catch is that hair keeps changing after burial.

The team showed that metal-loving bacteria deposit gold onto hair after death. They used gold as a tracer for that microbial activity. Bacterial deposits can mimic or mask the signals researchers want to read. The warning is practical: hair chemistry may report the graveyard more than the life.
plos-pone-0009435:
Hernan Bonomi and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE in 2010 on Brucella abortus. That germ causes illness in cattle and in people. The germ lives inside host cells, where it is hard to reach. To stay harmful, it must make riboflavin, also known as vitamin B2. Its way of making that vitamin is not the usual one.

The team showed that this odd path is vital for the germ to cause disease. Human cells do not use the same path to make the vitamin. A drug that blocks the germ path could thus spare the patient. The work names a clear weak point in a germ that is hard to treat.
plos-pone-0009535:
Vitali Sintchenko and co-authors mined the medical literature with computers in PLOS ONE in 2010. The PubMed database held more than eighteen million papers at the time. A large share deal with infectious diseases and their causes. No person can read even a fraction of them. The team used software to find links between germs and disease syndromes across that whole body of text.

Their associational study surfaced connections that single readers would miss. Some links confirmed known facts, and others suggested new ones to check. The work shows how knowledge can be synthesized by machine from published research. It is a step toward using the literature itself as a data source.
plos-pone-0009635:
Pengjing Xu and co-authors tested learning in patients with Wilson's disease in PLOS ONE in 2010. Wilson's disease lets copper build up in the body and harm the brain. The basal ganglia, deep brain structures, are hit hard. Those structures are known to matter for learning categories. The team measured both category learning and perceptual learning in treated patients.

Comparing the two kinds of learning shows which ones suffer when the basal ganglia are damaged. Some skills may survive through other brain systems. The results help separate the jobs of deep brain structures in learning. They also guide support for patients whose learning profile is uneven.
plos-pone-0009835:
A tiny sea snail drifts in both the Arctic and Antarctic oceans, or so it seemed. Brian Hunt and colleagues tested whether the two polar populations are really one species. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The snail is Limacina helicina, a pteropod with a delicate shell. Pteropods are sometimes called sea butterflies. Genetic tests showed the Arctic and Antarctic forms are distinct from each other. Two populations at opposite poles can look alike yet follow separate paths. The split matters for tracking how polar species respond to warming seas.
plos-pone-0009935:
Watching calcium flash inside living cells is a core trick of cell biology. Kenta Saito and colleagues built a new glowing indicator for that job. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Calcium spikes act as signals that trigger cell actions.

The indicator is auto-luminescent, making its own light without an outside lamp. It is also ratiometric, comparing two signals so readings stay steady. Genetically encoded means cells build the indicator themselves from inserted genes. Real-time imaging at the single cell level could sharpen studies of signaling. The imaging ran in real time, as signals rose and fell.
plos-pone-0010135:
The authors were Menachem Bitan, Lola Weiss, Michael Zeira, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used mice to test a transplant aid called heparanase. Heparanase is an enzyme that cuts sugar chains on cell surfaces. It is known for roles in cancer spread, new blood vessels, and inflammation.

In bone marrow transplants, mice making extra heparanase took grafts better. The enzyme also prevented graft versus host disease, where donor cells attack the patient. Both effects together could make stem cell transplants, a key leukemia treatment, safer and more reliable. Few transplant tools promise both gains together.
plos-pone-0010235:
The authors were Philip Cooper, A. Clementina Mesaros, Jie Zhang, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used mice exposed to ozone, a common air pollutant. Ozone makes airways overreact, a state called hyper-responsiveness. That reaction raises illness and death in people with asthma and other airway diseases, especially on high pollution days in cities.

The team proposed that oxidized lipids carry the effect inside the airways. They identified one lipid, 20-HETE, as the mediator of ozone-induced overreaction. Notably, the effect did not need neutrophils, a white blood cell often blamed in airway inflammation.
plos-pone-0010435:
Sven Sehlmeyer and colleagues studied detox enzymes in tiger moths for PLOS ONE in 2010. Insects face poisons from the plants they eat and from farm sprays. They survive by breaking those poisons down inside their bodies. One famous enzyme family does much of that work. This team examined a second family, the flavin-dependent monooxygenases, in the arctiid moth group.

Their results suggest this second family also serves as a detox route. Having two systems may explain how some moths handle very toxic plants. It may also affect how pests resist insecticides over time. Knowing all the detox routes helps design sprays that last longer. The study widens a field that had focused on one enzyme family.
plos-pone-0010535:
Hilary Zelko and colleagues asked researchers themselves how high-impact biomedical papers come to be in PLOS ONE in 2010. Innovation in science has fascinated historians and philosophers for generations. Few studies, though, asked working biomedical researchers how landmark publications actually develop. The team interviewed researchers and built a qualitative account. From those accounts they drew a causal model of the selection process.

High-impact work, in their model, is selected by layered filters, not born great in one step. Funders and journals shape what survives as much as authors do. Understanding that machinery matters for science policy and careers. It can also help young researchers aim effort where it counts. The study turns scientists into subjects of their own methods.
plos-pone-0010635:
Johanna Assies and colleagues compared blood fats in people with repeated depression, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cell membranes in the brain are rich in fatty acids. Earlier work linked low omega-3 fats to depression, but the full fat picture was rarely measured.

Each patient was matched with a healthy person of similar background. The team measured a wide range of fats in plasma and red cells. Several patterns differed between the groups, beyond the usual omega fats. The results keep open the idea that fat metabolism plays a part in recurring depression, and they define what to test next.
plos-pone-0010735:
Armando Arias and colleagues trimmed a small viral protein to find what makes picornaviruses damage cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Picornaviruses include the polio virus and common cold agents. Their protein VPg primes the copying of viral RNA, acting as a starter tag.

Deleting parts of VPg changed how much harm infected cells suffered. Some deletions hurt copying; others left copying intact but reduced cell damage. Damage and copying can thus be separated. That separation matters for designing weakened viruses and for drugs, since a treatment might blunt disease even when it cannot stop copying outright.
plos-pone-0010835:
William Precht, Richard Aronson, Ryan Moody and co-authors published this reef study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The threespot damselfish shapes life on Caribbean reefs by farming algae and guarding its patch, and it prefers thickets of staghorn coral.
