That coral has died back across most of its range in recent decades, hit by disease and other stresses.

Surveys from Jamaica, Florida, the Bahamas, the Cayman Islands, and Belize compared fish numbers with coral cover, reef shape, fishing pressure, and predator abundance. Damselfish patterns tracked live coral cover and complex reef structure more closely than predator numbers. Losing its favorite coral has forced the fish into new microhabitats. Precht and colleagues show how the fate of one coral can quietly rearrange a whole reef community.
plos-pone-0010935:
Thierry Granjon, Ofelia Maniti, Yolanda Auchli and co-authors published this enzyme study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Oxaloacetate decarboxylase is a membrane machine found only in oxygen-free bacteria, including the cholera germ. It harvests energy from a chemical reaction and spends it pumping sodium ions across the cell membrane, building a gradient that powers other work.

The enzyme has three parts, one holding the catalytic site. Using fluorescence and infrared methods, the authors watched how a stand-in for its fuel and sodium ions each changed the protein's shape and surroundings. Granjon and colleagues test which parts sense which partner, clarifying how the machine couples chemistry to pumping. Such details matter because this energy route exists in pathogens but not in people, a tempting drug target gap.
plos-pone-0011035:
Ke-Da Yu, Jun-Jie Li, Gen-Hong Di and co-authors published this breast cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Whether breast cancer has spread to the armpit lymph nodes is a key staging fact, and European studies had reported a bent, piecewise relation with age: risk dipping then rising. The authors tested whether that pattern holds in Chinese patients.

They analyzed several thousand women with operable breast cancer treated in Shanghai over a decade, then repeated the analysis in a second, later group of nearly two thousand patients. The European U-shaped pattern did not replicate; the age relationship in these patients was more straightforward and not piecewise. Yu and colleagues show that a risk pattern found in one population cannot simply be imported into another, a caution for applying foreign clinical data to Chinese practice.
plos-pone-0011135:
Cohen, Maoz, Turm and colleagues mapped breast cancer spread in PLOS ONE in 2010. For cancer to spread, tumor cells must push into nearby tissue. The team traced a protein relay that controls a receptor on the cell surface linked to that invasive step.

They set out the order of partners in the relay and its role in invasion. Each link in such a chain is a possible place to block spread with drugs. That matters because spread, not the first tumor, causes most breast cancer deaths. The study gives drug hunters a defined set of targets in this pathway.
plos-pone-0011235:
Coulon, Chebli, Cavelier and colleagues found a hidden mouse gene switch in PLOS ONE in 2010. A famous gene, switched on quickly when cells are stimulated, was thought to have one start site. The team discovered a second promoter inside the gene itself in mice.

That inner promoter answers to two known gene regulators and is itself controlled across development in living animals. Layered control like this lets one gene serve many roles at different times. Finding it changes how researchers read decades of work on this model gene. It also warns that other genes may hide extra promoters too.
plos-pone-0011335:
Kuo-Chen Chou and Hong-Bin Shen presented Plant-mPLoc in 2010, a computer tool for plant biology. A protein does its job in a specific place inside a cell, such as the nucleus or the wall. Knowing that address helps scientists guess what the protein does, but testing every plant protein in the lab is slow and costly.

Their tool predicts a plant protein's address from its sequence alone, and it can suggest more than one address when a protein works in several places. They built it with a top-down plan that first sorts proteins broadly, then refines the call. Tested against known cases, the tool gave researchers a fast first map of where proteins act. Such maps guide lab work on crops and on basic plant cell function.
plos-pone-0011435:
Katherine Holmes and co-authors traced in 2010 the chain by which a vessel growth signal switches on one gene in lining cells. VEGF commands blood vessels to grow, and one gene it raises, RCAN1.4, helps fine-tune the response. The team worked out each link the signal must pass through inside endothelial cells, the cells that line vessels.

The chain proved to require calcium, the calcium-activated enzyme calcineurin, and a further signaling protein, working in sequence. Charting that relay gives vascular biologists a detailed wiring diagram for a signal that drives both healing and the blood supply of tumors. Each link is a possible drug point, for boosting vessel growth in wounds or starving it in cancer. The paper turns a vague arrow on a diagram into named, testable steps.
plos-pone-0011535:
Sarah Meadows and co-authors showed in 2010 that blood gene patterns can reveal partial-body radiation exposure in mice. After a nuclear accident or attack, many people may be exposed unevenly, with only part of the body irradiated. Doctors must then sort the exposed from the spared quickly, to spend treatment wisely. Physical dosimeters are rarely worn, so a blood test that reads exposure from the body itself is needed.

Gene activity profiles in peripheral blood distinguished partial-body exposure and carried information about the dose the body received. A blood-based readout can be run on many people fast, which is what triage in a mass emergency demands. The mouse work is a step toward a human test, not the test itself, since human profiles must be charted separately. Still, it proves the body's own transcription can serve as a dosimeter when no meter was there.
plos-pone-0011635:
James Bull and Michael Bonsall used models to test a surprising idea about predators, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Wildlife often lives in scattered patches, where random bad luck can wipe out a small local group. Nearby patches can rescue each other by sending migrants, which keeps the whole network alive.

Their models show that predators can actually lower the overall risk of extinction in such noisy patchworks. By checking booms that would otherwise crash hard, hunters steady the system. The counter-intuitive result gives conservation managers a reason to think twice before removing predators from fragile habitats.
plos-pone-0011735:
Lise Lotte Husemoen and co-authors linked drinking, genes and disease risk in a white study group, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Past studies keep finding the same curve: both non-drinkers and heavy drinkers show more type 2 diabetes and heart disease than light drinkers. What drives that curve is still not clear.

The authors looked at alcohol intake side by side with variants in genes that break alcohol down, and set both against diabetes and heart risk factors. Since breakdown speed is set in part by genes, mixing the two views sharpens the picture. The method helps split alcohol's own effects from the drinker's inborn traits.
plos-pone-0011835:
Pradeep Marri and colleagues published this 2010 genome study of Neisseria, a bacterial group that includes harmless throat residents as well as the causes of gonorrhea and meningitis. Very little was known about the full gene content of the harmless members, or how closely they match their dangerous relatives.

By sequencing and comparing genomes across the group, the team found that genes tied to causing disease move between species far more often than expected. Harmless and harmful Neisseria appear to trade useful DNA rather than evolving in isolation. That sharing blurs the line between friend and foe, and it helps explain how new disease-causing strains can pick up ready-made tools.
plos-pone-0011935:
Michael Barton, Daniela Delneri, and Stephen Oliver examined in 2010 the energy bill yeast pays for its proteins. Every amino acid costs the cell something to build, and proteins made of costly parts are expensive to produce in bulk. Natural selection should favor cheaper proteins where the savings do not hurt function.

Taking a systems view, the team studied how these building costs have shaped yeast evolution. Cheap and costly amino acids are not spread randomly through the yeast's proteins; cost leaves a pattern. That accounting helps explain features of genomes that look arbitrary until the energy ledger is considered, and it gives biotechnology a rule of thumb for designing proteins yeast can make cheaply.
plos-pone-0012035:
Cheng Chen and co-workers studied in 2010 how bladder muscle cells soften under a sudden stretch, then firm up again. Cells in hollow organs such as the lungs, gut, and bladder face large brief stretches as routine. Earlier work had shown that a transient stretch makes an adherent cell promptly fluidize, loosening its internal structure.

Following human bladder smooth muscle cells through that cycle showed both the fluidizing and the resolidification that restores stiffness. A material that yields under a sharp pull, then heals, protects organs that must stretch without tearing. The cycle also offers a model for how mechanical forces alone, without any chemical signal, can reset a cell's state.
plos-pone-0012135:
Kazumune Ueshima, Takeo Fujiwara, Soshi Takao, and co-authors surveyed social ties and exercise in Japan for PLOS ONE in 2010. They asked whether social capital, the trust and connection people share in a community, goes along with being physically active. In early 2009 they surveyed a random sample of several thousand residents of Okayama city, chosen by neighborhood clusters.

People's answers let the team compare activity levels across levels of individual social connection. If connected people move more, then building community ties becomes a health tool, not just a social good. Population studies like this guide city health programs toward changes that can shift exercise habits at scale, cheaply and without medicine.
plos-pone-0012235:
Larissa Reifur, Laura Yu, and Jorge Cruz-Reyes studied RNA editing in the parasite that causes sleeping sickness, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Inside this parasite's mitochondria, messages are rewritten after copying, guided by small guide RNAs that must each find exactly the right message among hundreds of similar ones. The team suspected the message's folded shape helps or hinders that targeting.

Their tests weigh how the structure of a target message affects a guide RNA's aim. Editing this extensive exists in almost no other creature, which makes its machinery a tempting drug target: block it and the parasite's energy system fails. Understanding targeting is a first step toward jamming it.
plos-pone-0012335:
Brian Krueger, Katayoun Varzavand, Jeffrey Cooper, and co-authors worked out how a stored transcription factor gets released, in PLOS ONE in 2010. P-TEFb is required to make most messages, yet the cell keeps the majority locked in a particle called 7SK, where a partner protein holds it inactive. HIV's Tat protein famously springs that lock for its own ends, and the cell has triggers of its own.

The release, they found, includes a shape change in the 7SK RNA at the particle's heart. A structural account of the lock explains both the virus's trick and the cell's normal one. Since this factor also matters in heart growth and cancer, its release mechanism has audiences well beyond virology.
plos-pone-0012435:
Eric Lugada, Debra Millar, John Haskew and colleagues reported a fast, combined health campaign in rural Kenya in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The drive bundled HIV testing and counseling with malaria prevention and diarrhea prevention in one visit. Bundling can raise coverage and fairness in poor areas, where separate programs reach the same villages again and again at high cost.

A public-private partnership set up the campaign and rolled it out at large scale in a short period. The report details how many people were reached and what the logistics took. Its lessons guide other regions that want to deliver several proven health services in a single, efficient push.
plos-pone-0012535:
Soon-Kyung Hwang, Longzhen Piao, Hwang-Tae Lim and colleagues found that a mitochondrial protein suppresses lung tumor growth, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The protein LETM1 shapes mitochondria, the cell's power plants, yet its own job stayed unclear. The human version matches a yeast protein known to keep mitochondria in form, hinting at deep, conserved duties.

Raising LETM1 suppressed lung tumorigenesis in the team's models, while losing it favored tumors. A mitochondria-shaping protein acting as a tumor brake ties energy organelles to cancer control. The link adds to growing evidence that cancer is partly a disease of cell power management.
plos-pone-0012635:
Rajasekaran, Xiong, Fong and co-authors compared two helper switches on human killer T cells. Both CD28 and NKG2D can boost a CD8 T cell's attack, but their separate jobs in each T cell subgroup were unclear. Their 2010 study sorted T cells from blood and lung tissue to test them apart.

They found the two switches do different work rather than backing each other up. Knowing which switch drives which subgroup matters for cancer and infection treatments that aim to raise T cell power. The split also explains why one drug cannot boost all killer cells alike.
plos-pone-0012735:
Sievers, Billig, Gottschalk and co-authors showed that two guard proteins are needed for cancer cells to grow and stick. Prohibitin 1 and its partner prohibitin 2 sit mainly in the inner membrane of mitochondria, the cell's power plants. Their roles in cancer had been debated for years.

Their 2010 study removed them and watched cancer cells lose both growth and adhesion. Cells that cannot stick cannot spread easily, so the double effect is notable. The pair may serve as targets in cancers that lean on them heavily.  The study used several cancer cell types to check the effect held broadly.
plos-pone-0331535:
Hirata and colleagues studied emergency transport in Japan through the pandemic years in a 2026 paper. Some regions use hospitals staffed by dedicated emergency doctors, a model linked to faster transport before the pandemic. Nationwide records from 2015 to 2021 covered two such regions and one comparable region without the model.

Transport outcomes were compared before and during the pandemic across the three areas. The question was whether the dedicated-doctor advantage survived when ambulances were diverted and departments crowded. Findings can guide how Japan staffs emergency care for future surges, when the freedom to refuse patients distorts normal flows.
plos-pone-0335335:
Xingmin Han, Ruirui Xing, and Mi Zhou compared three leading language models as teachers about ADHD in 2026. Outside coaches and general teachers increasingly lean on such tools, yet accuracy and reading ease for non specialists were untested.

Thirty answers per model were collected on definitions, symptoms, and how medication interacts with exercise. All matched the standard diagnostic manual, but styles split: one model wrote broadly and variably, one stayed consistent and clinical, one was concise and strengths based. All were harder to read than ideal. The study advises schools to pick and supervise tools deliberately, not casually.
plos-pone-0335835:
Maximilian Berthold and five colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about tiny ocean life. Picocyanobacteria are among the smallest photosynthetic bacteria and huge in number in coastal seas. The authors study inter-strain diversity, how strains of these organisms differ from each other across salinity gradients, from fresher to saltier water.

Coastal waters shift in saltiness with rain, rivers, and tides, so strains sorted by salt tolerance reveal how these microbes partition their habitat. These bacteria fix carbon and feed marine food webs, making their diversity a basic fact of ocean ecology. Marine microbiologists are the readers for a strain-level map across the gradient.
plos-pone-0338535:
Lorna Katusiime and Frank Agbola study Uganda's digital credit boom in this 2026 paper. After the pandemic, mobile money use and phone-based lending grew fast in the country. The authors ask what drives the amount of mobile money loans actually handed out. They use monthly data from mid-2021 through the end of 2024.

A long-run link ties disbursements to outstanding loan values and past inflation. In the short run, yesterday's lending strongly shapes today's. Everyday behaviour matters too. Buying airtime and repaying earlier loans on time signal reliability, and disbursements rise with both. By contrast, higher transaction fees and heavy transaction volumes push lending down. The message for lenders and regulators is direct: cut user costs and reward good repayment to grow responsible digital credit.
plos-pone-0340735:
Vivian W L Tsang and colleagues evaluated a programme run from a children's hospital in British Columbia that lets community clinicians consult child mental health specialists by phone and video. The review covers six years of Compass Program records, with special attention to the province's rural north and to Indigenous communities, where specialists are scarce and travel is long.

Northern communities accounted for about a fifth of all consultations, and nearly half of all Indigenous consultations came from the north. Calls about Indigenous youth climbed steadily across the period, and medication questions led the reasons for calling. Anxiety was the most common concern everywhere. The authors present the programme as a working model for stretching specialist advice into underserved regions, while noting that demand keeps growing.
plos-pone-0342235:
Pei Shi and colleagues proposed a traffic forecasting network in 2026. City traffic forms patterns across linked roads and over time that simple models miss, and poor forecasts weaken signal control and trip planning.

Their network first builds shifting time and place codes, then reads road links through several graphs at once, including one it learns itself. Attention modules weigh which places and past moments matter most. On four public data sets the method reported strong accuracy. Designs that learn the map as traffic changes could give control rooms a clearer view of jams before they form.
plos-pone-0342635:
Anna Strnadová and coauthors published a study in PLOS ONE on hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, an inherited thickening of the heart muscle that can cause heart failure and sudden death. Diseased hearts burn lots of glucose, and glucose chemistry feeds production of hyaluronan, a gel-like sugar between cells. Working with mice carrying one faulty copy of a heart protein gene, the team mapped where hyaluronan gathers and whether two beta-blockers change the picture.

Mutant hearts held far more hyaluronan than normal hearts, scattered in patches. Where the gel piled up, heart muscle cells were enlarged, tying accumulation to the thickening. A gel-making gene was switched on higher in mutants, and one beta-blocker held it at normal levels while raising a related one. Neither drug reduced the gel or the cell enlargement. The spatial link they visualized makes hyaluronan a target worth attacking directly, the authors say.
plos-pone-0344235:
Ruichen Li, Hao Liu, and Yukie Nagai build a computer model of the body's automatic control systems to understand how they differ in autism, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Heart rate and blood pressure arise from two branches of the autonomic nervous system working together or in opposition. Their closed-loop model simulates both branches plus breathing, and they compared its behaviour against real tilt-table test data from autistic and non-autistic people.

In typical development the branches coordinated in distinct styles matched to the task. In the autism data the branch weights converged, with the calming branch staying unusually engaged when posture demanded the opposite. Adding deep breathing in the model improved pressure recovery — a hint that breathing training could be a practical lever.
plos-pone-0345135:
Samuel Duraivel and colleagues read the public mood about the metaverse in nearly fifty-three thousand English-language tweets. Automated tools scored each post's sentiment, and topic modelling sorted the chatter into four arenas: the metaverse in general, one flagship virtual world and its cryptocurrency tokens. A fourth arena covered virtual social events such as online concerts and weddings.

Enthusiasm led overall, with about forty-three percent of tweets positive, fuelled by excitement about immersive technology. About a quarter were sceptical, citing unreliable platforms, corporate control, and privacy. The flagship world drew a paradox of hopeful users venting frustration, while token talk cooled from price speculation toward practical uses. Virtual events earned the warmest feelings of all. The authors offer the map to developers and investors gauging readiness for the next wave of digital life.
plos-pone-0345435:
Anna Ogonowska-Slodownik and seven colleagues design a water-based balance training programme for older adults — with the future users in the room, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Practising recovery from a deliberate loss of balance prevents falls, but on land the drills frighten people and strain joints. Three older adult partners joined physiotherapists and researchers through design sessions, a practical pool trial, and feedback rounds.

Partners pushed for a support vest instead of a hip belt, clearer information about pool depth, and a starter pack explaining the programme. Safety, instructor support, and the social side of sessions mattered most for sticking with it. The resulting protocol is now ready for feasibility testing, shaped by the people it must persuade.
plos-pone-0346835: Akinwande and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE review on hunger among teen mothers in sub-Saharan Africa. The review covers girls aged ten to nineteen who are raising children while still teens themselves. As a scoping review, it maps what studies exist and where the gaps are. Teen mothers face high food risk, so a clear map of the evidence can steer aid and future research.
plos-pone-0347035:
Aja Louise Murray, Xuefei Li, and Tom Booth gave a first test to a new World Health Organization questionnaire measuring people's experiences of ageism. The fifteen-item scale covers insults people direct at themselves, treatment by others, and barriers built into institutions, and it is meant to work across ages and countries. The 2026 study ran it with four hundred two British adults of mixed ages.

Scores held together well, stayed stable when people retook the scale later, and lined up sensibly with related measures. Analysis supported treating self-directed ageism as one dimension. The authors say the early results justify adopting the scale in Britain and translating it for testing elsewhere.
plos-pone-0347535:
Joshin Joseph and co-authors surveyed tourists in Kerala, India, four months after deadly landslides in Wayanad, to ask what draws people to disaster sites. Such dark tourism raises ethical questions about whether visitors seek learning or a thrill from others' loss. Their 2026 study questioned more than four hundred tourists, measuring standard travel motives alongside a mild form of pleasure at others' misfortune.

Curiosity, learning, and bonding with companions all raised the intention to visit, while seeking fun lowered it. The misfortune-pleasure trait was the single strongest predictor, and it amplified the pull of novelty in particular. The authors urge destination managers to handle post-disaster tourism with explicit ethical care. They also note their one-region, one-time snapshot cannot prove cause and effect.
plos-pone-0348135:
H. C. Poorvi and P. K. Vinod searched for the shared molecular script of organ rejection by pooling gene data from six hundred seventy-two transplant biopsies of liver, kidney, and heart. Rejection is usually studied organ by organ, fragmenting the picture. Building gene networks for each organ and comparing them, the 2026 study looked for what repeats.

A six-stage immune cascade appeared in all three organs, alongside a twenty-four gene cell-division signature that switched on in rejecting tissue. A refined twenty-gene immune signature predicted rejection with excellent accuracy and also worked in an independent lung transplant group. The authors propose one cross-organ test for transplant monitoring.
plos-pone-0348435:
Anna Sára Bognár, Bálint Mihály Erőss, and co-authors pooled the research on psychological suffering among patients with pancreatic cancer, one of the deadliest cancers and one whose emotional toll is understudied. Their 2026 review searched three major databases and combined twenty-eight studies in a meta-analysis covering depression, anxiety, distress, fatigue, and sleep problems.

Roughly one patient in four experienced depression, and a similar share reported anxiety. Distress affected more than four in ten, fatigue about four in ten, and sleep disturbance about three in ten, though estimates varied widely between studies. The authors say the numbers make a plain case: psychological care should be built into pancreatic cancer treatment from the start, not added when crisis hits.
plos-pone-0348935:
Zhihong Xu, Gary Wingenbach, and co-authors surveyed alumni of a land-grant university to learn how agriculture programs should teach data analytics, a skill now demanded across food and farming careers. Learners differ in age, experience, and the words they use for their needs, and one standard curriculum may serve none well. Their 2026 study combined survey statistics with text mining of open-ended answers from more than five hundred graduates.

Two learner groups emerged. Younger, less experienced graduates wanted hands-on technical fluency: coding, visualization, and tools. Older, more experienced graduates prized strategy, leadership, and communication. Language patterns in their written answers confirmed the split. Communication skills mattered to both groups. The authors recommend split pathways, hands-on lab tracks for newcomers and strategy-focused modules for seasoned staff, rather than a single track.
plos-pone-0349135:
Tao-Ming Dai and colleagues mapped pain and low mood in older Chinese adults. Data came from a national ageing study. Waves ran from 2011 to 2020. Nearly thirty nine thousand adults took part. All were aged forty five or older. Seven learning models predicted low mood. Inputs covered background, habits, and pain by body site.

Pain tracked low mood most strongly. Leg pain and spine pain mattered most. Model accuracy stayed modest. The best model reached fair sorting power. Extra tools showed each factor weight per person. Pain care and mood care should be planned as one. Treating pain alone may leave mood risk untouched.
plos-pone-0349235:
RETRACTION: this entry is a retraction notice from the PLOS One Editors, and the study it describes should not be relied on. The withdrawn article had reported finding drug-resistant E. coli bacteria in chicken meat sold in Pakistan. After publication, readers raised concerns about several of its figures and one key table, and the journal investigated.

Gel images in the paper closely resembled images in another article, bands within the gels looked duplicated, and adjusted backgrounds showed suspicious breaks. A headline value in the table also fell below the range the paper itself stated. The authors explained the overlaps as shared methods and imaging artefacts, but the data they supplied did not settle the doubts. Some authors disagreed with the decision. The editors concluded the results' reliability could not be trusted and withdrew the article.
plos-pone-0349335:
Su Woan Wo and colleagues validated a Malay-language version of the Empathy Quotient, a widely used self-report scale of empathy, in five hundred eighty-six Malaysian adults. Translated scales can drift in meaning, and this one's structure has been debated since its creation. The team also checked that the scale measures empathy the same way across genders and across those who took it in Malay or English.

Analysis settled on two factors, emotional and cognitive empathy, across twenty-three retained items, with acceptable consistency and stability over time. The structure held broadly steady across groups, so score comparisons between men and women, and between language versions, are meaningful. A validated local instrument lets Malaysian researchers and clinicians study empathy without importing untested assumptions.
plos-pone-0349635:
Karolynn Siegel and colleagues asked middle-aged Latino adults in northern Manhattan which memory and thinking problems would actually send them to a doctor. Early Alzheimer's diagnosis depends on families treating early slips as medical, not normal aging. One hundred sixty-one participants, aged forty to sixty-four, judged five kinds of problems occurring repeatedly over a few months.

Participants often explained symptoms away with benign reasons, one reason diagnosis comes late. Getting disoriented was the problem most likely to prompt a visit. The study identified what pushed people toward or away from seeking care for each symptom. Health campaigns that ignore how people interpret early slips will miss their audience; this work shows which interpretations doctors and educators need to counter.
plos-pone-0350035:
Yizhang Tong and seven colleagues validate a way to screen for osteoporosis on scans patients are already having. Their 2026 prospective study enrolled two hundred fifty-two people undergoing routine chest CT. Bone density normally needs dedicated equipment and a separate appointment. A phantom-less software system instead measures density in the spine directly from the chest images. No calibration phantom is scanned with the patient. Its readings were compared against the phantom-based standard method.

Two choices of reference fat region were tested: the software's automatic pick, and a manual pick for comparison. Diagnostic performance, agreement, and consistency statistics were all computed. Five different CT scanners took part, checking whether the method travels between machines. Opportunistic screening is the prize. If chest scans ordered for lungs can quietly flag fragile bones too, osteoporosis could be caught years before the first fracture announces it.
plos-pone-0350135:
Sitthisak Chaiyasuk and colleagues reviewed research on how governments audit and govern data in public services, with a focus on whether disabled people are served fairly. Following standard review methods, they gathered one hundred twenty-five studies and official sources published between 2010 and 2025. The review asked how data rules shape openness and equal treatment.

Three forces worked together in the evidence: how services are delivered to disabled people, how audit data are governed, and whether agencies build a data-driven culture. When any one leg was weak, records went missing and unfair outcomes became harder to challenge. The authors combine the three into a framework that agencies can use to check their own systems.
plos-pone-0350335:
Klara Mogensen and colleagues tested whether smart software reading brain scans can predict who will benefit from a brain fluid shunt for a treatable walking and thinking disorder of older adults. Scans from one hundred and forty nine operated patients were classed by whether walking speed improved after surgery. Three software routes were tried: deep networks, a fused network, and hand built scan features with classic learning.

All routes performed poorly, with none reaching seventy percent discrimination. Hand built features did least badly. Scan appearance alone, the authors conclude, does not yet hold enough signal to pick shunt winners. Clinics should keep using gait tests and fluid trials rather than scan based software for this call.
plos-pone-0350435:
Dong Li and Liuyong He examined why fine grains make a magnesium alloy last longer under repeated loading, in 2026 work. The alloy is light and strong, which suits sports gear, but it must survive many cycles without cracking.

Samples with fine grains beat coarse ones in strength and in fatigue life, lasting far longer at the same load while staying just as stretchy. Under the microscope, fine grains blocked the twinning and slip bands that seed cracks, and spread tiny strengthening particles more evenly. The clear mechanism gives makers a route to lighter sports equipment that still endures hard use.
plos-pone-0350735:
Zakir Ullah, Jiqin Han, and Aftab Anwar surveyed close to three hundred rice farming households in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, in early 2025. Rice feeds and funds many rural homes, yet costs, climate swings, and thin support squeeze growers. The survey charted uptake of greener methods like rotation, natural fertilisers, and water saving, and weighed their payoff.

Just over half of farmers used at least one greener method. Schooling, larger farms, credit and subsidy access, nearby markets, and training each raised uptake. Adopters harvested notably more rice per hectare and earned more, with stronger returns per cost. Matching checks backed the gains. Support that joins training with credit, the authors argue, spreads both greener and richer farming.
plos-pone-0350835:
Maobao Yang and four colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One survey study of whether auditors who are skilled with digital tools are less likely to cut corners on audit quality. Corner-cutting is a known threat to trustworthy audits. Drawing on nearly five hundred valid questionnaires from auditors, the authors modeled digital literacy's effect through two stepping stones: confidence with digital tools and actual task performance.

Greater digital literacy was tied to less corner-cutting, partly because digitally confident auditors performed their tasks better, and that performance gain formed a chain from confidence to behavior. Prosocial attitudes, caring about the wider good, changed how strongly these links operated. The authors advise firms to build auditors' digital confidence and competence as a concrete route to protecting audit quality.
plos-pone-0350935:
Doctors in Lesotho, a small mountain kingdom in southern Africa, worked through COVID-19 with thin resources. Laura Holdsworth and co-authors interviewed seven of them about well-being during the pandemic, in this 2026 PLOS One qualitative study.

Five themes emerged. Doctors felt swamped, unprepared, and out of control, and lived with constant uncertainty and threat. Isolation cut both ways, since colleagues, friends, and family also became lifelines. Many coped alone at first, yet several described new perspectives they carried forward. The authors discuss what national and local support should look like so doctors are not left to manage such strain by themselves.
plos-pone-0351135:
Katarina Zorcic and co-authors describe in 2026 a newsletter that uses a large language model to sum up major clinical trials for busy doctors. Software gathers trial reports from top journals, pulls key facts from each summary, and drafts plain language briefs. Fifty issues went out over nearly two years to several hundred readers.

Checked against hand review, the briefs reported most trial facts correctly, with the best scores for patient group and study stage. Readers who answered a survey rated the service highly and said it helped them keep up. Promotion at meetings grew the audience far faster than quiet days did.
plos-pone-0351335:
Knowing which habitat fills a landscape helps protect wildlife, and Mahdis Tourian and colleagues taught a computer to name habitats from ordinary ground-level photos. Their 2026 PLOS One study, built with Natural England, sorts each picture into one of sixteen classes under an established English habitat framework.

The team adjusted and balanced thousands of photos, then fine-tuned a deep learning model first made for outlining objects in images. Repeated cross-checks measured how often the model agreed with human labels. Because the method needs only photos, it could tap the huge supply of pictures from volunteers and field visits, widening habitat mapping beyond satellite views.
plos-pone-0351635:
Davina Sharma and colleagues present a protocol for mapping how health systems manage rehabilitation for people living long-term with serious brain injury. A severe traumatic brain injury is now understood as a chronic condition, yet care after the first year varies wildly across Europe's differently funded systems. The review will collect evidence on the management practices, at personal, organizational, and national levels, that shape access and continuity of rehab.

Searches will cover studies of adults at least a year past injury, published since twenty eighteen, across four databases, following standard scoping methods. As a protocol, it reports no results. The eventual map should show where systems hand patients off well and where they drop them, giving advocates and planners a shared picture on which to press for steadier long-term care.
plos-pone-0351735:
Xuehua Li authored this 2026 PLOS One simulation study on how rock containing two crossing sets of cracks breaks under pressure. Such cross-shaped fracture patterns are the most typical found in rock masses, and their growth is a main reason rock fails in mines and tunnels. Using specialized failure-simulation software, Li varied the angle between the main crack and the pressing direction and tracked how damage spread.

Changing that angle reshaped the stress around crack tips, which changed how much energy new cracks needed to grow. The effects showed up as clear differences in the rock's strength and in the crackling signals it emitted while failing. The author argues the results help engineers predict which cracked rock masses are closest to collapse under load.
plos-pone-0351835:
Enkang Li and four colleagues map the geography of China's listed food manufacturers. Their 2026 study assembles records on seven hundred seventy-seven companies. It asks where these firms sit, how similar their business lines are, and how they expand between cities. Richer regions host more firms, and bigger ones. Beyond that simple pattern, the detail gets interesting.

Firms rarely share the same business scope, even when neighbours. Similarity fades quickly with distance. Still, the similarity network shows small-world structure, with clusters shaped by place and sub-industry. The hiring network tells a different story. When firms recruit across cities, transport links matter most. Easy travel knits distant plants into one corporate web. For regional planners, the study links factory geography to the roads and rails that let companies grow.
plos-pone-0351935:
Gonzales-Huerta and colleagues tested how a tuberculosis-related molecule affects immune cells fighting a fungus in a 2026 lab study. Many patients develop a lasting lung fungus infection after tuberculosis, and the mycobacterial coat molecule is known to blunt immune pathways. Mouse immune cells were treated with two forms of the molecule, then challenged with the fungus.

Cell death, signal release, and fungus killing were measured by several methods, including live imaging. The work probes why the fungus gains a foothold after tuberculosis damages lungs. Understanding that handover could guide combined treatment for patients facing both infections, a group numbering over a million worldwide.
plos-pone-0352335:
Lina Yan and Xin Gu assess how city landscapes control rainwater runoff in this 2026 study. Their test site is a dense urban community. Sealed surfaces and fragmented green space push rain into drains fast. The authors classified the landscape into eight digital types using mapping software, satellite imagery, and weather records. An ecosystem services model then simulated runoff, calibrated against real measurements.

The model proved reliable at this small scale. Where sealed surfaces covered about thirty-seven percent of the area, runoff ran deep and fast. The team then tested an optimised layout. Adding green space and stitching green patches closer together changed the picture. Mean annual runoff depth fell from roughly forty-two millimetres to about twenty-seven. Such numbers give neighbourhood planners a concrete lever: modest greening, arranged well, can meaningfully cut the water a community sheds during storms.
plos-pone-0352435:
M S Amithalal and co-authors made silver nanoparticles, tiny specks prized for killing germs, using leaf extract of the tree Falconeria insignis instead of harsh chemicals. Plant juices can both form the particles and coat them, a greener route to a material eyed for wound care and coatings. The team confirmed the particles with light, X-ray, and microscope checks.

The plant-made particles were irregular in shape, very small, and wrapped in natural compounds from the leaf. Against Staphylococcus aureus, a common wound germ, they killed far better than either the leaf extract or silver solution alone. Statistical tests backed the gap. One tree's leaves will not stock a factory, but the work adds a candidate species to the search for clean ways to make germ-fighting materials.
plos-pone-0353235:
Dong, Yang, and Chen studied whether pretending to be green pays company bosses in a 2026 paper. Greenwashing means talking up environmental care beyond what a firm truly does. The team tested whether such talk links to higher executive pay, and through what paths.

Firms that greenwashed more tended to pay their executives more. The link ran through better short-term results and a stronger reputation for the boss. The effect was larger in private firms and in firms with stock-based pay plans. Findings like these warn boards and investors that green talk can reward leaders personally, even when real environmental gains lag behind.
plos-pone-0353835:
Ami Yamasato and colleagues test in 2026 a digital twin idea meant to ease first meetings for young people who feel nervous talking with strangers. Each person saw a generated video chat before a real online talk. One group watched their own twin talk with their partner's twin, while the other watched two strangers' twins.

Heart rate change, the main measure, did not differ clearly between groups overall. Still, the twin group calmed after the preview and stayed steadier, while the other group grew more tense before talking. They also reported less anxiety and more wish to keep talking. The authors call the signs early and in need of firmer testing.
plos-pone-0353935:
Peter G. van der Velden and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE asking whether life's troubles come first for people who end up as physically aggressive conspiracy believers. Using a Dutch population panel, they recorded six psychosocial problems, from severe anxiety and money trouble to trauma and low life satisfaction. Months later they surveyed the same people about conspiracy beliefs and aggression, sorting everyone into four groups.

People carrying earlier problems were far more likely to land in the aggressive groups, whether or not they believed conspiracies. The concentration was striking among aggressive believers: roughly two-thirds of respondents with four or more problems fell in that group, compared with only a small fraction of those with none. Individual problems differed in weight, but the count mattered most. Preventing aggression around conspiracy movements, they suggest, may start with ordinary social support, before beliefs harden.
plos-pone-0354035:
Tang and colleagues, in a 2026 cell study, untangle a chain of genetic switches that helps cow muscle cells grow, and that a ketosis chemical disrupts. Dairy cows often fall into ketosis after calving, flooding the body with a fuel molecule called BHBA, which can hinder muscle development. The team worked with satellite cells, the stem cells that repair and build muscle.

BHBA slowed the cells' maturation, and more BHBA slowed it more. Two players pushed back: a long noncoding RNA and a growth gene it protects. Between them sits a small RNA that does the opposite, slowing growth and deepening BHBA's block. The long RNA works as a sponge, soaking up the small RNA and freeing the growth gene. Tests confirmed the three are directly linked. The authors say the chain offers a new angle on muscle loss in ketotic cows, and a possible target for protecting herd condition.
plos-pone-0354135:
Alessandra Burgio and four colleagues project how many Italian babies will be conceived with medical help by 2050, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Italy is famous for very late childbearing, which pushes more couples toward fertility treatment. The team combined official 2023 data with nine scenarios, varying how fast mothers' ages rise and how fast treatment rates grow.

Changes in the age mix of women, they found, would barely move the share of assisted births. Later childbearing and wider use of treatment mattered far more, lifting the share from a little over four percent in 2023 to roughly eleven or twelve percent by mid-century. Planners, they argue, should prepare for that growth.
plos-pone-0354235:
Postler and colleagues, in a 2026 study, compare outcomes when the lower thigh bone is replaced with a prosthesis after a break versus as a planned revision. This operation is often the last chance to save a leg when the bone above a knee replacement is badly damaged. The two routes to it may carry very different risks.

Ninety-three patients at one center were followed for about five years on average. Patients whose bone broke had fewer earlier operations and reported higher satisfaction afterward. Yet their death rates were much higher, reflecting the frailty that comes with such breaks. Planned revision patients needed far more repeat surgery by five years, but died less often. Being female lowered repeat-surgery risk, while an earlier stiffer knee implant and a planned indication raised it. The authors advise surgeons to weigh these opposite patterns when counseling patients.
plos-pone-0354335:
Bashar Al Qaroot and colleagues ran a randomized trial to find the best height for wedge insoles, a simple shoe insert prescribed to unload the painful inner side of arthritic knees. Their 2026 study gave thirty-four patients with mild to moderate inner knee osteoarthritis either escalating custom wedges or standard care, tracking X-ray alignment, joint space, and symptom scores.

A mid-height wedge performed best. It straightened the bowed alignment in the non-dominant leg, stopped the joint space from narrowing further while untreated knees kept thinning, and eased pain and overall symptoms. The tallest wedge was abandoned because most patients could not tolerate it. The dose lesson is practical: enough wedge to correct, not so much that patients quit wearing it.
plos-pone-0354635:
Lin Tao and co-authors surveyed young breast cancer survivors in China about existential distress during rehabilitation. Existential distress, anguish over meaning, death, and identity, can shadow recovery long after treatment ends. Their 2026 survey covered several hundred women under fifty within five years of treatment, using standard scales for adaptation, support, resilience, and distress.

Poorer adjustment to life after cancer came with clearly higher distress. Two stepping stones carried much of that effect. Social support alone passed along about half of the indirect influence, and resilience formed a second route, including a chain through support into resilience. Tao and colleagues say rehabilitation should build support networks and coping strength, not only treat the body.
plos-pone-0354735:
Ratchanok Phonyiam and three colleagues published this 2026 study protocol on life after childbirth for Thai women with type 2 diabetes. Income, housing, work, and support shape health after delivery as much as medical care does, yet nobody had studied these women's postnatal experience. The plan first adapts a well-being questionnaire into Thai, then surveys women, then interviews selected mothers in depth.

The two strands will be merged to show how social conditions drive well-being scores. As a protocol, it reports intentions, not results. Phonyiam aims to guide fairer postnatal care for diabetic mothers.
plos-pone-0355335:
Jijie Fan and colleagues present in 2026 a method to judge whether heart tracings from wearable devices are clean enough to trust. Noise from movement, power lines, and drifting baselines can spoil readings and mislead later diagnosis. Their method needs no hand labelled training set, a common limit in real use.

Fake noise was added to clean tracings to teach the system what damage looks like. A rebuilding step then highlighted the damaged zones, and scores from the whole signal and from those zones were combined. Tests on four public sets gave strong scores, suggesting the joint view generalises better to unseen noise.
plos-pone-0355735:
Weilue He, Julie Osborne, and Megan Frost test a new way to sterilize medical equipment in their 2026 paper. Hospitals and device makers now rely heavily on ethylene oxide gas, which works well but is highly toxic to people and the environment. Their candidate replacement is nitric oxide gas, used at ordinary room temperature and normal air pressure.

The team exposed hardy bacterial spores, the standard test for sterilization, to nitric oxide and tracked how fast they died off. The gas killed the test spores in a steady, predictable pattern and also inactivated two bacteria that commonly cause infections. The dose that workers or users might encounter stayed well below the level classed as immediately dangerous, pointing to a safer, greener option.
plos-pone-0355835:
Dan Kuang and colleagues measured how temperature shaped deaths and costs in Chengdu, a basin megacity in southwest China. Both heat and cold raise mortality, but their local weight was unquantified. Their 2026 study modelled seven years of daily death records across twenty-three counties against weather, then priced the burden for a recent year.

The risk curve was U-shaped, with a safe middle band. Just over seven percent of non-accidental deaths were tied to temperatures outside that band. Cold accounted for most of the share, several times the heat portion. Kuang and colleagues argue basin cities should plan for cold snaps as seriously as heatwaves when protecting public health and budgets.
plos-pone-0355935:
Holly Tuten and co-authors report the first years of a public tick reporting programme in Illinois. Tick-borne illness is rising in the United States, and two biting species are spreading into new ground. Their 2026 account covers submissions from residents between 2018 and 2023, with lab testing of a subset.

Residents sent in eight tick species, led by the lone star tick and the blacklegged tick. Submissions arrived nearly all year and came mostly from people, dogs, and deer. Testing found six disease agents, including the Lyme disease bacterium in about one in seven adult blacklegged ticks. The authors say public submissions widen surveillance cheaply and reveal year-round exposure risk.
plos-pone-0356235:
Leila Verena da Conceição and six colleagues develop artificial seeds for cassava, a staple crop that feeds hundreds of millions, in this 2026 study. Cassava is normally planted from stem cuttings, which multiply slowly and carry disease. Their synthetic seeds wrap tiny axillary buds in beads of sodium alginate gel. The team varied the gel strength and the chemical used to set it. They then measured how well buds pushed through and grew outside sterile conditions.

The setting chemical proved decisive. Beads set with calcium chloride hardened into tight networks that strangled emergence, stopping it entirely at higher gel strengths. Beads set with calcium hydroxide let up to four fifths of buds emerge with strong growth, though plain uncoated buds still did slightly better. A dilute gel near one percent balanced sturdiness and emergence best. Storage and field trials come next.
plos-pone-0356735: Chagonda and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE plan for a review on early signs of a dangerous pregnancy condition. Preeclampsia can strike without warning later in pregnancy. The planned review covers tests that measure two urine chemicals, glycolic acid and methylsuccinic acid, in the first trimester. A cheap early urine test could flag risk months ahead, when watchful care helps most.
plos-pone-0357035:
Chia-Wei Tsai and co-authors break a recently published quantum messaging scheme that claimed ironclad security. The scheme let two parties exchange secret bits both ways under a controller's supervision, using four-particle quantum states, and its proof leaned on wiretap channel theory. The critics assume the controller is fully untrusted, exactly as the original design allowed, and show how that controller can cheat with a classic Trojan horse trick.

By sneaking probe light into the equipment, the controller can quietly read off the private keys and then reconstruct every secret bit both parties sent, the attack shows. Because the probes leave the checked particles untouched, the scheme's own error alarms never fire. Tsai and colleagues argue the proof failed by ignoring the physical layer, a warning for quantum security claims generally.
plos-pone-0357735:
Sidra Rashid leads a team of six teaching self driving systems to guess where cars will go next, in PLOS ONE in 2026. A vehicle's future path depends on its neighbors, but not equally: one close truck matters more than five distant sedans. Earlier models either watched a small neighborhood or treated every neighbor alike, and their errors grew over longer horizons. The team's model pairs a memory network with a multi head attention system that ranges across the scene.

Attention scores let the model weight the vehicles that influence the target, and position aware features capture long range patterns. On a public highway dataset, the model beat every established rival. At the five second horizon its prediction error fell by more than half compared with the next best method. For a car planning a lane change, that margin is the difference between a calm decision and a late swerve.
plos-pone-0358135:
Aleksandr Diachenko and Detlef Gronenborn wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article in archaeology. It looks for signals of social dynamics in archaeological time-series, long sequences of finds ordered by age. The authors study how the way culture is passed on, and the biases of makers, shape the diversity of assemblages, the collections of artifacts found together.

How people copy each other's styles, and how makers favor certain forms, can raise or lower the variety in the record. Untangling those forces matters because archaeologists read past societies from exactly these patterns. If bias alone can create a trend, social conclusions drawn from artifact counts need extra care.
plos-pone-0358235:
Weilong Zheng and Huanhuan Zheng mapped cell states inside melanoma tumors, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. A tumor is not uniform; where a cancer cell sits shapes how it behaves. The pair studied the spatial layout of melanoma cell states and the neighborhoods formed with support cells called fibroblasts.

Their map reveals tumor cells beside cancer-associated fibroblasts that show enhanced capacity to multiply. That geography points to where the tumor grows fastest and where therapy should strike. It also suggests that cutting the support fibroblasts provide could slow growth. Spatial studies like this are changing cancer from a list of cell types into a map, and maps suggest routes of attack.
plos-pone-0358335:
Lingzhu Huang led a team of seven authors studying a fast, deadly heart illness in children, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Fulminant myocarditis is severe heart inflammation that can kill within hours, yet it can look like a stomach bug at first. The team searched emergency department records for warning signs.

Huang's group described the clinical traits of children with the condition and flagged signs visible early in the emergency visit. A short list of red flags helps emergency doctors act before the heart fails, with intensive care and heart support ready. For parents, the wider lesson is that rapid worsening after a seeming stomach illness deserves urgent care.
plos-pone-0358535:
Joseph Resch and Mark Handcock wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article in statistics. It assesses variational likelihood estimation, an approximate computing method, inside network formation models. Those models explain how social and other networks form their links, one tie at a time.

Exact likelihood calculations for networks grow impossibly slow as networks enlarge, so researchers lean on approximations. Assessing one approximation honestly shows when its answers can be trusted and when they drift. Statisticians who model networks, from friendships to trade, are the audience for this check on a common shortcut.
plos-pone-0359335:
Yongwei Fan and six colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It aims at diagnosing Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia early, a lung infection common in children and young adults. The authors develop and test a model that predicts the illness from signs and tests taken in a routine examination.

A model built from ordinary examination findings could flag this pneumonia before specialized tests return, guiding early treatment choices. Development plus validation means the model was built on one set of patients and checked on another. Clinicians who treat children and lung disease, facing look-alike pneumonias, are the audience for such a model.
plos-pone-0359535:
Tiffany Chen and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It works at county level in the United States. The authors study links between walking and bicycling data gathered automatically by devices, and self-reported data on activity outside work, what people say they do.

Passive data from phones and counters could give health officials cheap, current activity maps if it matches what surveys show. Comparing the two sources tests whether the automatic stream can stand in for costly surveys. Public health agencies planning activity programs county by county are the readers for this check.
plos-pone-0359635: Viktorisson and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on work absence after a mini-stroke in Sweden. A transient ischemic attack is a brief stroke-like event that soon passes. The team used national registers to follow working-age adults and their sick leave. Knowing how long people stay off work after such an event helps doctors, employers, and insurers plan support and return-to-work steps.
plos-pone-0359835:
Ting Zhang, Sheng Ye, Liang Ye, and Zekai Qian published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It concerns the tomb of Yue Fei, a famous Chinese general from the Song dynasty. Stone relics at the tomb need cleaning, and the authors evaluate that cleaning with infrared thermography.

Infrared thermography uses heat images to reveal surface conditions that the eye may miss, such as damp or hidden damage. A non-destructive check suits fragile heritage stone, where testing must not harm the object. Conservators caring for stone monuments can apply this evaluation approach before and after cleaning other historic sites.
