Kirtland, Ohio printed the first Doctrine and Covenants in 1835, the young church's book of revelations. Joseph Smith and his counsellors, Oliver Cowdery, Sidney Rigdon, and Frederick G. Williams, stood behind the edition. It gathered the revelations Smith had received, the commandments guiding the Latter Day Saints.

Bound with the revelations stand the Lectures on Faith, seven talks on doctrine later dropped from the book. That pairing makes the 1835 edition precious: later printings changed the contents. As the founding doctrinal text of the movement, this first form shows Mormon scripture before it settled into its standard shape.
social-security-act-1935:
Franklin Roosevelt signed the Social Security Act in 1935, amid deep depression. The New Deal law creates old-age pensions for American workers. Jobless insurance and aid to the needy stand in its other titles.

The act founds what later ages call the American welfare state. Old age, the law pledges, need not mean poverty and fear. Workers and bosses pay in, and the retired draw their checks. Critics then and since have fought over its costs and reach. No New Deal law has touched more lives for so long since 1935. Its monthly checks remain the floor under old age in America.
swan-speculum-mundi-1635:
John Swan, an English minister, published Speculum Mundi in 1635. The Latin title means a mirror of the world. Swan set out to survey all creation in order, as an act of both learning and devotion, for readers who wanted the world explained in one book.

Beasts, stars, waters, and wonders pass in review through its chapters. Among them sits the famous tale of the Edam mermaid of 1403. Dutch fishermen, Swan reports, caught her and kept her for years. Such stories stand beside plain teaching without apology. The book shows a pious, curious mind taking in the whole of creation at once.
tob-0035:
For about two decades the Central Intelligence Agency backed a strange experiment: could trained viewers describe distant places by mind alone? Files from that effort, run under names ending with the Stargate Project, were later declassified. Protocols, session records, and official reviews survive in the paperwork.

Remote viewers sat in offices and reported images of bases, hostages, and hidden sites. The agency's own reviewers weighed hits against misses and judged the results too weak for real spying. The files remain gripping as Cold War history: careful men in gray offices filing reports on psychics. Espionage has no odder chapter.
tob-13335:
Evelyn Underhill published Mysticism in 1911, a study of the nature and growth of man's spiritual awareness. She wrote as a scholar who also practiced the life she described. The large book at once became the standard English work on its subject.

Underhill traces the mystic way through awakening, purification, illumination, the dark night, and union, drawing on saints and writers from many ages. She quotes widely and treats mysticism as a real, testable side of human life. Her book brought the mystics to modern general readers and founded the modern study of the subject in English.
tob-14435:
The Sentences of Sextus gather 451 short sayings on how to live, credited to a sage named Sextus. Pagans and Christians of the ancient world both prized the set. A copy turned up at Nag Hammadi, and church writers quoted it for centuries.

The sayings urge control of the tongue, freedom from passion, care for the soul, and a life made like God's. Many lines run to a single sharp sentence a reader can carry all day. Origen cited the collection with respect. It stands as proof that moral wisdom in the ancient world crossed the lines between faiths.
tob-4135:
A. E. Waite published The Doctrine and Literature of the Kabalah in 1902, the first full English study of Jewish mysticism's teachings and books. The Sefer Yetzirah, the Book of Formation, and the Zohar, the Book of Splendor, receive long treatment. Later Kabbalists and their schools fill out the survey.

Waite reads the tradition as a secret doctrine of the soul's return to God, a view colored by his own mystic hopes. Scholars now correct him often, but for decades his book was the doorway. Verified from the 1919 edition, it shows Victorian occult scholarship at its most serious and industrious.
tob-4235:
William Smith edited the Dictionary of Greek and Roman Antiquities, and the revised edition of 1870 became the Victorian classicist's constant companion. Article by article, the dictionary covers law, war, religion, dress, coinage, and daily life in the ancient world. Smith marshaled a team of scholars to write it.

A student with a question about a Roman court, a Greek ship, or a festival calendar found the answer here, with sources cited. Illustrations of tools, arms, and buildings crowd the pages. Verified from the 1919 edition, the dictionary served schools and universities for a century, and antiquarians still pull it down.
un-ga-res-35: Five states knocked on the UN's door in 1946 and got no answer from the Security Council. Albania, Mongolia, Transjordan, Ireland, and Portugal had all applied, and the Council had made no recommendation on any of them. Resolution 35, passed on 19 November 1946, sends the five bids back. The Council is told to judge each one on its own merits, by the test of the Charter.
un-ga-res-a-69-35:
Zones free of nuclear arms now cover the southern half of the earth, and Resolution A/69/35, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, marks their reach. The text recalls the rules of the 1978 disarmament session on such zones. It backs the 1999 guide lines on how zones should be set up, by free deal among the states of a region.

Four pacts are named: Tlatelolco for Latin America, Rarotonga for the South Pacific, Bangkok for Southeast Asia, and Pelindaba for Africa, with the Antarctic Treaty beside them. All the southern zones, the text notes with pleasure, are now in force. One hundred fifteen states stand as parties to such pacts. Joint work among them, through shared meetings, is urged on.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 35 was adopted on 19 November 1946, at the forty-ninth plenary meeting. It took up five stalled membership bids. Albania, the Mongolian People's Republic, the Hashemite Kingdom of Transjordan, Ireland, and Portugal had all applied. But the Security Council had sent the Assembly no recommendation on any of them. Membership stands open to peace-loving states able and willing to meet the Charter's terms. Recalling that, the Assembly urged the Council to weigh each bid again on its own merits.

General Assembly resolution 69/35 (2014) celebrates the nuclear-weapon-free southern hemisphere. It welcomes the contribution of the Antarctic Treaty and the treaties of Tlatelolco, Rarotonga, Bangkok, and Pelindaba. It notes that all southern-hemisphere nuclear-weapon-free zones are now in force. They cover 115 states parties and signatories. The Assembly calls for adherence to the zones' protocols by the states concerned. It calls for withdrawal of reservations by nuclear-weapon states. It calls for closer cooperation among the zones. It reaffirms freedom of the high seas and rights of passage.
un-sc-res-1035: Bearing number 1035, this resolution of the Security Council is dated 1995 in the catalog. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-1335: Holding number 1335 in the Council series, this resolution carries a 1999 date in the library catalog. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-135:
In May 1960, a planned summit of the leaders of France, the Soviet Union, Britain, and the United States fell apart, and public hopes for easing the Cold War fell with it. Resolution 135, adopted on 27 May 1960 by nine votes to none, speaks to that moment of disappointment and rising tension.

The Council warns that the arms race adds to the danger. It recommends that the governments concerned settle their disputes by talks or other peaceful means, as the Charter provides. It appeals to all member governments to avoid the use or threat of force, and to respect each other's sovereignty, land, and political independence.
un-sc-res-1435:
Israeli troops had surrounded the Palestinian leader's compound in Ramallah in September 2002. On 23 September 2002 the Security Council demanded an end to the siege measures. It repeated its call for a complete halt to violence. Terror attacks, provocation, and destruction all had to stop. The Council condemned bombings against civilians in Israel days earlier. It also condemned an attack in a Palestinian school.

Israel had to stop destroying Palestinian civilian and security buildings. Its forces had to pull back fast to the positions held before September 2000. The Palestinian Authority had to bring those behind terror acts to justice. The vote was fourteen to none. The United States abstained.
un-sc-res-1535:
The Counter-Terrorism Committee was rebuilt with a professional arm on 26 March 2004. Resolution 1373 (2001) had set every state's duties after the September 2001 attacks. The committee of Council members had checked state reports for two years. Its report on revitalization, S/2004/124, proposed a stronger structure. States were reminded that counter-terrorism steps must respect human rights, refugee, and humanitarian law.

The Council endorsed the revitalization report. The renewed committee would pair a plenary of Council states with a bureau. A new Counter-Terrorism Committee Executive Directorate, CTED, headed by an executive director, would do the expert work. The director had to file an organizational plan within thirty days of taking office. The plan would go to the Council for its blessing. The committee would keep reporting to the Council at regular times. CTED became the standing expert staff of the Council's counter-terrorism watch.
un-sc-res-1635:
MONUC was extended through Congo's election year on 28 October 2005. The Pretoria transition deal still framed the country's path. Elections were the base for lasting peace, the Council stressed. Militias and foreign armed groups in the east kept fighting and threatened the polls. Rights abuses by those groups were deplored.

The Council extended MONUC's mandate until 30 September 2006. The temporary rise in strength granted that September would stay part of the mission until that date at the latest, and its short-term character was stressed. Transitional bodies and all Congolese parties were called to keep the elections free, fair, and on time. The unity government had to press security sector reform and the disarmament of fighters. Donors were urged to keep funding the process as a matter of urgency. MONUC, within its means, was asked to support the electoral work and protect civilians under threat.
un-sc-res-1735:
Sanctions on Al-Qaida and the Taliban are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1735, adopted on 22 December 2006. Attacks in Afghanistan were rising, and the groups were spreading their message online. The sanctions list had grown for seven years, yet states applied it unevenly. Fairer listing steps had become a pressing demand.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council restates the asset freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo on everyone on the list. States proposing new names must now file a detailed statement of case. Listed people must be told why they were named and how to seek removal. The committee gains clearer rules for taking names off. Freeze rules are spelled out to reach money of every kind, even funds behind web services.
un-sc-res-1835:
Iran's nuclear file returned to the Council in Resolution 1835, adopted in September 2008. Earlier rounds had already placed sanctions on Tehran over uranium enrichment. This text restated those demands and pressed Iran to answer inspectors' questions about possible military work.

The members call again for Iran to suspend enrichment and to cooperate fully with the International Atomic Energy Agency. No new sanctions were added, which itself signaled division among the major powers. For readers, the resolution is a snapshot of a standoff hardening: the demands stay fixed while the pressure stalls.
un-sc-res-1935:
Resolution 1935 brought Darfur under a formal Council decision, adopted on 30 July 2010. Security had worsened again that year. Rebel attacks, air strikes by the government, and tribal fighting all rose. Peacekeepers faced ambushes, and one helicopter pilot had been seized. Some armed groups still refused to join peace talks.

The Council extends the African Union-United Nations force, called UNAMID, for twelve months to 31 July 2011. Guarding civilians across Darfur comes first in every use of its strength. Safe and open aid access ranks second. The mission must draft a full strategy to reach those aims. All sides are told to stop fighting and to stop attacking civilians, aid staff, and peacekeepers at once.
un-sc-res-235: The record catalogued as Resolution 235, dated 1967, preserves one formal decision of the United Nations Security Council. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-2735:
Resolution 2735, adopted in June 2024, put the Security Council behind a ceasefire plan for the war in Gaza. The plan, announced by the United States, set out stages meant to end the fighting that began in October 2023. The Council welcomed the proposal and urged both sides to accept it.

The stages in the text move from a first halt in fighting and hostage releases to a permanent end of hostilities and Gaza's reconstruction. It also rejects any change to Gaza's territory. The resolution matters as the Council's clearest shared call to close that war, after months of divided votes.
un-sc-res-335: Two German states were recommended for United Nations membership by the Security Council on 22 June 1973. The Council had taken up the applications of the German Democratic Republic and the Federal Republic of Germany one by one. It recommended to the General Assembly that the German Democratic Republic be admitted. It recommended in the same terms that the Federal Republic of Germany be admitted. The recommendations opened the way for both states to take seats that autumn, a marker of the Cold War division being managed rather than settled.
un-sc-res-35: The Council spoke on Committee work through Resolution 35, adopted on 3 October 1947 by nine votes to none, with two abstentions. A Committee of Three had been formed under an earlier text that year. The Council asks the Secretary-General to call the committee together and arrange how its work is organized. It also asks the three members to take up their duties with the utmost speed. The short text settles only the machinery, leaving the substance to the committee itself.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Security Council resolution 1035 was adopted unanimously on 21 December 1995. It follows up the General Framework Agreement for Peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina and resolution 1031, which authorized the multinational implementation force IFOR. Acting on the Secretary-General's report of 13 December 1995, the Council approves his proposals for the United Nations part in carrying out the Peace Agreement.

The Council establishes a United Nations civilian police force, the International Police Task Force (IPTF), for one year. The year runs from the transfer of authority from the United Nations Protection Force to IFOR. A United Nations civilian office is established together with it. The Task Force takes the police tasks set out in Annex 11 of the Peace Agreement. It works under the Secretary-General's authority, with coordination by the High Representative. It is to be reported on at least every three months.

For the Prevlaka peninsula, the disputed coastal strip between Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, calm on the ground still did not settle who owned the land. United Nations observers, UNMOP, watched that the zone stayed demilitarized. This text of 12 January 2001 decides how long they would stay.

The observers were authorized to keep working until 15 July 2001. The Council welcomed the open crossing points in the zone, which let civilians and trade pass safely in both directions. It still flagged breaches of the demilitarization rules and limits on the observers' freedom of movement, and it urged both sides to resume talks toward a negotiated settlement.

Days after a four-power summit in Paris collapsed, this text of 27 May 1960 speaks to a frightened world. Hopes for a meeting of the leaders of France, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom, and the United States had just failed. Public worry about rising tension and the arms race runs through every line.

Governments are urged to settle their disputes by talks and other peaceful means under the Charter. All states are asked to avoid force or threats and to respect each other's borders and independence. The four powers are pressed to keep working on full disarmament under world control, an end to nuclear tests, and talks against surprise attack.

Israeli tanks surrounded Yasser Arafat's headquarters in Ramallah in September 2002. The siege followed suicide bombings inside Israel on 18 and 19 September. Troops had also re-entered other Palestinian cities. Resolution 1435 was adopted on 23 September 2002. Fourteen members voted yes. The United States abstained.

The Council demanded an immediate end to the measures around Ramallah. Destruction of Palestinian offices and services had to stop. Israeli forces were told to withdraw quickly to positions held before September 2000. Terror attacks on civilians were condemned on all sides. The Palestinian Authority had to bring attackers to justice. Support flowed to the Quartet's peace efforts.

Resolution 1535, adopted unanimously on 26 March 2004, builds a professional staff for the Council's counter-terrorism watchdog. The Counter-Terrorism Committee, created after the September 2001 attacks, reviewed how states carried out their duties to suppress terror financing and deny safe haven. Member states were praised for cooperating with it, and reminded that counter-terrorism measures must still respect human rights, refugee, and humanitarian law.

The Council approved the committee's revitalization plan and created its Executive Directorate, CTED, staffed by experts who would visit countries, assess gaps, and arrange technical help. The directorate was set up as a special political mission for an initial period ending in December 2007, subject to review. Later resolutions kept extending it.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo's move toward elections is the focus of Resolution 1635, adopted on 28 October 2005. The UN Organization Mission there, MONUC, backed a transition set out in a 2002 peace deal. Militias and foreign armed groups still fought in the east, abused civilians, and threatened the planned vote. Illegal mining and the arms trade helped feed the conflict.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends MONUC until 30 September 2006. It allows 300 more troops so an infantry battalion can deploy in Katanga for extra safety during the election period. It marks that rise as temporary. It calls on Congolese leaders to hold free, fair, and calm elections on the agreed timetable. It also calls on them to merge the armed forces and national police into one service with proper pay and supplies.

The Al-Qaida and Taliban sanctions machinery is tightened in Resolution 1735, adopted on 22 December 2006. The 1267 Committee's Consolidated List was growing, states were listing names with uneven evidence, and listed people often learned of it late.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council confirms the asset freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo on listed Al-Qaida, Taliban, and associated persons and entities. It stresses that the freeze reaches economic resources of every kind, including internet hosting services. States proposing listings must file a detailed statement of case on a standard cover sheet, marking what can be made public. The Secretariat must notify the states concerned within two weeks of a listing, with the public case summary and delisting procedures. The Committee must keep developing delisting guidelines, weighing mistaken identity, death, or severed association. The window for objecting to basic-expense exemptions grows from 48 hours to three working days.

Iran's nuclear programme is taken up again on 27 September 2008, without new sanctions being added. The atomic energy agency's September report described continued non-compliance. The six negotiating powers had restated their two-track approach: talks and incentives on one side, pressure on the other, and that framework is backed again.

Earlier positions are reaffirmed: the presidential statement of March 2006 and the four Iran resolutions that followed it. Commitment to an early negotiated solution is restated, and continuing efforts toward one are welcomed. Iran is called on to comply fully and without delay with its duties under those resolutions and the agency's requirements, above all suspending enrichment work. The matter stays under review.

Darfur's hybrid mission is extended with civilian protection as its first priority in Resolution 1935, adopted on 30 July 2010. Security in Darfur was deteriorating. There were ceasefire violations, rebel attacks, government aerial bombardment, and inter-tribal fighting. Attacks on humanitarian workers and peacekeepers restricted aid access. UNAMID was nearing full deployment, and Sudan and Chad had normalized relations in January 2010 with a joint border force.

The Council extends the African Union-United Nations Hybrid Operation in Darfur, UNAMID, for twelve months to 31 July 2011. UNAMID must give priority to protecting civilians across Darfur and to safe, timely, unhindered humanitarian access. It must develop a comprehensive strategy for both and support the AU-UN political process and the Joint Chief Mediator. The Council strongly condemns attacks on UNAMID, demands Sudan remove obstacles to its movement and comply with the Status of Forces Agreement, and requires ninety-day progress reports against benchmarks.

During the Six-Day War, Israel and Syria each announced that they accepted the Council's demand for a cease-fire. Resolution 235, adopted unanimously on 9 June 1967, followed two resolutions passed earlier the same week. The Council confirmed those calls for an immediate cease-fire and an end to all military action. It demanded that hostilities stop at once. The Secretary-General was told to contact both governments immediately, arrange full compliance, and report back within two hours. That deadline shows how fast events were moving that day.

A three-phase cease-fire plan for the war in Gaza won the Council's backing on 10 June 2024. Egypt, Qatar, and the United States had been mediating between Israel and Hamas. A new proposal had been announced on 31 May 2024. Resolution 2735 deals with that proposal.

The Council welcomed the plan and noted that Israel had accepted it. Hamas was called on to accept it too, and both sides were urged to carry it out in full. The first phase would bring a complete cease-fire and the release of hostages. Women, the elderly, and the wounded were named in particular. The second phase would end the fighting for good, free the remaining hostages, and pull Israeli forces out of Gaza. The third phase would start a major rebuilding plan for Gaza, lasting several years.

Two German states enter the United Nations in a single text, Resolution 335, adopted on 22 June 1973. The Council considered the applications separately: one from the German Democratic Republic in the east, another from the Federal Republic of Germany in the west. Their applications arrived days apart in June, after the two states had signed a treaty regulating relations between them.

The Council recommends that the General Assembly admit the German Democratic Republic, and then, in a parallel line, that it admit the Federal Republic of Germany. The paired recommendation was a landmark of Cold War diplomacy, accepting divided Germany into the UN as two states. Both took their seats that September.

Early Council business often ran through small committees. Resolution 35, adopted on 3 October 1947, concerns one such group, a committee of three member states. Poland and the Soviet Union abstained in the vote. The committee itself had been created days earlier by Resolution 31.

The text gives the Secretary-General a practical task. He must call the three members together. He must also arrange how their work is organized. The committee, for its part, is told to move fast. It should begin exercising its functions with the utmost dispatch. The resolution is two sentences long, a glimpse of the Council's working habits in 1947.

Armenia emerged from the Soviet Union's collapse as an independent republic. It applied for a UN seat within weeks of the old union's end. Resolution 735, adopted without a vote on 29 January 1992, considered that application. The meeting was the Council's 3041st.

Members recommended that the General Assembly admit the Republic of Armenia. The Assembly did so in March 1992. Armenia joined alongside a rush of former Soviet republics. Each arrival redrew the UN's map of Eurasia. For Armenia, membership confirmed its sovereignty in law. It also gave the small Caucasus state a voice while war with Azerbaijan over Nagorno-Karabakh was intensifying.
